name: The Cradle and the Crescent

covenants.name: Dar al-Hikma
covenants.notes:
Story seeds:
Yahya's Connections: Yahya the Barmakid is said to have kept lasting Arcane Connections to every member of the First Council; they may lie in his grave in Baghdad, in his house, or in his cell in the abandoned prison, which has an evil name.
The Two Wanderers: Al-Zill Habib and Al-Hajjaj left Baghdad in the mid-800s after a visit from the Sufi Fozail-e Iyaz and told their pupils not to follow; travellers still share meals with a young man in white and a hooded companion in black who seem not to have aged in four centuries.

diary.name: The caliph's first wazirs
diary.details: About this time three summoners swear lifelong service to the Umayyad caliph and take the title wazir, then meaning a bearer of magic for the caliph. Distrusted at first, they prove their worth when the armies meet foreign wizards who rain fire and raise the sea, for their spirits withstand such magic. Three become thirty and thirty more than a hundred, and they learn to command jinn and lead them into battle. (The book says about 700.)

diary.name: War with the jinn
diary.details: The wazirs have treated the spirits they summon as slaves, many of them believing jinn whom the Prophet's teaching forbids enslaving. Beings of other worlds turn on them, and by about this year the wazirs are so busy defending their homes against a magical war that they can no longer help the armies, and the conquests slow and stop. The caliphs blame their people, not their wazirs. (The book says about 720.)

diary.name: The jinn besiege Damascus
diary.details: While the 'Abbasids' supporters gather in Khurasan, more than a hundred jinn are said to surround Damascus and demand two wazirs hiding inside. After many such reprisals few summoners are left, the word wazir loses its link with wizardry, and their cruel kind of summoning survives only on the empire's edges.

diary.name: Harun's council
diary.details: Harun al-Rashid becomes caliph. His mother al-Khayzuran, a Yemeni woman skilled in enchanting music and tales, urges him to gather a council of wizards to advise him and secure his rule; he wants thinkers more than warriors. His old tutor and grand vizier, Yahya ibn Khalid the Barmakid, an unGifted scholar of potions and elixirs, writes to invite the best minds of Islam.

diary.name: The First Council
diary.details: Five answer: Jabir ibn Hayyan, Gifted alchemist and summoner, whose discovery lets the council join its many styles into one tradition; the astrologer Muhammad al-Fazari, maker of the first armillary sphere, whose father became a spirit to guard him and showed him how to open the unGifted to the art; Bakhtyshu, a Nestorian physician admitted on trial, who earns his place by casting out a demon that plagued the caliph and teaches the True Names of hundreds of spirits; Al-Zill Habib, the cloaked outlaw-hero with a band of jinn and yatus; and Al-Hajjaj, poet and mathematician, who claims al-Khidr as his teacher and never looks older than twenty-five. With Yahya and al-Khayzuran they make a shared language of their magic and invent the five Solomonic arts, answering to the caliph alone. The house in Baghdad where they teach will become the Dar al-Hikma.

diary.name: Al-Khayzuran vanishes
diary.details:
The caliph's mother complains of a headache, collapses, and is carried to her rooms, where her body and belongings disappear before her son and his advisers. Yahya retires to his studies and his Gifted son Ja'far becomes grand vizier and head of the council; Harun moves his palace north, away from the sahirs, and speaks to them only through Ja'far. (The timeline calls her a grand vizier; she was the caliph's mother, and the Order had no grand vizier until 805.)

Secrets
Sahirs who are sensitive to spirits feel a woman's presence in her old chamber, and some say a faerie queen made of the tales about her now lives there.

diary.name: Ja'far beheaded
diary.details:
Harun has grown wary of Ja'far and listens to other counsellors: Christopher Coronus, a young Hermetic magus said to come from Charlemagne's court, who writes often to Tremere and once threatens Jabir with a duel; the Sufi Fozail-e Iyaz; and an eastern miracle-worker called Dawud al-Kharita. Rumour paints Ja'far as a sorcerer after the throne, and when Harun's sister, whom Ja'far loves, pleads for him, Dawud says he has bewitched her. The caliph has Ja'far executed and the Barmakids killed or jailed; Yahya is spared, in prison.

Secrets
Another telling makes Ja'far guilty: too ambitious for his post, he tried to make Harun adopt him and, failing to enchant the caliph, ensnared his sister instead, until Harun's other advisers foiled him.

diary.name: The Suhhar Sulayman founded
diary.details: Months pass with no new grand vizier, and the five surviving masters meet Yahya secretly in his prison. At his urging they found a society that governs itself, free of the court's intrigues: the Suhhar Sulayman. Its founding document admits anyone who comes with a sponsor and shows he can summon a spirit, bars neither women nor non-Muslims, asks a quarter of each member's wealth on top of zakat, and expels any sahir who holds a thinking being in thrall; everything else is left to Islamic law. Harun, assured that they do not plot against him, blesses it on condition that its sahirs remain his loyal subjects. The first Majlis meets, and its members keep calling themselves viziers and their head the grand vizier.

diary.name: The golden age of the houses
diary.details: The Suhhar flourishes. The council's house in Baghdad becomes a great academy, the Bayt al-Hikma (now the Dar al-Hikma), and sahirs carry the art across Islam; great communities grow round houses of learning in Damascus, Gundeshapur, Cairo and Cordoba, each sending viziers to the yearly gathering. Being apart from the court keeps the Suhhar strong as the caliphate later splinters. Africa, central Arabia and the frontiers stay dangerous, prowled by spirits still angry at the Umayyads. (The book gives no year: the years after the founding.)

diary.name: Al-Zill and Al-Hajjaj depart
diary.details:
After years of teaching in Baghdad, the two founders leave without warning soon after a visit from Fozail-e Iyaz, and tell their followers not to come after them. Travellers from the Pillars of Hercules to the far east later tell of sharing meals with a young man in white and a companion hooded in black. (The book says the mid-800s.)

Secrets
Some say the two still live, unchanged in 1220.

diary.name: Cairo's twelve viziers
diary.details: Cairo has so many sahirs that it sends twelve viziers to the gathering, one for every house of more than two.

diary.name: The viziers and the solitary sahirs
diary.details: The grand vizier rules that each community's vizier also speaks for the sahirs living alone or in pairs nearest it, and must seek them out before every gathering. Until now most viziers had avoided the hermits, many of them Gifted and unpleasant company.

diary.name: A sahir who can be summoned
diary.details: A sahir complains to the Majlis that another has learned to summon him and shared the formula with friends, who keep calling him from his studies with absurd bargains; his tormentor, made vizier for the occasion, says no law forbids it. The grand vizier rules that one who can be summoned is no longer a sahir but a supernatural being, outside the Suhhar's laws and free to take what revenge he likes. Ever since, spirits and other such beings may not be members. (The book says only the tenth century.)

diary.name: The Iberians meet at Cordoba
diary.details: Perhaps wary of the long journey through hostile lands, the Iberian sahirs begin holding their own gatherings at Cordoba. Baghdad sends envoys for years to talk them out of it.

diary.name: The Iberians expelled
diary.details: Baghdad gives up its attempts at reconciliation and expels the Iberian sahirs from the Suhhar Sulayman. Many of them had called themselves Ashab al-Halqa, for the outer ring of Solomon's Seal.

diary.name: The Iberians join the Order of Hermes
diary.details: The Iberian council, meeting on its own since its expulsion, votes by a majority to join the Order of Hermes. The two groups have had little to do with each other since, though many sahirs now want to learn how Hermetic magic differs from theirs. (The timeline gives only this year for the split; ch03 has it run from 912.)

diary.name: Driven from North Africa
diary.details: With the Fatimid caliphate's rise, rumours spread of Berber wizards fighting for it whom the sahirs' spirits cannot beat, and many sahirs flee east into Egypt; those of the frontier retreat to the cities or vanish. With the Iberians gone, the Suhhar now holds only Egypt, Arabia and Persia, and turns inward to study in peace. The Berbers press no further. (The book says the mid-900s.)

diary.name: Three friends at Nishapur
diary.details: By the middle of the century the Suhhar's magic is the tradition it is in 1220. At Nishapur's house of wisdom three apprentices, 'Umar Khayyam, Hasan-i Sabbah and Abu 'Ali al-Tusi, swear that whichever of them becomes great will share it with the others. Al-Tusi rises to be vizier to the Seljuk sultans, as Nizam al-Mulk, and grand vizier of the Suhhar; 'Umar asks only for the means to study, and is given a pension. (The book says the middle of the eleventh century.)

diary.name: Hasan-i Sabbah at Alamut
diary.details: Hasan-i Sabbah takes the post his friend offers only to get close to him, being secretly an Isma'ili, and at the sect's bidding murders the grand vizier. The outraged Suhhar holds back its vengeance, as Nizam al-Mulk asked as he died, but no reconciliation is possible, and Hasan takes Alamut, where Prince Nizar has fled after a split among the Isma'ilis. There he teaches his followers Solomon's art, making a rival society of sahirs: they walk unseen, bend minds, poison and cross great distances in a moment, and the Seljuk governor cannot stop them even with the Suhhar's help. The two have tried to destroy each other ever since. (The year is the timeline's for Alamut; the book places the murder before it and gives it none.)

diary.name: The Crusaders take Jerusalem
diary.details: The Frankish knights' sieges of Antioch and Jerusalem shock the sahirs, who had turned wholly inward and were quite unprepared; a few try to save Tyre. Those sent to watch the European wizards find most proof against Solomonic magic, and those who fight magi in the field are beaten and many killed. Most survivors decide that God was with the invaders and Jerusalem is theirs by right, but the Asala al-Sakhr calls them Hell's tools, and a party against the crusaders grows round him among the Syrian viziers. The Suhhar stays aloof in public, yet relaxes its rules on fair dealing with non-Muslim spirits and names crusading magi enemies of Islam, leaving each sahir to strike back as he sees fit. (The timeline runs the First Crusade from 1095 to 1109.)

diary.name: 'Umar Khayyam dies
diary.details: The astronomer, poet and sahir dies at Nishapur, where he trained and later led the house of wisdom, leaving books on algebra, Euclid and the stars and the poems of the Rubaiyat.

diary.name: Edessa retaken
diary.details: Working in secret, sahirs teach magic to Muslim leaders, use the Magic Realm's geography to fall on the Franks' rear and plunder their camps, and read the stars for the moment to strike. Their help wins Edessa back from the crusaders when Zangi takes it.

diary.name: The Second Crusade broken
diary.details: The same hidden war helps bring the Second Crusade to nothing before Damascus.

diary.name: Guides for Nur al-Din and Salah al-Din
diary.details: By custom a vizier may disguise himself as a nameless old sage, as al-Khidr does, to offer magic or aid to a promising Muslim leader or scholar without committing the Suhhar: 'sending a guide'. Both great men of the late century are sent one. Nur al-Din declines, saying al-Khidr himself has taught him, and the two exchange wisdom in a famous text now kept in Baghdad; Salah al-Din refuses without a reason, and the sahirs must help him unasked. (The book says the late 1100s; this is the year Salah al-Din begins to unite the Muslim Levant.)

diary.name: The House of the Heavens empties
diary.details:
Soon after the vizier of Nasibin and the Asala al-Najm come home from the Majlis, they and every sahir of the city leave in a body near the end of summer, some packed and ready, some walking away from half-done work. Astrologers find that all seven planets stood in Libra then. Neither leader has been heard of since; the family's sahirs now wander in caravans with their laboratories, and Meriq of Savah, who took the Asala's place, insists the house is still at Nasibin, waiting for them to come back.

Secrets
Most sahirs think they scattered to help Salah al-Din win at Hattin and retake Jerusalem the next year; others, that they went to set in motion a plan to remove Rashid al-Din Sinan of the Syrian Nizaris.

diary.name: Kha'trazh elected grand vizier
diary.details: The viziers elect Kha'trazh of Basra, a Follower of the Heart, who takes the laqab al-Wazir al-Dall as a pledge not to abuse his seat. They will keep him there for some thirty years. (The book says he has led the Order for nearly thirty years by 1220.)

covenants.summary:
The Followers of the Heart's great academy in Baghdad and the Order of Suleiman's first house: the house where the First Council studied and taught grew into it after 805. It stands north of the caliph's palace, halfway between the Bab al-Sham and the Bab al-Khurasan, a building as grand as the Golden Gate palace and mosque, and nearly a hundred sahirs, young and old, live and study there. Its observatory is exceptional, with perhaps the best astrolabe yet made.

Baghdad has seven other houses of wisdom besides, and about a thousand sahirs in all, more than any other city. The house chooses its leader, and so its vizier at the Majlis, by what its members achieve; by custom its vizier acts as grand vizier when the seat falls empty between meetings.
covenants.what_matters:
Library: the Order's oldest, its contents not given in the book.

Tension: Niya's views make her succession to the acting grand vizier's place, should Kha'trazh die, hard to hold.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Savah
covenants.summary: The Followers of the Star's house in Savah, a town of camel-drivers and herdsmen, where every sahir is of that family. It keeps the tall domed tower attached to the great mosque and its hospital: the library on the lower floors, the best magical library in Persia, and the observatory at the top. Meriq, the family's Asala, is of this house.
covenants.what_matters:
Library: the finest collection of magic in Persia, with Meriq's own books on Artes Liberales and Solomonic Astrology; the book gives no scores.

Site: its observatory, Magic 5, gives +3 to astrology.

covenants.name: The House of Healing
covenants.summary:
The Followers of the Hand's academy at Gundeshapur and the town's largest house of wisdom: its great medical school and hospital, run by the descendants of its founder Bakhtyshu. Its sahirs work in laboratories dug far below, out of the Divine aura that covers the house.

Nizari visitors have come to see its vizier, Nil, here more than once.
covenants.what_matters: Tension: the Order suspects its vizier of Nizari sympathies.

covenants.name: Dayr Qunna
covenants.summary: A house of wisdom a mile east of Dayr al-'Aqul, near al-Mada'in, posing as a Nestorian monastery: a large building behind walls so high and strong it looks a fortress. Its sahirs and their followers live as monks and are posted there to watch the caliphs. The townsfolk of Dayr al-'Aqul, who suffer some hidden enemy, wonder whether its 'monks' are sorcerers.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Sana'a
covenants.summary: The house in Sana'a where 'Arkhaman was born in secret and raised. Its older sahirs have made him their vizier and are sending him to the Majlis this summer, hoping he will meet other Gifted sahirs before his Gift drives him mad.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Muscat
covenants.summary: A large company of sahirs of Solomonic Travel in Muscat, the port lately taken from the 'Abbasids by the Yahmad tribe, whose house is given to finding the fabled islands of Sinbad the Sailor's voyages.

covenants.name: The Houses of Wisdom of Nizwa
covenants.summary: Several houses of sahirs in Nizwa, the royal city of 'Uman, and the country round it, taken here as one record. Nizwa also has a name for witches and sorcerers, who are not of the Order.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Merv
covenants.summary: The house in Merv, keeper of the magical library of Nizam al-Mulk, the Seljuk grand vizier, among the city's famous libraries. Taught by the Ghuzz sack and fearing Genghis Khan, its sahirs are copying every irreplaceable book they can, since the colleges and madrasas will not move theirs.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Nishapur
covenants.summary: The house where Hasan-i Sabbah, Nizam al-Mulk and 'Umar Khayyam learnt the Solomonic arts. 'Umar later led it, until his death in 1123, and his books are in its keeping.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Bukhara
covenants.summary: Bukhara's own house of wisdom, which paid for the new mausoleum over Job's Spring at the edge of the farmers' market; one of its sahirs visits the spring each year. As 1220 opens, Genghis Khan's horde is before the town.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Ramhurmuz
covenants.summary: A few sahirs in Ramhurmuz, a rich town of silk and perfume, with a modest library. Long ago they took in a sorcerer of Soqotra, learnt his island's secrets and perfumes and made a trade of them; when he saw he had been cheated he left a curse behind, and the district swarms with gnats and biting midges every year.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Damascus
covenants.summary: The seat of the Followers of the Stone at Damascus, outside this book's lands and the heart of the sahirs' war on the crusaders and their magi. The town is the Levant pack's to describe; this record has no place.

covenants.name: The House of Wisdom of Cairo
covenants.summary: The great academy of the Followers of the River at Cairo, outside this book's lands and still the centre of the family's art; the city once sent twelve viziers to a single Majlis. The town is the Levant pack's to describe; this record has no place.

neighbours.name: The Order of Suleiman
neighbours.summary:
The Suhhar Sulayman, the great society of sahirs, whom Hermetic magi have long whispered about as a rival Order bent on their ruin. Its members are mostly unGifted Muslim summoners who command jinn and other spirits and work spells and devices much like the Order's; they claim Solomon's powers, taught him (they say) by al-Khidr. About five thousand live east of the Levant, with two or three thousand more in Syria and Egypt, perhaps one in ten of them Gifted; they outnumber the magi about five to one. Founded in 805 by the First Council's heirs, it has a grand vizier elected for life (Kha'trazh, of the Heart, for some thirty years), five Asalat who lead the families, and a vizier for every community of three or more.

The Majlis, its council, meets in Baghdad's summer bazaar for three days each August; only viziers sit, one vote each. Its chief rules: enchanted items go to sahirs only, extracted vis is never sold to magi, a sahir who can be summoned counts as a spirit and may not belong, a sahir silent for five years is lost, and the penalty is expulsion or a fine of vis or service; quarrels go to duels or trials of boasts, stories or champions. When the grand vizier's seat is empty the vizier of Baghdad's Dar al-Hikma acts by custom.

Long turned inward, the Suhhar was shaken by the Crusades. Its sahirs met the invading magi, found most of them proof against Solomonic magic, and lost when they fought them openly; so they worked in secret, guiding rulers, ambushing through the Magic Realm and reading the stars, and helped retake Edessa and break the Second Crusade. By custom a vizier may go in disguise as a nameless sage, 'sending a guide', to offer a promising leader help; Nur al-Din declined, having been taught by al-Khidr himself, and Salah al-Din refused without a word.

In 1220 the Suhhar still counts itself at war with the crusaders and every Hermetic magus among them. It welcomes magi into its lands, where they are easier to watch, studies them closely, and is planning a Solomonic counter-crusade against the Levant. It never signed the Treaty of Baghdad that binds the Levant's magi and the caliph's court, and it treats the Nizaris as traitors.

Its summoning, naranj, Al-Iksir and the rest are the Sahirs tradition's chapter and The Cradle and the Crescent's chapter on the Order.

details.rules: Enchanted items go to sahirs alone; no extracted vis is traded to Hermetic magi; a sahir who can himself be summoned may not be a member.
details.wants: To drive the crusaders, and the magi who came with them, out of the lands of Islam.
details.offers: Solomonic magic, and a guide for a promising ruler or scholar.

neighbours.name: Ashab al-Sakhr, the Followers of the Stone
neighbours.summary:
The family of Solomonic Alchemy, heirs of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the one Gifted member of the First Council. Its seat is Damascus, once the Umayyads' capital and now the heart of the sahirs' war on the invading soldiers and magi. Its members are devout, almost never anything but Muslim, cold to Europeans, proud of their honour, and fond of good steel: many fight with blades rather than spells, or with blades their magic has strengthened. An Asala of the Stone first called the crusaders the Infernal's tools and led the counter-crusade among the Syrian viziers; the family's Asala is usually chosen by a test of arms.

Its house at Damascus is a bayt of the Order of Suleiman, not a Hermetic covenant.

details.wants: War on the crusaders and the magi with them.

neighbours.name: Ashab al-Nahr, the Followers of the River
neighbours.summary:
The family of Solomonic Travel, the art of journeys between worlds: Faerie and the Magic Realm, the Divine and Infernal places, dreams and the land of the dead. It was thought a lesser art until the Nabatean Ibn Wahshiyya, two generations after its founder al-Hajjaj, read its secrets out of the old Egyptians' writings. Its great academy is in Cairo, still the centre of the family's magic. Both founders were known for passion that ended in madness, and the family's sahirs are an eccentric lot.

Its house at Cairo is a bayt of the Order of Suleiman, not a Hermetic covenant.

neighbours.name: The jinn
neighbours.summary:
In Islamic teaching God made three thinking peoples: angels of light, jinn of smokeless fire, and humans of clay. Jinn, like men, can be saved or damned; many have taken Islam, others tempt men and refuse the faith. Iblis was once among the mightiest of them. A jinni's body is Faerie glamour, Infernal power or pure magic, by its realm, usually of Vim and sometimes of an element; most can take a body of matter and change shape.

There are no Divine jinn. The faerie jinn are pious or impious, the magic jinn pagan spirits, genii loci and elementals, the Infernal jinn corrupt. They divide into tribes, said to number 112, which follow their realms loosely: the jann, lesser faerie jinn who keep Islam and pass for merchants, nomads or shepherds; the shaitan, dark faeries and demons; the ghul, faerie predators and Infernal eaters of the dead who haunt graveyards; the marid, ancient spirits of water, wind and weather, mostly in Arabia; and the 'ifrit. Every jinni has a true name, belongs to the lands of Islam, speaks Arabic and knows its theology. The bismillah, the four Quls and the Throne Verse are their weaknesses, and a hajji resists some of their powers.

Many things the common folk call jinn are not: ghosts, naddahas, nisnases, shiqq and the rest, the Persian divs, yazatas and peris, the Soqotran jinniyah, and the planetary spirits the Arabs call al-Nujum, the Stars. Sihr commands true jinn only.

Their lands: Jinnistan, the Mountains of Qaf, Amerabad the City of Amber, Golden Baghdad, Khashgar and the ocean al-Khadar.

neighbours.name: Jinnistan
neighbours.summary:
Wherever jinn make their homes, just out of a man's sight: behind a door that cannot fit between two houses, round the last corner of a bazaar alley, under the ground, in the wilds, in ruins, and beyond this world in regiones and the otherworlds. All of it is Jinnistan. Perhaps it began in the Magic Realm; the tales now put most of it in Arcadia, with branches into Eudokia and perhaps into Hell. Its jinn live much as their human neighbours do and pass freely between the two, and whole jinn cities lie within it, Amerabad the City of Amber among them.

Travellers say it lies past the great rivers, past the eastern mountains, or over the edge of the sea; they are right and wrong at once, for where jinn are, Jinnistan is.

neighbours.name: The Mountains of Qaf
neighbours.summary:
In Muslim lore a ring of peaks around the known world, green as emerald and impassable, the wall between the lands of men and the homes of the jinn and the jinn's homeland. Geographers have put it in the Caucasus, the Pamirs, the Hindu Kush, even the Urals or the Atlas, and the learned match it with the Greeks' great eastern range at the end of Alexander's world.

It may be the very idea of mountains in the Magic Realm, with other worlds behind it, or Faerie's distillation of every tale ever told of mountains no one can cross.

neighbours.name: Iraq
neighbours.summary: The land of the Tigris and Euphrates, settled for thousands of years and in 1220 still thick with towns along the rivers. The faerie gods who once ruled it are seen no more, though their ziggurats still tower over passers-by. Since the 'Abbasids took power in 750 it has been the political heart of Islam, whatever the caliph's real reach; the caliph rules it directly now. North of it lies the Jazira, mostly under quarrelling Ayyubid princes and cities that honour them only in name.

neighbours.name: Baghdad
neighbours.summary:
The caliph's city and so the political centre of Islam, founded by al-Mansur in 762. Its heart is his Round City on the west bank, three walls round the first palace of the Golden Gate; the caliphs spread it over both banks with mosques, palaces and gardens in its golden age. Fire, flood and civil strife have ruined much of it since: on the west bank each quarter stands walled off among ruins, and only the third of the city round the caliph's palace on the east bank thrives. Shi'is and Sunnis, and the Sunni schools of law, quarrel and sometimes fight; the Sufis prosper in the ribats the caliphs build them.

Each summer a vast fair fills the streets and open ground south of the city for most of the season, where anything at all may be bought, from vendors who appear only when their wares are wanted, or whose tents swallow the careless. The Order of Suleiman holds its Majlis there in August. About a thousand sahirs live in the city, more than anywhere else, in eight houses of wisdom, the greatest the Dar al-Hikma north of the palace, with nearly a hundred sahirs and a famous observatory.

neighbours.name: Mosul
neighbours.summary: On the east bank of the Tigris across from the ruins of Nineveh, behind a double wall, a strong citadel and the river; a broad road runs north to south through it and many houses are of marble, with gardens and suburbs outside. Its mosques hold the tombs of Jonah and of St George, a prophet to Muslims too; it has a healing spring, a squash tree the Prophet planted, colleges and Christian monasteries. Its people are Muslims, Christians and Yazidis, and its cloth gives muslin its name.

neighbours.name: Georgia
neighbours.summary: A Christian kingdom of mountains, hills and high plains, with lowland only on the Black Sea coast and along the Rioni and Kura. Its capital Tiflis sits on great trade roads, the Silk Road among them, behind double walls and three strong gates, and for all the wars fought over it is a tolerant city where mosque, church and synagogue may stand side by side.

neighbours.name: Greater Armenia
neighbours.summary:
East of Asia Minor and south-west of Georgia, a war-torn land of mountains, high plains and valleys, with winters of eight months and more. Taken by the Muslims in the seventh century, tributary and free in the ninth, fought over by Muslims and Byzantines (many Armenians left for Lesser Armenia then), and lost to the Turks in the eleventh, it is contested still: the Ayyubids hold some of the south, Trebizond a piece in the north-west, and local dynasties the rest. Greeks, Armenians and Turks grow grain, fish, mine silver and salt, and weave, dye and embroider.

Its remote sites keep strong Magic auras, and its politics leave room for a new covenant that does not grow too strong for its neighbours, if it can be supplied through the winters.

neighbours.name: The Pit of Harut and Marut
neighbours.summary: Beneath the ruins of Babylon hang Harut and Marut, the two angels who taught men magic, chained there for it; some sahirs say they spread the dark, Infernal form of Solomon's art as a test of mankind's faith. The ruins above saw the Tower of Babel, the Jews' exile, Nebuchadnezzar's Hanging Gardens and the Persians' overthrow of Belshazzar. Ancient Magic says more of the city's mysteries.

neighbours.name: Caliph of Baghdad
neighbours.summary:
The 'Abbasid caliph, Commander of the Faithful, al-Nasir, who has reigned since 1180 and is a forceful one. The 'Abbasids have ruled from Baghdad since 762, as figureheads under others for much of three centuries, but since al-Muqtafi (1136 to 1160) the caliphs have governed Iraq themselves, and in 1157 drove the Seljuk sultan from the city. His real realm is little more than Iraq, sometimes the Jazira and parts of Persia too; most Sunni rulers honour him in name, the Ayyubids among them, and he has yet to recognise the Khwarazm-shah's claim to be shah. He has built ribats for the Sufis and restored mosques, shrines and colleges to heal the city's quarrels.

His court is party to the Treaty of Baghdad with the Levant's magi (Blood and Sand). If history holds he reigns until 1225; the Mongols take Baghdad in 1258 and kill the last caliph by rolling him in a carpet and trampling him, so that no royal blood touches the ground.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Egypt
neighbours.summary:
Al-Kamil, sultan in Cairo since 1218, the head of Salah al-Din's family, the Ayyubids, whose princes rule Egypt, Syria, the Jazira and Yemen and spend much of their time plotting against one another. The Hijaz, Mecca and Medina are his in name; his kinsman al-Mas'ud Yusuf holds Yemen and 'Asir more closely.

In 1220 the Fifth Crusade sits in Damietta, taken in 1219 after he offered, and was refused, all the old Latin lands west of the Jordan for the Crusade's leaving Egypt and a thirty-year truce. He camps at al-Mansura. If history holds he reigns until 1238.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Aleppo
neighbours.summary: Al-'Aziz, Salah al-Din's grandson, who has ruled Aleppo since 1216 and holds Edessa, taken from the crusaders by Zangi on Christmas Eve 1144, where most of the people are Christians of several churches. Edessa's Mandylion, the cloth bearing Christ's face, went to Constantinople in the tenth century and was lost in the sack of 1204. If history holds he reigns until 1236.

neighbours.name: Emir of Mosul
neighbours.summary: Mosul has been the Zangids' since 1128; their founder 'Imad al-Din Zangi, who died in 1146, is famed for taking Edessa from the crusaders. In 1220 the real ruler is the mamluk Badr al-Din Lu'lu', regent for the emir al-Qahir Mahmud, who owns the Ayyubids as overlords and the caliph above them, in name.

neighbours.name: King of Georgia
neighbours.summary: Giorgi IV Lasha, king since 1213, of a Christian kingdom free of Muslim rule only since Dawid II took Tiflis in 1121, after centuries of war with Muslim overlords. His people are Georgians, Armenians, Turks, Persians and Alans, Christian and Muslim; the Georgian church answers to neither the pope nor the emperor. His troops prop up the Emperor of Trebizond. If history holds he reigns until 1223.

neighbours.name: Lord of Alamut
neighbours.summary: The dai'd-duat, grand master of the Nizari Isma'ilis, who has held Alamut and its castles in Daylam, Quhistan, Qumis and Fars since 1210. Jalal al-Din Hasan has done what none thought possible and turned the sect Sunni in public; his followers take it for taqiyya and obey, and many think him the imam-qa'im. He looks for friends against the Khwarazm-shah, the caliph in the west and Genghis Khan in the east, has allied with the rulers of Arran and Azarbayjan, and has married the emir of Gilan's four daughters. The Syrian Nizaris at Masyaf answer to him.

neighbours.name: The Nizaris
neighbours.summary:
The Nizari Isma'ilis, whom the crusaders call the Assassins (a slander from Syria; the ascetic Nizaris take no drugs) and the Persians the Batiniyya or the heretics. Their founder Hasan-i Sabbah, a sahir, murdered the Suhhar's grand vizier, fled to Alamut and taught his faith's followers Solomon's art, so that the Nizaris walk unseen, bend minds, poison and cross great distances in an instant. The Suhhar and the Nizaris have tried to destroy each other ever since, with equal losses; the Suhhar still calls them traitors and will not treat with them, while the Nizaris kill sahirs, as anyone else, only when they stand in the imam's way.

Seven ranks: the fida'i and lasiq, uninitiated killers who make the sect's name; the mustajib, the first initiates and its magicians; the da'i, the hujja over each territory or jazira, and the dai'd-duat, grand master of Alamut; and the imam-qa'im, the immortal teacher who was once Elijah, Enoch, Khidr and 'Ali. They seek the hidden meaning of the Qur'an, live by the fifty-one epistles, and hold that the law no longer binds those who know it, so they reject the Pillars and the caliph alike. Members call one another rafiq, comrade.

Besides Daylam, Quhistan and Qumis they keep hidden communities in the southern Zagros (Shardiz among them) and cells in most great cities. The Syrian branch holds Masyaf and a stronghold near Aleppo; its most famous chief, Rashid al-Din Sinan, the crusaders' Old Man of the Mountain, died in 1193.

details.rules: The imam's word is absolute; taqiyya, hiding one's faith, is lawful in danger.

neighbours.name: Sultan of Rum
neighbours.summary:
The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum holds the Anatolian plateau, lost to the empire after Manzikert, and in the north reaches the Black Sea at Sinope, splitting Nicaea from Trebizond. It drove north between them in 1214, killing David Komnenos, but could not reach Trebizond through the mountains. Its sultan Kaykhusraw I died at Antioch-on-the-Maeander in 1211, and the Maeander has been the border with Nicaea since. Trebizond still fears it.

The book names no sultan for 1220. History has Kaykhusraw's son Kaykaus I reign from 1211 to his death about 1220, followed by his brother Kayqubad I, who is named as ruler here.

neighbours.name: Emperor of Trebizond
neighbours.summary:
Alexios Komnenos, thirty-eight, grandson of the Emperor Andronikos Komnenos, who seized Trebizond with his brother David in 1204, the very year Constantinople fell, and calls himself 'Emperor and Autocrat of the Romans'. David pushed west into Paphlagonia and Heraclea, provoking Rum and then Nicaea, which won back most of his gains in 1212; Rum killed him in 1214. Alexios rules on, propped by Georgian troops and Latin and Seljuk mercenaries, cut off from Nicaea and still threatened by Rum, and also rules Cherson and Kerch across the Black Sea; Cherson pays him tribute.

He lives with his family in the castle behind the city. Like his grandfather he patronises art and letters, giving titles and stipends to astronomers, alchemists and experimental philosophers, and his Silk Road market and its taxes make Trebizond very rich.

neighbours.name: The Fifth Crusade
neighbours.summary:
In 1218 the Crusade chose to strike at Egypt, the heart of Muslim power, and laid siege to Damietta. Al-Kamil offered every old Latin land west of the Jordan and a thirty-year truce if it would leave Egypt; it refused, and Damietta fell in 1219. The legate Pelagius claims the conquests for the Church, not the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and the Muslim armies are working their way back toward the city.

Both orders of wizards watch it. Foothold and the Levant's crusading magi want the Treaty of Baghdad voted down in 1221 so they can help it, and the True Cross has opened a covenant in Damietta itself; the Order of Suleiman is planning its own counter-crusade against the Levant.

details.antagonist: The crusaders at Damietta, and the papal legate Pelagius

stages.title: The legate and the king fall out
stages.clues: Pelagius and John of Brienne quarrel over who commands and who keeps what is won.
stages.ignored: John leaves the camp, and the Crusade loses its momentum.

stages.title: The Nile rises
stages.clues: The host marches south toward al-Kamil's camp at al-Mansura.
stages.ignored: The flood cuts the crusaders off; Pelagius agrees an eight-year truce and the Crusade leaves Egypt.

neighbours.name: The Mongol Conquest
neighbours.summary:
As 1220 opens Genghis Khan is camped before Bukhara with a great part of his horde. He has come for the Khwarazm-shah, whose governor at Otrar killed his merchants and who shamed and killed his envoys, and the shah's empire from the Jaxartes to the Gulf is about to fall. The cities the Mongols sack and leave empty may take Infernal auras of wrath, which draw lesser demons, dark faeries, ghuls and evil jinn in the horde's wake, and the unburied dead wander.

If history holds, the Mongols take Persia, Georgia, Armenia, northern Iraq and Asia Minor in the decades after, sack Baghdad in 1258, and are stopped only by Egypt's Mamluks in Syria in 1260. The Levant's magi know almost nothing of them yet.

In Russia and Poland, if history holds, they come twice: a reconnaissance that breaks the princes on the Kalka in 1223, and from 1237 a conquest that burns Ryazan, Vladimir, Chernigov and Kiev, ravages Poland and Hungary, and lays the Mongol yoke on Russia for two centuries. Their spirits run ahead of them: since 1206 wingless thunder wyrms have raided Slavic Arcadia in the Onslaught, and their spies and shamans work among the princes long before the horde returns.

stages.title: Bukhara falls
stages.ignored: The town falls within a fortnight; its defenders are killed, its people enslaved or driven off, and fire leaves it in ruins under an Infernal aura of 3, save round the Kalyan minaret.

stages.title: Samarkand and the Jaxartes towns
stages.ignored: The horde, swelled by Turkish recruits, destroys the oasis towns along the Jaxartes as far as Khojend and takes Samarkand.

stages.title: Gurganj and the shah
stages.ignored: Gurganj falls and its great dykes are broken; the shah is hunted across Khurasan to die on the Caspian shore; Baylaqan in the west is razed.

stages.title: Into Persia
stages.ignored: Balkh, Merv, Nishapur and Herat are sacked, the shah's son is driven over the Indus, and Jebe and Subadei ride north into Russia.

stages.title: The Kalka
stages.clues: Refugee Cumans beg the Russian princes for help; Mongol envoys come with gifts.
stages.ignored: Subadei, having bought off and then destroyed the Cumans, draws the princes' host into a nine-day pursuit and routes it on the Kalka: nine princes die, the Prince of Kiev smothered under a carpet for the murdered envoys. Then the Mongols ride home past the Volga Bulgars, and the Russians forget them.

stages.title: The return
stages.clues: Mongol spies along the steppe; the princes at war over Kiev.
stages.ignored: Great Bulgar is razed; in December the horde enters Ryazan, then burns Vladimir and kills the Grand Prince. Northern Russia submits in four months; Novgorod is spared by the thaw.

stages.title: Kiev falls
stages.ignored: Chernigov and Pereyaslavl are crushed, and on 6 December Kiev is stormed and left a field of bones.

stages.title: Legnica and the Sajo
stages.ignored: Two toumens sack Sandomierz and Krakow and destroy Henry the Pious's army at Legnica; a day later Batu and Subadei annihilate the Hungarian host on the Sajo.

stages.title: The horde turns back
stages.ignored: Word of Ogedei's death recalls Subadei; Batu withdraws to the Volga steppe, razing as he goes, and rules Russia from Sarai.

neighbours.name: Arabia
neighbours.summary:
The peninsula where Islam began, holding its two holy cities, Mecca and Medina, which every Muslim should visit on the hajj once in a lifetime if he can. It is not all sand: stony desert fills the north, mountains run behind most of the coasts with thin, fertile plains below them, a high plateau in the east (the Najd and Yamama) has green valleys of crops, sheep and goats, and in the south the hills of Yemen and Hadramawt are wooded, well watered and rich in incense trees, the Romans' Happy Arabia. The old incense road through the deserts is gone; its trade now goes by ship round the coasts. Three great deserts lie within: the Nefud in the north, the Empty Quarter in the south and the Dahna between them, with burning sun, short water, dry quicksands, sandstorms, brigands and the jinn who conjure false oases for the thirsty.

Its people are townsfolk round the oases, mostly farmers, and Bedouin herders who trade with them, guide and guard the caravans and pilgrims, and now and then quarrel with them. Most are Muslims of one kind or another, with many Christians and Jews among them. Local dynasties rule the settled lands and most honour the 'Abbasid caliph in name; the Ayyubids, Salah al-Din's family, share the Hijaz, 'Asir and Yemen.

Beneath the sands lie buried cities, across the land holy shrines, and in the ruins jinn and stranger beings, some of whom live openly in the towns. The Bedouin treat date-palms, rocks carved by the wind and precious wells almost as gods: many such places are home to an 'ashira, a 'close friend' spirit appeased with gifts, and are where auras and elemental vis are found. The strongest 'ashira are Magic jinn, genii loci who were the gods of the Ignorance before Islam, or Infernal jinn who have taken their places: Abgal of the camel-drivers, Dhu'l-Khalasa of oracles, Dhu Shara of the mountains, Hubal of the moon and divination, Ishtar, Manaf whom women worshipped, Nakhla of the date-palm, al-Qawm of war, night and caravans, Sa'd, Wadd and Yaghuth. One name may cover several spirits a few miles apart, of different realms and power, from little elementals of Might under 10 to the spirits of great lonely landmarks near 50.

The Bedouin prize the camel above every beast, then their Arabian horses, saluqi hounds and falcons, and their falconry, al-Qanas, puts food on the winter fire more than it entertains. Their birds are the enduring saqr and the swift shahin. The Arabian phoenix, the anqa, red, orange and gold, flies to its eyrie above the Mountains of Qaf when it grows old, burns and is reborn as a black egg; a magus who watches this for a season may count it as a significatos in Animal, Ignem or Vim.

Falconry's great authority is an untitled Arabic book by the falconer Moamyn, which no house in the book is named as holding: a summa on Animal Handling (falconry), level 4, Quality 7, with a tractatus on Hunt (hawking), Quality 7. Master Theodore of Antioch will put it into Latin for Frederick II within the decade (Quality 6), and by 1250 the emperor's own corrected and glossed version, De arte venandi cum avibus, reaches Quality 8.

Kohl, the black or blue eye powder women wear across the Middle East, is said to come from the jinn, and the hidden folk sell it in the bazaars of Golden Baghdad for prices seldom paid in coin. The commonest magical kohl, a Bedouin folk witch's brew, grants Second Sight for a day; other kinds give Keen Vision, Magic Sensitivity, Piercing Gaze or Wilderness Sense at a score of 2 or 3. As a material it gives +3 to affect sight; its base is burnt frankincense.

Story seeds:
The List of Suleiman: Solomon is said to have written down the True Name of every jinni in a book that amends itself as jinn are born and die; sahirs claim to have found its pages bound into other books of Lore, where old names come and go between readings, though whether these are true fragments or faerie forgeries no one knows.

the whirlwind jinn of the sands

neighbours.name: The Hijaz
neighbours.summary:
The holy land of Islam on the Red Sea coast, home to Mecca and Medina, with more traffic than all the rest of Arabia: pilgrims above all, and ships putting into its many harbours on the run between Egypt and the Indian Ocean. The sultan of Egypt holds it in name.

Sahirs are few here, and live far from the great cities: the thick Divine auras and regiones make magic hard, and wizards of every kind, Gifted or not, keep out of the religious authorities' sight. Infernal jinn crowd the pilgrim roads, planting doubt and impious thoughts.

Non-Muslims may not enter the harams, the sacred ground reaching some five miles round each holy city. The book offers a troupe four ways round this: going in disguised or hidden by magic (a grave sacrilege if caught, with the high auras against any spell), sending only the Muslim characters, a special arrangement under local escort, or simply letting non-Muslims into the mythic cities. Either way a visit should be a deeply religious experience. Each haram has a Divine aura of 3, with the Calm trait at +3 unless noted, and the cities 4 or more; fighting and killing are forbidden there, save for slaughtering animals for food or putting down savage or sick ones, and God has been known to strike down the impious with Ignis Domini, the Smiting of the Lord, or by swallowing them alive.

The hajj, one of the five pillars, is set out in Realms of Power: The Divine. A Muslim who completes it gains Pious +3 and 3 Faith Points; going again can restore them, but never takes the trait past +3.

neighbours.name: The Najd and Yamama
neighbours.summary:
A high plateau tilting down from west to east. Yamama is thick with oases and farming villages; the Najd is rockier and more mountainous, its villages in valleys that catch the rain's run-off. Most of the people are Bedouin, though some towns are big. The Jadis and the Tasm, two old tribes of faerie jinn, still roam here, known for their strange wares, their spotless honour and the most wonderful hospitality anywhere.

Yamama tells of Zarqa al-Yamama, a blue-eyed witch of the days of Tasm and Jadis who could see a rider thirty miles off. A king of Yemen who conquered the land killed her and had his physicians cut out her eyes for the secret; they found them smudged with kohl.

In the north the Jews of Tayma' and Khaybar keep their own towns.

Story seeds:
The Stone Lovers: wizards who settle by two man-shaped rocks in a remote Magic aura offend the Bedouin, who count the stones as kin: the giant lovers Aja and Salma, banished there for five hundred years; dark jinn haunt the rocks by night, and too much magic may wake the giants.

links.note: a jinni racehorse of the Bedouin races

neighbours.name: Bahrayn
neighbours.summary:
The eastern coast of Arabia and the islands off it. From 899 to 1076 it was held by the Qarmatians, Isma'ili Shi'is who in 930 sacked Mecca and Medina and carried off the Black Stone of the Ka'ba. It came back in 951, left in a sack in the great mosque of Kufa with a note saying that it had been taken, and was now returned, on command; most credit the Fatimids of North Africa with talking the Qarmatians round, but no one knows. The stone came home broken in seven. The Sunni Uyunids drove the Qarmatians out and rule in 1220, though some Qarmatians still live here.

The busy markets round the fortress of al-Mushaqqar, with good wages and cheap wine, are where the jann guide Jumayl likes best to be found.

Story seeds:
The Fate of the Black Stone: while the Qarmatians held it, a renegade sahir stole the Black Stone for a ritual of unknown purpose and was killed at great cost, the stone broken in seven; now he has been seen again, and the heirs of those who fought him are dying one by one.

links.note: a jann caravan guard who drinks in its markets

neighbours.name: The Empty Quarter
neighbours.summary:
Rub' al-Khali, the trackless desert dividing north from south Arabia. No caravan has crossed it since the kingdom of 'Ad fell in the third century and its frankincense trade with it, and even the Bedouin keep to its edges. Some miles past the last settlements the dunes rise a thousand feet, and beyond them the traveller is in the realm of al-Khali, 'the Empty One', a mighty elemental jinni, a Magic daimon and genius loci, said to guard the lost lands of the times before Islam.

Few Magic auras in the Middle East are as vast or as strong: past the great dunes it climbs quickly to 10, lower only at the fringes, and the land dissolves into shifting brightness, full of regiones of blank sand. Some travellers pass straight into the Twilight Void without noticing any regio, most often near the edge of the provinces of Auram, Imaginem or Terram; some tell of the ghosts of old cities or wandering tribes, or of provinces of other Forms. Some old magical disaster, and a power of ritual strength of al-Khali's, seem to have made the way so easy, and the empty land echoes the emptiness of the Void.

Local sahirs, and the few magi who know of it, call it the Valuable Quarter: great stores of vis and of the Magic Realm's riches lie within reach of any wizard, though getting back out is far harder than going in, and those who return often come back Warped; a few mundane folk have come home knowing Sihr and a Solomonic art, and are never quite trusted by other sahirs. Criamon magi wonder whether it hides a way into the Counter-Cyclical Alam, Merinita magi whether it rings a hidden gate to Arcadia where the old gods of Arabia lie trapped. Some sahirs think Al-Hajjaj and Al-Zill of the First Council vanished into it, and will return like King Baluqiya.

Suggested vis sources (not in the book), for the storyguide to use, change or ignore: glassy tears of fused sand on the crests of the great dunes after a lightning storm, 4 pawns of Terram a year; the whistling wind at the Quarter's edge at dawn, caught in a sealed jar, 3 pawns of Auram a year; the shimmer over the bright sands, gathered as a mirage-glass, 3 pawns of Imaginem a year.

Story seeds:
The Valuable Quarter: local sahirs call the Empty Quarter the Valuable Quarter, for the Twilight Void and the Magic Realm are easy to enter there and rich in vis; coming back is far harder, and those who do return changed, some even initiated into Sihr and never trusted again. The Primi of Criamon and Merinita, at odds over what lies at its heart, are recruiting young magi for a joint expedition.

levels.name: The bright sands
levels.see: Shining, featureless sand where the dunes should be.
levels.enter: Only unawares, but with frightening ease: +6 to the roll to enter.
levels.notes: Many pockets lie within the Quarter, traps for the careless. Leaving one is hard: -3 to the roll, so those without Second Sight, Magic Sensitivity or some such power may never find the way out.

neighbours.name: 'Asir and Yemen
neighbours.summary: The south-west of the peninsula, under the Ayyubid sultan of Yemen. Most of its people are Sunnis or Zaydi Shi'is, with scattered Tayyibis, Isma'ilis of the Fatimid line who await a hidden line of imams. The Tayyibis are great traders and keep up dealings with Soqotra to the south, an island of non-Hermetic sorcerers described in Rival Magic, and Yemeni seafarers are pushing into the old Ethiopian lands of Africa and across the sea to al-Sind.

neighbours.name: Hadramawt
neighbours.summary:
A backwater of the Muslim world: dry, thinly peopled valleys, and hills sometimes thickly wooded but too steep to farm or coppice. Few pilgrims or strangers come so far south, and the locals are startled to meet one. It is known only for the nisnas, a half-man of its forests whose flesh the people find sweet, and as the source of much of the incense and spice carried up the coast to Europe. Its remoteness, its wild magic and its little-known Magic jinn make it a possible first home for Hermetic settlers, if they can find magical answers to its poverty and distance.

Frankincense and myrrh come from twisted trees on its foggy mountains, with groves too in 'Uman, Ethiopia and Soqotra. Harvesters cut the bark and wait three months for the sap to harden into tears, worth more than their weight in gold. White flying serpents, the syrenii or iaculii, guard the trees and are driven off with the smoke of storax brought from Anatolia. Frankincense, olibanum, pale yellow tinged with green, quickens the blood: as a material it gives +3 to medicine and +5 to promote life. Myrrh, reddish brown, darker and clearer the better it is, flavours wine and goes into embalming and the Orthodox holy oil: +3 to ease arthritis or inflammation, +5 to preserve, +2 to sanctify.

links.note: the winged serpents of the incense trees

neighbours.name: 'Uman
neighbours.summary: The eastern tip of the peninsula: hot, dry desert inside, cooler and fertile coastal mountains and plains where crops grow, and ports through which Arabia trades with the Indian Ocean. Most of its people are Ibadis. The last giants of 'Ad live in Magic regiones deep in its deserts, and weaken if they stay too long outside their strong auras; now and then one comes out to build for a sorcerer or emir in return for some secret of eternal life.

neighbours.name: The Haram of Mecca
neighbours.summary: The sacred ground reaching about five miles out from Mecca, closed to non-Muslims, where no blood may be shed. Its Divine aura is 3, with Calm at +3; inside the city itself every aura is a point higher than it would be elsewhere, so 5 in its streets. God's favour shows plainly: the weather is gentle beyond nature, plants grow lush but never run wild, and peace hangs over the streets.

neighbours.name: The Haram Mosque
neighbours.summary:
The holiest of mosques, at the heart of Mecca: a great courtyard ringed by richly decorated halls of many rows of columns, with twenty gates and seven minarets. Off its north-west hall is the Dar al-Nadwa, where the scholars take counsel with the Grand Sharif; off the south-west hall the house of the Maliki scholars. Its Divine aura is 10, overwhelming; a Muslim may invoke baraka here for any of the Saint Powers of Realms of Power: The Divine, and the site counts as Divine Might 100 where that matters.

In the courtyard stands the Ka'ba, which Adam built under the angels' guidance and Abraham and Ishmael rebuilt: a cube of about forty feet a side and forty-six high, its upper walls hung with the green kiswa. In its eastern corner, five feet up, is set the Black Stone, which fell from Heaven to mark the spot for Adam and Eve, white once and blackened by the sins it has soaked up; pilgrims touch or kiss it to be forgiven. Since the Qarmatians stole it, it has been seven pieces held in a silver band. A door seven feet up the north-east wall, reached by wheeled wooden steps, opens on marble of many colours, three pillars, a stair to the roof, old and precious Qur'ans and the records of those who restored the shrine. Muslims may seek baraka from the Prophet inside the Ka'ba and just outside it.

About twenty yards east of the Ka'ba, under a marble dome, is the Well of Zamzam.

levels.name: The Ka'ba within
levels.see: A still richer Ka'ba, which holds more worshippers than the shrine could.
levels.enter: Pious Muslims who go in on the days it is opened to all, most Mondays and Fridays.
levels.notes: Here, as at the spot near the south-west wall where the Prophet prayed, a crowd may all pray in the same place without jostling.

neighbours.name: The Well of Zamzam
neighbours.summary:
The spring God showed to Hajar, Ibrahim's wife, when she searched for water for her thirsty son Ishmael, older than any building of Mecca. Its water is clean and pure, and pilgrims drink it as an act of devotion, but most of the year it has no power.

Vis: on the night after Ramadan ends the Divine aura over the well sinks a little, and its water, drawn by moonlight, is an unusual Extraordinary Aquam vis: each mouthful restores all of a character's lost Fatigue levels by an unknown non-Hermetic effect of ritual strength. The book gives no number of pawns.

Story seeds:
The Restoring Waters of Zamzam: on the night Ramadan ends the Divine aura at the well dips and its water can be drawn by moonlight as Aquam vis; each mouthful restores all lost Fatigue, and magi may covet it as a path to an Insight on the Limit of Energy.
neighbours.secrets:
Zamzam is also a name: an ancient Magic marid lies trapped in a smothered Magic regio at the bottom of the well, its powers crushed by the Divine aura. What strength it keeps goes into keeping the water so pure, and it has come to hate its prison. It remembers far back, and knows things of the past no other source can tell.

Story seeds:
The Marid of the Well: the marid Zamzam lies in a smothered Magic regio at the foot of the well, keeping its water pure and hating the Dominion that holds it; it knows things of the distant past no one else does, but how could anyone speak with it unseen in Islam's holiest shrine, and what would it do if freed?

neighbours.name: The Mosque of the Jinn
neighbours.summary:
On Mecca's northern edge lies al-Ma'la, the cemetery of many of the Prophet's kin and companions, his mother Amina, his first wife Khadija and his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib among them. Beside it is the mosque where a band of jinn heard the Prophet recite the Qur'an and took Islam.

It has become the jinn's own centre of worship. At the hours of prayer, and above all at Friday noon, it teems with faerie jinn of every shape and size, and even its officials are jinn who do not trouble to disguise themselves. By an unspoken rule they take no shape too monstrous or too big for the room. A few humans pray here too, sahirs and other wizards among them, and respectful mortals are always made welcome, sometimes a little too warmly. The jinn draw their vitality from human worship beside them, not from any aura of the Divine.

Its Faerie aura is 4, and 5 while the jinn are at prayer.

Story seeds:
The Mosque of the Jinn: a Merinita magus hires the characters to study the faeries who worship there without making a Divine aura; the jinn, who feed on human prayer, resent being watched rather than joined.

neighbours.name: The Haram of Medina
neighbours.summary: The sacred ground about five miles round Medina, closed to non-Muslims, where no blood may be shed: Divine 3, with Calm at +3. As at Mecca, every aura inside the city is a point higher than elsewhere, so 5 in its streets, and the city is full of mosques, shrines and places of the Prophet's life. Old lava fields, long cooled, ring the plain.

neighbours.name: 'Ukaz
neighbours.summary:
A small oasis town halfway between Mecca and Medina, whose yearly poetry contest goes back to the Ignorance: the seven Suspended Odes, the Mu'allaqat, that now hang on the Ka'ba were first heard at its fair. Each year a different tribe of jinn sponsors it, and the prize is always precious and never the same: the hidden way to 'Abqar, kinship with the tribe for ever, a young jinni's service without condition. The competition is fierce and the poetry astonishing.

Story seeds:
The Poetry Festival at 'Ukaz: each year a tribe of jinn sponsors the old poetry contest at 'Ukaz between Mecca and Medina, and the prize changes: the way to 'Abqar, kinship with the tribe forever, or a young jinni's service; magi and sahirs come to compete.

neighbours.name: Al-Qudayd
neighbours.summary: The lost sanctuary of al-Manat, goddess of fortune and fate, one of the three Daughters of Allah, somewhere about ten miles from Medina; no one now knows where. The cult of the Daughters at Ta'if is searching for it.

neighbours.name: The Nest of Lukman's Falcons
neighbours.summary:
Lukman, son of 'Ad, once heard a voice and found here a nest of two falcon chicks. He raised the stronger, and in its eighty years of life he did not age a day; when it died he found another chick, and so on through seven birds, the last of them Lubad, until five centuries fell on him at once and he died. The nest lies in a Magic regio somewhere in the western mountains.

Each fledgling raised as a companion keeps its trainer from every Aging roll for eighty years, at a Warping Point a year, and no Longevity Ritual works beside it; when the bird dies its owner ages quickly until he raises the next. The falcon itself makes no Aging roll and dies suddenly at eighty, unless killed: it has Magic Might 8 and is unaffected by The Gift.

Story seeds:
The Seven Falcons of Lukman: Lukman of 'Ad stayed young through the lives of seven falcons from one nest, each living eighty years; the nest lies in a Magic regio after a hard climb in western Arabia, and a fledgling raised there spares its trainer all Aging rolls for eighty years, at a Warping Point a year and a quick ageing when it dies.

levels.name: The falcons' eyrie
levels.enter: Only after a hard climb in the mountains of western Arabia.

neighbours.name: The Stone Lovers
neighbours.summary:
Two oddly shaped outcrops of rock in a remote Magic aura. The local tribe counts them as 'ashiras and so as members of the tribe: its legends say they were the giants Aja and Salma, lovers banished here who lived on the spot for five hundred years and slowly turned into the half-human stone sentinels seen today. Dark faerie and Infernal jinn haunt them by night, and the tribe fears that wizards will wake the giants or draw the jinn. Vis can be had from the site, the book says, without saying what.

Suggested vis sources (not in the book), for the storyguide to use, change or ignore: grit that weathers from the stones' faces on the night of the full moon, 2 pawns of Terram a year; dew that gathers in the hollow between the two figures at dawn, 1 pawn of Corpus a year.

neighbours.name: The Valley of 'Abqar
neighbours.summary:
In the times before Islam jinn lived in this valley and breathed inspiration into the greatest Arab poets, as their muses. It may be a faerie regio reached both from Yemen and from southern Jordan, a town in Arcadia, or both at once.

Story seeds:
Poets and Qareen: the 'abqari, poets with an artistic qareen, can lampoon their foes into misfortune; a journey to 'Abqar may be part of a Merinita Keepers of Tales initiation, or draw Jerbiton and Redcaps who love the Thousand and One Nights.

levels.name: 'Abqar
levels.enter: From Yemen or from southern Jordan; the poets' fair at 'Ukaz sometimes gives the way as its prize.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Ma'rib
neighbours.summary:
East of Sana'a, the remains of the capital of Balqis, the Queen of Sheba, whose priest-kings, the mukkaribs, served the sun, moon and stars as al-Shams, 'Ilmaqa and al-Zuhara. Suleiman heard of her sun-worshipping land from the hoopoe and invited her to talk of faith; she came with riddles and a caravan of gold, spice and jewels, found her own throne fetched ahead of her and disguised, mistook his glass floor for water, and acknowledged the one God.

Most of its palaces, temples and gardens are ruins, with small Magic auras scattered through them where pagan jinn who served the queen at Suleiman's command still live. Upstream, in the mountains, the great dyke that held back the Wadi Udhana and its wild water elementals lies broken. The book calls the land round it a good site for a covenant, for those who can supply so remote a place and face its hostile spirits, who love neither wizards nor summoners.

Story seeds:
King Suleiman and the Queen of Sheba: Sheba's sun-worship may survive at Ma'rib, its gods faeries or demons posing as a heavenly trinity; the mukkaribs' magic may have commanded celestial spirits; the hoopoe's kin could guide or serve; the queen's throne and glass hall may still be somewhere; and perhaps Suleiman and the queen never died.

neighbours.name: The Temple of Ghumdam
neighbours.summary: The great temple the jinn built at Ma'rib, still standing alone and silent among the ruins, with a Magic aura of 6.

neighbours.name: Iram, the City of a Thousand Pillars
neighbours.summary:
Ubar, capital of the giants of 'Ad, who ruled Yemen, Hadramawt and 'Uman five generations after the Flood from their homeland of al-Akhaf. They worshipped idols, rejected the prophet Hud whom God sent from among them, and held to their idols through the drought sent to warn them, until a great storm destroyed them, all but Hud and the few who listened, and drove the city deep under the sand.

A wide hollow in the dunes above it has a Magic aura of 5. Below, in a vast cavern, the city stands whole, full of its people's riches and their dried corpses, its Magic auras still strong: a tempting covenant site, though everything is built for folk some twelve yards tall.

Story seeds:
Discovering the Lost City: a map, a survivor's descendant or a fall through dry quicksand leads to Iram whole in a cavern under the sands, full of riches and dried corpses, strong in Magic and built for giants twelve yards tall: a covenant site, if the last stonesmith giants of 'Ad allow it.

links.note: the giants of 'Ad in the deep desert

neighbours.name: The Trees That Cry Blood
neighbours.summary:
A grove of five ancient mogar trees in Hadramawt's hills above the sea, growing straight out of the rock and standing up to the monsoon storms. The locals know the complicated timing of its harvests well, and dread the large, savage flock of flying serpents that nests in its branches, which shrugs off storax smoke and ordinary wards.

Vis: frankincense gathered from these trees during a violent storm comes as unusually pure tears, each holding one pawn of Rego Terram vis; each tree gives several pawns a harvest.

Story seeds:
The Trees That Cry Blood: five old trees in Hadramawt's coastal hills give frankincense holding Rego Terram vis when tapped in a storm, guarded by fierce flying serpents that ignore storax smoke and wards; rivals soon learn of the harvest, and too much magic may wake the trees themselves.

neighbours.name: The Haunted Shores of Hajar
neighbours.summary:
In 350 the Persian king Shapur II sent his armies against the Arabs on both shores of the Gulf, and they killed, looted and carried off thousands round Hajar and on the Persian coast across the water. The dead walk those shores still: each night they come out and beg whoever they meet for help against their tormentors, until invisible soldiers cut them down, with weapons that are said to kill the living as well. So no one goes out after dark; they stop their ears to the screaming and the frantic hands beating on their doors.

The sahirs of Hajar suspect the ghosts in any trouble by night, but cannot command the dead.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Yemen
neighbours.summary:
Al-Mas'ud Yusuf, sultan of Yemen since 1215, the Ayyubid prince who holds 'Asir and Yemen, far more firmly than his kinsman the sultan of Egypt holds the Hijaz. He rules from Sana'a.

If history holds, when the Grand Sharif Qatada is killed this year he marches in to end the bloodshed at Mecca and rules it as a soldier until his death in 1229, when the sharifs take it back.

neighbours.name: Grand Sharif of Mecca
neighbours.summary:
Qatada, Grand Sharif since 1201, governor of Mecca, a descendant of the Prophet through his grandson al-Hasan and of the Hawashim clan. He takes counsel with the scholars in the Dar al-Nadwa off the Haram Mosque, and owes the sultan of Egypt allegiance in name.

If history holds, in 1220 his son al-Hasan kills him and many of the family in a massacre to make his own succession sure; the Ayyubid sultan of Yemen then takes the city in hand until 1229.

neighbours.name: Uyunid Emir of Bahrayn
neighbours.summary: The Uyunids, a Sunni Arab dynasty, rule Bahrayn in 1220, having driven out the Qarmatians, who had held it from 899 to 1076.

neighbours.name: Nabhanid King of 'Uman
neighbours.summary: The Nabhanids, the Ibadi kings of 'Uman, rule from Nizwa, their royal city.

neighbours.name: Yahmad Lords of Muscat
neighbours.summary: The Yahmad, a local tribe who have lately taken Muscat from the 'Abbasids and want to push its trade further east.

neighbours.name: Mecca
neighbours.summary:
The holiest city of Islam, in a valley among mountains that shelter it from the desert's wind and heat: houses, and shrines, convents, colleges and a hundred mosques, the greatest of them the Haram Mosque with the Ka'ba at its centre. It is always crowded: townsfolk who serve its needs, scholars who live and teach in its mosques, and pilgrims of almost every Muslim persuasion who stay a fortnight or a few years and move on. Most of its people are Sunnis, with many Zaydi Shi'is.

Muhammad left it for Medina in 622, the first year of the Muslim calendar, and took it in 630; the Qarmatians sacked it in 930.

Story seeds:
The Lost Lords of Mecca: the Jurhumites, jann-blooded lords of Mecca before Islam, live on as dark Faerie jinn with a few jinn-blooded sahirs adopted into the clan; they know secret ways into the closed cities and may court magi in their feud with Mecca's rulers. Are they behind Medina's lava, or scapegoats for renegade sahirs?

neighbours.name: Medina
neighbours.summary:
Madinat al-Nabi, the City of the Prophet, Islam's second holy city, on a flat plain held between mountains and old lava flows where several valleys and passes meet. Its soil is unusually rich in fruit and grain. Strong walls with watchtowers enclose it, built in 1162 by Nur al-Din, sultan of Syria. Its governor owes the sultan of Egypt allegiance but the city largely runs itself. It has long been a city of scholars: Malik ibn Anas, who died in 795 and whose followers became the Maliki school of law, lived and taught here.

Story seeds:
The Lava Flows of Medina: the earthquakes that crack the old lava fields round Medina are no accident but the work of enemies trying to melt them again and drown the holy city in fire.

neighbours.name: Ta'if
neighbours.summary: A town on the mountain slopes about sixty miles south-east of Mecca, famous for its orchards, which feed Mecca and other towns with fruit. Before Islam a great idol of al-Lat stood here, goddess of fertility, shepherds and caravans; it was destroyed when the Muslims took the town in 631. The Cult of the Daughters of Allah lives here in secret.

neighbours.name: Sana'a
neighbours.summary:
The seat of government of Yemen and 'Asir, high in the Yemeni hills where the air is fresh and cool, and home of the Ayyubid sultan. Its Salt Market, the Suq al-Milh, sells every kind of curiosity to whoever searches long enough, and its food is famous for being good.

Story seeds:
The Food of Sana'a: a cooking pot from Sana'a carries a hedge enchantment that makes every meal delicious and slowly Warps whoever eats from it; if such pots are common the whole town may be Warping unawares, and someone made them.

links.note: the Infernal jinni bound to Sana'a's young vizier

neighbours.name: Muscat
neighbours.summary: A coastal town, perhaps Ptolemy's Hidden Port or Pliny's Moscha, and a leading point of departure for voyages beyond the Middle East; many who sail from its quays dreaming of riches never come back. The Yahmad tribe lately took it from the 'Abbasids and want its trade to reach further east. A large house of sahirs of Solomonic Travel is here, seeking the islands of Sinbad's tales.

neighbours.name: Nizwa
neighbours.summary:
The royal city of 'Uman, a centre of faith, trade and art, with many finely decorated mosques and palaces and busy markets famous for silver jewellery and fine daggers. Several houses of sahirs are in the city and the country round it.

It also has a dark name as a home of witches and sorcerers.

neighbours.name: Hajar
neighbours.summary:
The chief city and port of Bahrayn, its link with the Persian coast across the Gulf. Its people never go out at night, for the ghosts of Shapur II's massacre of 350. A community of sahirs lives here.

Story seeds:
The Ghosts of Hajar: a child is lost in Hajar's streets at night, and the local sahirs, who cannot command the dead, ask for help before the ghostly soldiers find it; laying the ghosts and lifting the curse could become a long tale.

neighbours.name: Tayma'
neighbours.summary:
Tayma', Khaybar and the towns near them have long been a refuge for Jews, and in 1220 they are free towns that owe no sultan anything. Jews are most of the people, and fierce, clever fighters: their children learn war young, and they keep in practice with raids on other Arabian settlements beside some of the Muslim Bedouin tribes. They can raise an army very quickly, but traditional Judaism thinks little of magic or those who use it.

Story seeds:
The Jews of Tayma' and Khaybar: the Jewish towns can raise fierce armies in days, allies worth having against a sudden host, but their elders distrust magic and must be convinced that the characters' cause is just.

neighbours.name: Khaybar
neighbours.summary: Tayma', Khaybar and the towns near them have long been a refuge for Jews, and in 1220 they are free towns that owe no sultan anything. Jews are most of the people, and fierce, clever fighters: their children learn war young, and they keep in practice with raids on other Arabian settlements beside some of the Muslim Bedouin tribes. They can raise an army very quickly, but traditional Judaism thinks little of magic or those who use it.

neighbours.name: The Bedouin Sahirs
neighbours.summary:
Far more Bedouin than townsfolk have supernatural power, and the Bedouin sahirs are Gifted more often than sahirs anywhere else in the Middle East. Most of Arabia's sahirs belong to a tribe, and few live in towns or houses of wisdom: they make their alliances by kin and blood. Arabia's vis is rich, and they trade it to their cousins in the towns for rare books on the Solomonic arts or for teaching.

Most work Solomonic Storytelling or Solomonic Travel; some scorn the arts and only summon and bargain with jinn. Each keeps a favourite falcon or saluqi which is really a faerie jinni bound by a khadim bond. Every tribe has at least one sahir, often helped by women wise in folk magic, the hakima or kahina (soothsayers), like Folk Witches of the Faerie realm but with Animal Healing and Entrancement in place of Cursing and Flight, or by the shai'ir, poets in the old pagan manner. Most tribes have elders of jinn blood, a wandering sahir vizier with an 'afrit or marid in his service, and families of faerie jann among their kin, who take the shapes of camels, falcons, hounds and horses. To a Bedouin, man or jinni, Muslim or pagan, the clan comes first and the family second.

Poetry is the Bedouin's pride. Poets (shai'ir, not to be mistaken for sahir) and reciters (rawi) are historians, soothsayers and praise-singers at once, carrying verses in praise of the tribe (qit'ah) and savage mockery of others (hija'). Bedouin sahirs still settle feuds by zajal, a mock battle in verse: opposed rolls of Communication + Solomonic Storytelling (Communication + Folk Ken between mundanes), +2 for Arabic 6 or more. Enchanting Poetry and Entrancement are common even among poets who are no wizards; the satirist Abu Nuwas of Harun's court passed into Golden Baghdad's tales as a faerie of Elysium.

neighbours.name: Muru'a, the Bedouin Code
neighbours.summary:
The code the northern nomads kept from before Islam, all of them Sunni Muslims in name: hospitality (diyafa), courage (hamasa) and honour (sharaf for men, ird for women) above all, with forgiveness, loyalty and self-sacrifice, and colouring town life too. Dutybound (Bedouin code) is nearly universal among Bedouin; a few from the deep desert are still Pagan.

Knowledge of muru'a is an Organization Lore like a non-Hermetic Mystery's, through which the tribe's hakima, as Mystagogue, initiates faerie-aligned Virtues useful to a nomad: Arcadian Travel, Animal Ken, Art of Memory, Dowsing, Death Prophecy, Cursing, Entrancement, Enchanting Poetry (as Enchanting Music), Greater Immunity to thirst, Puissant Arabic, Wilderness Sense, Spiritual Pact and Ways of the Desert; Enchanting Poetry is the Major Virtue most often gained. Scripts differ from tribe to tribe, with ordeals tied to the code that leave Flaws such as Generous, Higher Purpose, Overconfident, Oversensitive to slights on honour, Proud, a Vow to keep one's word, or Weakness.

A foreigner who shows the virtues the Bedouin admire may be taken into a clan and initiated, gaining Dutybound (Bedouin code) and Close Family Ties to the clan. To the tribe and its jinn that bond, 'asabiyya, outweighs every other, so a magus may have to choose between it and the Code, and a quaesitor come for him may find a whole tribe of jinn-blooded Bedouin standing behind him.

details.rules: Hospitality, courage, honour; loyalty to the clan above all; always keep your word.

neighbours.name: The Cult of the Daughters of Allah
neighbours.summary:
Before Islam three goddesses were worshipped round Mecca: al-Lat at Ta'if, al-Manat, goddess of fortune and fate, at al-Qudayd near Medina, and al-'Uzza, of strength and of Venus, at a sanctuary outside Mecca. The pagans called them the Daughters of Allah, whom they already held to be the high creator. The story of the 'Satanic Verses', still argued over by scholars, says Iblis once slipped verses into the revelation that let Muslims ask the Daughters to intercede, and that God at once sent verses rejecting them.

A single family of Ta'if has kept their worship alive in secret through the centuries, always three strong, each member able to channel one goddess. Two sanctuaries, al-Lat's and al-'Uzza's, they have already found; they are hunting for the third. 'Abd al-Qadir speaks for al-Lat, with power over growth in men, beasts and plants and over swift travel; his son Yusuf for al-Manat, bending chance and the dice; and Yusuf's wife Farida for al-'Uzza, with great strength and power over beauty, love, performance and speech. The book suggests playing them as Spirit Votaries, or, if the cult is corrupt, as diabolists.

Story seeds:
Farida's Fears: the Cult of the Daughters finds al-Manat's sanctuary and begins a three-part rite that may bring back the goddesses or harm the Ka'ba; Farida, the family's newest member, has doubts, and may fear the child she carries is meant to replace her.

details.wants: To find al-Qudayd, al-Manat's lost sanctuary, and bring back the worship of the three goddesses.

neighbours.secrets: Farida, the newest of the three, has doubts: her Muslim upbringing, what she is asked to do, or the child she may be carrying, who would replace her in a family that is never more than three.

neighbours.name: The Witches of Nizwa
neighbours.summary:
The witches and sorcerers of Nizwa's dark reputation, who are not of the Order of Suleiman. They are said to travel in an instant by stepping over a line drawn in the sand, and, worse, to make people seem to die, take the 'corpses' and keep them as mindless slaves. The book has no tradition record for them.

Story seeds:
