The Witches of Nizwa: the witches may be Infernalists, faerie wizards, exiled Soqotran witches, agents of the Olibanum King working against the Suhhar, or heirs of Sheba's astral sorceresses; or the rumours may be false, which matters if the characters want a covenant nearby.
neighbours.secrets: The book leaves their nature open: Infernalists, faerie wizards, Soqotran witches in exile, agents of the Olibanum King working against the Order of Suleiman, the last of Sheba's astral sorceresses, or nothing but slander.

neighbours.name: The Jurhumites
neighbours.summary:
An ancient tribe who ruled Mecca and parts of the Hijaz before Islam. They refused the faith, seemed beaten by the first Muslim armies, and now live on in the old tales of the pagan tribes: every one of them is a dark faerie jann, with more elemental power, of Auram and Terram, than most of their kind, though a few jinn-blooded sahirs are secretly counted as adopted kin. As Mecca's old masters they know hidden ways into the closed places.

Other tribes of old survive, the Bedouin say, as faerie jinn clans: the Jadis, the Tasm and the Thamudites.

details.wants: Mecca back, and their old feud with its rulers.

neighbours.name: Mesopotamia
neighbours.summary:
The political heart of Sunni Islam and its north-western provinces, from Iraq up through the Jazira to the Caucasus. Nearly every ruler owns the 'Abbasid caliph at least in name, but most provincial lords govern as they please and look to Baghdad only when its blessing helps their claim. The land falls into three: fertile plains between and along the Tigris and Euphrates, watered in Iraq by canals thousands of years old that shifting ground and neglect have badly worn down; mountains to the north, east and north-west, farmed only in the valleys; and the Syrian desert to the west, running south into Arabia's Nefud. Most people are Muslims, with many Christians and Jews, living in towns and villages, with nomads and oasis folk in the desert.

The old gods of the land were faeries, and are starving: their worship lingers only at a few cult centres, at Harran, Mardin, Ashshur and Mosul, whose priests, many of them yatus, walk the streets unafraid in their tall conical hats. Too few to feed them, so the gods have hidden in regiones for centuries and crave attention, some dreaming of their cults reborn, some only of friends, and none quite understanding mortals. Among them: Anu of the sky at Uruk, head of the elder Anunnaki; Ea of the waters under the earth, of craft, magic and wisdom, at Eridu; Ellil of the earth at Nippur, head of the younger Igigi, who keeps the Tablet of Destinies; Ishtar of love, fertility and war at Uruk, Nineveh and Erbil; Dumuzi of flocks and fields, her lover, half of each year in the underworld; Adad of storms, canals and liver omens at Aleppo; Mami the great mother at lost Kesh; Nergal of war, plague and fire and his weeping queen Ereshkigal at Kutha; Sin of the moon at Ur and Harran; Shamash of the sun and justice at Sippar and Larsa; Marduk at Babylon; and Ashshur at Ashshur.

Tiamat, the first mother, bore the gods with her consort Apsu, then tired of the young gods' din and bred eleven kinds of monster to destroy them, until Marduk killed her and made the world from her body; students of the Magic Realm will see in it a Titanomachia, faerie gods taking power from primordial Magic beings. Her brood serve the fading gods still: the seven-headed dragon mushmahhu, the lion-dragon ushumgallu, the horned snake bashmu sixty leagues long, the snake-dragon mushhushshu, the hairy giant lahamu, the lion-headed, bird-footed ugallu, the lion-bodied man uridimmu, the scorpion-man girtablullu, the fierce storm umu dabrutu, the merman kulullu and the bull-man kusarikka. Colossal statues of the winged bulls, the aladlammu and apsasu, guard many old ruins, and a land that has one may call on the faerie against disease and demons.

Demons throng the land, some busy since ancient times: the uttuku, Infernal jinn of the Mazzikim's kind; the galla, great spirits of disease, whom the aladlammu fight; the lilu, ghuls of the wastes who prey on children and women with child, and their female counterparts, the lilitu succubi; and the gidim, ghosts who come back to torment the families that mourn them. Realms of Power: The Infernal places the Mulhidun, an Infernal tradition, mostly in the Jazira.

Story seeds:
The Unholy Trinity: Mahound, Termagant and Apollyon, the three gods Europe wrongly thinks the Muslims worship, are real demons of the False Gods who stir up hatred between Christian and Muslim wherever they can; a troupe with friends of both faiths may spend a saga hunting them.
Disputes over the Caliphate: the 'Abbasids missed at least one Umayyad, and perhaps more; a hidden heir of that house, or a Shi'i claimant, asks the characters to help him to the throne, with an old relic or a power of his own to make the request hard to refuse.
The Corruption of the West: almost every Infernal being of these lands is a jinni, and so open to Sihr; but Europe's demons have followed the Crusades into Outremer, and as merchants, missionaries and magi travel further east they will bring their own sins and devils with them, the Unholy Trinity among them.
The Dark Sufis: a heretical Sufi path honours Iblis for refusing to bow to Adam, taking it for love of God alone: unwitting diabolists, one of whom poses as a holy man to lead a Criamon magus astray.
Sorcery, Treason, and Plot: the characters foil a magical attempt on the King of Georgia's life and are told to find the culprit: a magus would have broken the Code, and anyone else is a power the Order should know of.

neighbours.name: The Jazira
neighbours.summary:
The fertile country north of Iraq between the rivers, mostly under Ayyubid princes who spend their days plotting against one another, so that the towns they do not hold outright own them in name only. Nearly all its rulers, the Ayyubids included, honour the caliph, to little effect.

Story seeds:
Tensions in Mosul: a wizard with the Blatant Gift who went to find a magical cause for Mosul's famed kindness has turned its people against one another instead, and needs mediators while he undoes his meddling.

links.note: the scorpion-men who guard the old ruins

neighbours.name: Azarbayjan
neighbours.summary:
A mountainous province north of the Jazira, ruled lightly by the Atabegs of Azarbayjan from Tabriz and mostly left to local governors. Its people are Turks, Persians and Caucasians, Muslims, Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians and others; its communities are scattered by the mountains and its greatest centres no more than big towns. A Turkic tongue is the common speech, with local dialects beside it.

Story seeds:
Khidr and the Water of Life: al-Khidr makes the best of mysterious advisers, whose strange counsel always proves right; those who seek the Water of Life need his guidance, and he gives it only to the pure in purpose.

neighbours.name: Arran
neighbours.summary: The province north of Azarbayjan, held by its atabegs in name, though they do little here. Most of its people are Armenian Christians, with a large Sunni community that includes most of the ruling class.

neighbours.name: Mukan
neighbours.summary: Mostly a marshy plain running from the north-western mountains down to the Caspian, much of it farmed for rice and wheat.

neighbours.name: Shirvan
neighbours.summary: A mountainous province north of Arran and Mukan, its towns in the valleys, ruled for centuries by the Shirvanshahs, a Persianised Arab dynasty, from Shamakhi. Most of its people are Sunnis, like their rulers, or Christians.

neighbours.name: Gilan
neighbours.summary: A backwater, neither rich nor famous: mostly jungle-clad mountains, with a fertile coastal plain of rice and wheat on the Caspian. Its rulers pay tribute to the lords of Jibal to the south and are otherwise left alone.

neighbours.name: The Palace of Shirin
neighbours.summary:
Qasr Shirin, a big walled village on the road up to Jibal under the mountains of the Persian plateau, named for Shirin, wife of the Persian king Khusraw II Parviz, who lived here. Her palace is a ruin, but at every full moon it fills with faerie Shirins, Khusraws, the sculptor Farhad and their courtiers, playing out Shirin's courtship over and over, best known in al-Nizami's telling (he died in 1209): the king loves the Armenian princess, the mighty Farhad becomes his rival, Khusraw sends him to cut through the Behistun cliffs for water and, when he does it, sends word that Shirin is dead, and Farhad leaps from the cliff; his pomegranate-wood axe grows into a tree whose fruit cures any sickness, and Shirin at last weds the king after he proves himself, killing a lion bare-handed to save her.

Visitors at the full moon are drawn into the parts of the tale, and may win rewards or wisdom by playing them.

neighbours.name: The Palace of Ctesiphon
neighbours.summary:
The ruins of the Persian emperors' capital at al-Mada'in, witness to the end of the Sasanids. Over what was the throne room still stands a vaulted arch more than 110 feet high at its peak, of great interest to the Mystery of Hermetic Architecture. The townsfolk distrust foreigners who poke about the ruins.

Story seeds:
The Ruined Palace: the great arch over the Persian emperors' throne room at Ctesiphon draws students of Hermetic Architecture, perhaps as an initiation task, though the locals eye foreigners digging in the ruins.

neighbours.name: Dayr al-'Aqul
neighbours.summary:
The first of three Nestorian monasteries down the Tigris from al-Mada'in, linked to one another without knowing it. It stands on the river bank in a sizeable town of the same name, which has a great mosque. Its monks take a toll from the river traffic and share it with the town, which lives on it, but lately the banks have been changing fast and the river is drifting west, away from them. Nothing they try stops it, monks and townsfolk alike think something supernatural is at work, and some whisper that the 'monks' of Dayr Qunna, a mile east, are sorcerers out to ruin them.

Story seeds:
The Enemies of Dayr al-'Aqul: someone is turning the Tigris, and the monks of Dayr al-'Aqul rescue the characters from its sudden shift: the sahirs of Dayr Qunna, who dislike the Dominion near them, or a spirit too strong for them, or Dayr Hizqil's monks after the river toll, or one of Hizqil's madmen (a sahir Dayr Qunna left there, his mind blasted by what he called), or a sorcerer feigning madness, or a demon or faerie enjoying it all.

neighbours.name: Dayr Hizqil
neighbours.summary: A monastery in the town of al-Nu'maniyya, twenty miles south of Dayr al-'Aqul, where the monks keep a madhouse for the insane: plain, strong men able to hold down their charges when they must.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Babylon
neighbours.summary:
The ruined city of southern Iraq that saw the chaining of Harut and Marut, who hang bound beneath it, the building of the Tower of Babel, the Jews' exile, Nebuchadnezzar's Hanging Gardens, and its fall with Belshazzar's kingdom to the Persians, in 539 BC. Ancient Magic tells more of its mysteries.

Story seeds:
The Sacred Vessels: the Temple vessels Belshazzar drank from may never have gone back to Jerusalem; turned Infernal, they pass from owner to ruined owner, or, still holy, they wait in Babylon's ruins for someone worthy.

links.note: the winged bull guardians against demons

neighbours.name: The Great Swamp
neighbours.summary: South of Babylon a great marsh fills the land between the two rivers until they meet. Its air is foul and insects swarm, yet stubborn villagers have drained patches to farm and live in scattered villages and towns, getting about in shallow boats. They keep the old religion in fragments, with no priests left, but one tale they have recited faithfully for generations: the Epic of Gilgamesh.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Uruk
neighbours.summary:
A great stepped ziggurat rising from the middle of the swamp, all that is left of a temple of Ishtar, with a Faerie aura of 2. The locals keep away: some who went never came back. A doorway choked with rubble is a faerie Guardian, and whoever breaks through it passes, unawares, into Elysium in the Faerie Realm; the Threshold is 33, but those who come to the temple and cross the doorway gather the points they need without fail.

Within, Gilgamesh asks one or all of them to take the part of Enkidu in his tale, which sets them on a Path of Destiny. The tale: the gods send the wild man Enkidu to distract the unloved king; tamed by Shamhat, he wrestles Gilgamesh to a draw and they become friends; they kill Humbaba in the Pine Forest and the Bull of Heaven that Ishtar sends when Gilgamesh spurns her; the gods strike Enkidu dead for it; Gilgamesh wanders past the scorpion men to Siduri and Utnapishtim, fails to win eternal life, and comes home wise enough to rule well. Whoever dies as Enkidu is sent back through the Guardian alive, with what he came for; a player who knowingly lets her character take that part and die gains an Unmitigated Success and, the book suggests, a Confidence Point.

Story seeds:
In Enkidu's Place: those who step through the temple door at Uruk find Gilgamesh, who wants one of them to be his Enkidu and sends them into the wild to wait for Shamhat.

neighbours.name: The Whirlpool at Ubulla
neighbours.summary: In the late eighth century a savage jinni made itself a whirlpool in the Shatt al-'Arab off Ubulla and wrecked every ship that came near, cutting Baghdad off from the Gulf. Zubayda bint Ja'far, Harun al-Rashid's wife, learnt in her studies that stone was its bane: she had ships loaded with stones and sunk in its maw, burying it in the river bed, and the waters grew calm. It is imprisoned there, not dead.

neighbours.name: Nimrod's Furnace
neighbours.summary:
A huge tower of hardened ash in the town of Kutha, all that is left of the furnace of the tyrant Nimrod, builder of the Tower of Babel. He threw Abraham, son of his own vizier Terah, into it; God bade the fire be cool, and Abraham walked out unhurt while the furnace itself burnt away, leaving the Tower of Ashes.

Story seeds:
Nimrod's Furnace: God's rescue of Abraham made the furnace holy and shut its fire demon inside; a corrupt cabal would light it again by weakening Kutha's faith and burning holy men in it.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of al-Husayn
neighbours.summary:
At Karbala', in the desert, Umayyad troops cut down al-Husayn, son of 'Ali and grandson of the Prophet, and his followers in 680, as he pressed his claim to the caliphate after Mu'awiya's death. All Muslims remember it with sorrow and the Shi'is mourn it each year on 'Ashura', the tenth of Muharram. A small town has grown up round his tomb (his head is in Cairo), a great Shi'i pilgrimage: a domed shrine in a garden pool, with a silver gate the pilgrims kiss before going in, gold and silver lamps within, and silk curtains over its other doors.

Its Divine aura is 8, and al-Husayn has Divine Might 75. Visitors may seek his baraka for these Saint Powers. To heal: Mass Healing, The Faithful Made Whole and Straighten the Crippled. Against evil: Expel Demons, Acknowledgement of Evil, Resist Temptation and Celestial Immunity. Besides these: Apparition, Grant of Serenity, Humility of Caesar and Terrify the Unbeliever.

neighbours.name: The Shrine of 'Ali
neighbours.summary:
'Ali, struck down at Kufa in 661, asked that his body be set on a camel turned loose, and buried where it knelt. His followers kept the grave secret from the Umayyads until in 791 Harun al-Rashid, hunting, chased a deer into a thicket that neither his horse nor his hounds would enter, had it dug up, found the body and built a tomb. Enlarged since, it is the heart of Najaf and draws thousands of pilgrims a year: a gold dome with a great portal and silver doorstep on each side, glazed tiles, thick carpets, gold and silver lamps and silk on doors and walls, the tomb itself fenced by engraved gold plates fixed with silver nails.

Its Divine aura is 8, and 'Ali has Divine Might 75. Visitors may pray for his baraka for these Saint Powers. To heal: Cure Blindness, Mass Healing, The Faithful Made Whole and Straighten the Crippled. Against evil: Expel Demons, Acknowledgement of Evil, Resist Temptation and Celestial Immunity. Besides these: Apparition, Grant of Serenity, Rebuke the Unfaithful, Humility of Caesar and Terrify the Unbeliever. The shrine is famed for healing, so powers of that kind are invoked at +1.

neighbours.name: The Jinni's Gorge
neighbours.summary:
The Siq al-Majnun, a narrow canyon on the lower course of the Lesser Zab, the Tigris tributary called Majnun, 'the mad river', for its wild currents. Here Ighraq al-Siq, 'the drowning flood of the gorge', an ancient pagan spirit of the Tigris who once roamed the whole river, is penned, and his fits bring the violent spring floods through the canyon. The canyon has a Magic aura of 6.

He is shut in a Jinni Block, a strange tower tomb of the kind set at the gates of some lost cities, and while there can neither act nor be detected, being part of the stone; the block takes his Magic Resistance but can still be worn away or broken. Something unknown frees him whenever anyone intrudes on the canyon, to drive them off. The ground round the block is a fixed Arcane Connection to him (+1 to the Penetration multiplier), and standing barefoot on it or touching it a stronger one (+3) that also shares his Magic Resistance. A sahir, summoner or magus there may try to command him by Sihr or by scouring, even unaware he is there, but a failure frees him in a rage.

Vis: clear rainwater that gathers each year in a niche cut into the block, 2 pawns of Aquam.

Story seeds:
The Jinni Block: Ighraq al-Siq sleeps in a tower tomb of stone at the gorge, loosed when intruders trip some unknown trigger; whoever stands on the block may try to command him with Sihr or scouring, but a failed attempt frees him, angry.

links.note: the drowning flood of the gorge

neighbours.name: Mount Judi
neighbours.summary: Where the Muslims hold that Noah's Ark came to rest, as Christians and Jews say it did on Ararat in Armenia; both are right, for its remains lie in a regio that can be reached from either mountain. A mosque on the summit marks the spot. At its foot is the town of Thamanin, 'eighty', whose people claim to descend from the eighty companions of Noah who, they say, founded it.

levels.name: The resting place of the Ark
levels.enter: Walk through the mosque's mihrab, though it looks to be solid marble.
levels.notes: The same regio can be reached from Mount Ararat in Armenia; Ancient Magic describes it.

neighbours.name: The Battlefield of Siffin
neighbours.summary:
Across the Euphrates from Raqqa, where 'Ali and Mu'awiya fought in 657. After months of skirmishes Mu'awiya asked for arbitration; 'Ali agreed, and some of his followers left him over it, among them Ibn Muljam, who later killed him. 'Ali's dead lie buried here, and from a distance their uncorrupted bodies can be seen through the earth, though they vanish as one comes near. It is a Shi'i place of pilgrimage.

Story seeds:
The Dead of Siffin: one of the dead at Siffin looks like a character's ancestor, hinting at unknown kin or a magical line, or like someone still alive, perhaps a warning; finding out means a closer look at a grave others would not want disturbed.

neighbours.name: The Sanjah Bridge
neighbours.summary:
A superb bridge over the Sanjah, a tributary of the Euphrates: a single arch over two hundred paces long, of huge dressed stones, built long ago by a sorcerer in a local ruler's service with the help of a talisman he carried. That talisman now sits high in the arch's keystone; what it does, and what removing it would do, nobody knows. The villages round about depend on the bridge to get their crops to market.

Story seeds:
The Missing Talisman: the talisman set in the bridge's crown has been stolen and the bridge is crumbling far too fast; the villages that need it ask the characters to find the thief and restore its power in time.

neighbours.name: Lake Urmiya
neighbours.summary:
A lake of startling blue, smooth as glass, named for the town on its western shore. Fishermen on a small island at its centre catch the odd dog-headed fish that live in it. The leavings of an old sorcerer's work and the beauty of the place give the lake a Magic aura of 2, and 3 on the island.

Story seeds:
The Sorcerer's Tower: the lonely tower by Lake Urmiya would make a covenant, or an old-fashioned delve: the sorcerer who bred the lake's dog-fish surely left other hybrids in it and the tunnels below.

neighbours.name: The Sorcerer's Tower of Urmiya
neighbours.summary: The ruin on Lake Urmiya's island where a mighty sorcerer of old bred and experimented on the lake's fish, until a failed experiment blew up most of the tower and him with it. Catacombs remain under the ruins, very likely full of his hybrid creatures. The book suggests it as a site for a new covenant.

neighbours.name: The Fountain of the Water of Life
neighbours.summary: The spring of the Water of Life, which is said to make whoever bathes in it immortal, and from which al-Khidr, the Green One, drank. Bajarvan in Mukan and Shamakhi in Shirvan both claim it is near them, so seekers might start where the Cyrus and the Araxes meet; no one has found it, or no one who did has come back. Al-Khidr will guide only those whose purpose is pure.

neighbours.name: The Rock of Moses
neighbours.summary:
The stone at Shamakhi that marks where Moses met al-Khidr: the fish Moses and his servant laid on it came alive and swam away, and the townsfolk still come to pray here for the dying. For Muslims it is a relic of Faith 3 with the Saint Power The Faithful Made Whole. The aura is the city's.

Moses asked al-Khidr to teach him and was allowed to follow only if he never questioned; he protested when al-Khidr holed a boat, killed a boy and rebuilt a wall for people who had refused them food, and on the third time was told why (a king was seizing boats, the boy was an unbeliever whose parents would have a better child, the wall hid orphans' treasure) and they parted. Sufis take it as the model of student and master; it would serve a Mystery's Initiation too.

neighbours.name: The Armenian Highlands
neighbours.summary:
A candidate covenant site. Greater Armenia's many remote sites have kept out mundane folk and may hold strong Magic auras, and its tangled politics let a newcomer set up independently, so long as the covenant does not grow strong enough to alarm its neighbours. The cruel winters make it hard to supply, and as the Tribunals fill, other magi may be looking for sites here too and contest the best.

Story seeds:
A Greater Armenian Covenant: Greater Armenia's isolated sites may keep high Magic auras and its politics leave room for newcomers who stay modest; but its winters make supply hard, and other magi may race the characters for the best sites.

neighbours.name: Atabeg of Azarbayjan
neighbours.summary: Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek, atabeg since 1210 and head of the Atabegs of Azarbayjan, who rule Azarbayjan and, in name, Arran, from Tabriz. He rules lightly, leaving much to local governors; he owns the Khwarazm-shah as overlord and pays tribute to the king of Georgia. Jalal al-Din Hasan of the Nizaris has made an alliance with him. If history holds he rules until 1225.

neighbours.name: Shirvanshah
neighbours.summary: The Shirvanshahs, a Persianised Arab dynasty and Sunnis, have ruled Shirvan for centuries from Shamakhi. Two of the royal house share power now: Farrukhzad I ibn Manuchihr III, who came to the throne after 1187, and his son Garshasp I, who has reigned with him since 1204. If history holds both are gone by 1225.

neighbours.name: Emir of Gilan
neighbours.summary: The ruler of Gilan, who pays tribute to the lords of Jibal and otherwise governs alone. He has been pushed into alliance with Jalal al-Din Hasan, head of the Nizaris, who has married his four daughters.

neighbours.name: Al-Mada'in
neighbours.summary: A small, crowded town south-east of Baghdad, once, in the seventh and eighth centuries, a great cluster of seven towns, long in decline. Its mosque is much admired, with the tomb of Salman the Persian, a close companion of the Prophet, beside it, and the ruined palace of Ctesiphon stands here. A large town like this can keep fifty sahirs, split between its quarters. Downriver lie the monasteries of Dayr al-'Aqul, Dayr Qunna, which is really a house of wisdom, and Dayr Hizqil.

neighbours.name: Basra
neighbours.summary:
An important city of southern Iraq on two canals running into the Shatt al-'Arab, full of shrines and mosques. The best known, built by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, has a minaret that shakes or stays still as an oath sworn before it is true or false, a miracle that can be neither fooled nor resisted. Its library is said to hold more than 15,000 books. Like al-Mada'in it can keep fifty sahirs; the grand vizier Kha'trazh comes from here.

Story seeds:
The Thief of Basra: a man caught stealing books of lore from Basra's library swears a sorcerer holds his family; the qadi gives the characters a week to prove it before the hand comes off, unless the thief lied and slips away while they look.

neighbours.name: Ubulla
neighbours.summary:
A busy town of palaces, mosques and markets on the north side of a canal into the Shatt al-'Arab, by the buried jinni's whirlpool.

Story seeds:
The Whirlpool at Ubulla: the jinni chained on the riverbed is not dead, and sorcerers mean to free it as a weapon against the caliph; stop them directly, or warn the caliph while they work?

neighbours.name: Kufa
neighbours.summary:
A city about seven miles north-east of Najaf, lively once, now declining and much of it ruined. In its eastern part the Great Mosque still stands in good repair: there 'Ali received his death wound from Ibn Muljam's poisoned sword in 661, at the spot a mihrab now marks, and Shi'i pilgrims still come on their way to or from Najaf. In 951 the stolen Black Stone was left in a sack in its great mosque.

Story seeds:
The House of Ibn Muljam: the poisoned sword that killed 'Ali lies buried in a Kufa house where his murderer hid, tainting it and binding his ghost there; a friend who has bought the house asks for help, and by the time the characters arrive the ghost has possessed him.

neighbours.name: Najaf
neighbours.summary: A city of the greatest importance to the Shi'is, grown up round the shrine of 'Ali, with a vast graveyard where several prophets and many Shi'i nobles lie, and madrasas, mosques and other religious houses. It has several houses of wisdom.

neighbours.name: Hilla
neighbours.summary:
A city on both banks of the Euphrates, most of it on the west, joined by a bridge of boats held by great iron chains. Many Twelver Shi'is live here waiting for the twelfth imam, who is to return at the end of time at one of its shrines, and it is a centre of Twelver learning, home to many scholars.

Story seeds:
The Scholars of Hilla: a crippled Shi'i sahir sends the characters to Hilla with questions for the scholar Muhammad ibn Muhammad, and they find three of that name who loathe one another; getting all three answers without offending any takes tact.

neighbours.name: Samarra
neighbours.summary:
The 'Abbasid capital from 836 to 892, then a sprawl of rich palaces and mosques on both banks of the Tigris where the caliphs lived as prisoners of their guards, who fought one another for them. Once the caliphs went back to Baghdad it fell to ruin, save the huge Great Mosque of al-Mutawakkil (who reigned 847 to 861), still mostly whole, with its spiral minaret some 180 feet high.

Most of its people in 1220 are Twelver Shi'is, staying by the tombs of the tenth and eleventh imams and a mosque with an underground room where the twelfth imam vanished and may one day come back, as he may at Hilla. Its wide ruins may hide Magic auras and devices of the old court sorcerers, and its wells and canals still work: a possible covenant site, if its people would bear foreign wizards.

Story seeds:
A Samarran Covenant: the sprawling half-ruined palaces may hide Magic auras and devices left by the caliphs' sorcerers, and the wells and canals still work: a covenant site, if the townsfolk will have foreign wizards.

neighbours.name: Kutha
neighbours.summary: The old cult centre of Nergal and Ereshkigal, where Nimrod's furnace stands as a tower of ash.

neighbours.name: Nasibin
neighbours.summary:
A seat of Nestorian learning and of a bishop, its people Christians and Muslims. It is famed for its gardens, forty thousand of them it is said, full of unusually large and sweet-smelling white roses, and for the swarms of its scorpions, whose sting is particularly deadly. Here stood the House of the Heavens, empty since 1186. Its ruler and Mosul's each say the thieves of Barqa'id are the other's problem.

Story seeds:
The Battle for Nasibin: the roses and the scorpions of Nasibin are the outward signs of a stalemate between an angel and a demon fighting for its souls; either may ask the characters' help, and the demon may pass itself off as the angel.

neighbours.name: Barqa'id
neighbours.summary:
A city travellers avoid, peopled almost wholly by thieves who rob visitors and the caravans on the Nasibin road. With fewer travellers passing, they have grown bolder and raid the towns and villages round about, whose appeals to Mosul and Nasibin have gone unanswered.

Story seeds:
Against the City of Thieves: the characters beat off raiders from Barqa'id, and the grateful village that saw it expects them to destroy the robbers' town.

neighbours.name: Amid
neighbours.summary:
A city of black basalt, heavily fortified by its Turkish lords: thick walls, many watchtowers, iron gates, a citadel on a high hill at its centre, and walled suburbs outside. Its great Sunni mosque and great Jacobite church, both of black basalt and iron, are famously beautiful. The walls are for the vast faerie armies, armed with wood and stone and armoured in some unknown old leather, that have attacked it for centuries, always at the spring equinox; the city prepares for them with weary resignation, and the shared enemy has made its Muslims and Christians firm friends.

Story seeds:
The Death of Tenik: Amid's faeries re-enact the old raid of Tigran and Vasdes but cannot end it, for no one remembers that Tenik died between the warbands to stop the fight; the faerie host grows with the city, and someone must play Tenik without dying.

neighbours.name: Raqqa
neighbours.summary: Once a residence of Harun al-Rashid, reviving under the Ayyubids, with thriving markets and famous blue-glazed pottery. The battlefield of Siffin lies across the Euphrates.

neighbours.name: Harran
neighbours.summary:
An Ayyubid town of ancient name: Abraham lived here, and in the eighth century it was the first home of the scholars who put the classical learning into Arabic. About nine miles south a shrine marks where Abraham and Sarah lived. It was the centre of the Sabians, monotheist star-magicians, and a strong cult of Ashshur, the Assyrians' patron god, is here still. Travellers complain of its heat, shadeless and stale-watered.

Story seeds:
The Heat Is On: the Sabian magi left in Harran are making the town hotter to drive its people out so they can dig for their tradition's treasures and revive their cult; magi may sympathise, or seek a compromise.

neighbours.name: Edessa
neighbours.summary:
A city that has changed hands many times, Byzantine, Muslim and others; the crusaders took it in 1098 and made it the seat of one of their four states, Zangi won it back on Christmas Eve 1144, and the Ayyubid sultan of Aleppo, al-'Aziz, holds it now. Most of its people are Christians of several churches. Its churches' great relic was the Holy Mandylion, the cloth with Christ's face that he sent to King Abgar, which the city's Muslim rulers traded to the Byzantine emperor for prisoners in the tenth century and which vanished when the crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204; the people hope for a miracle to bring it home.

Story seeds:
The Holy Mandylion: the Image of Edessa is held by Otto de la Roche, Duke of Athens, excommunicated and all but invincible with it; an Armenian lord or magus, or an evil threatening Edessa, sends the characters to bring it home.

neighbours.name: Arzanjan
neighbours.summary: A busy market town, mostly of Armenian Christians, famed for its craftsmen, above all its brass-smiths, whose work takes beautiful shapes no other town's smiths can match.

neighbours.name: Tabriz
neighbours.summary: The seat of the Atabegs of Azarbayjan.

neighbours.name: Maragha
neighbours.summary:
A city that seems to enjoy some supernatural being's favour: round it grow rich orchards of a strange melon, green outside, red within and sweet as honey, and its sky is never clouded, so astronomers love it.

Story seeds:
Dim Skies and Rotten Fruit: clouds gather over Maragha, which never sees them, and the melons rot overnight: the spirit that kept the town prosperous has turned against it, and someone must learn why and make amends.

neighbours.name: Baylaqan
neighbours.summary: The chief city of Arran, in a river valley fed by many streams, with many mills, gardens and orchards. Its people are divided over a popular preacher who raves of a storm gathering in the east that will soon swallow them: some want him locked up or killed, others call him a seer.

neighbours.name: Bajarvan
neighbours.summary: A modest town, one of Mukan's chief cities, famous for being near the spring of the Water of Life.

neighbours.name: Shamakhi
neighbours.summary: The Shirvanshahs' capital, built wholly of stone at the foot of a mountain among gardens. It too claims to be near the Water of Life, and it keeps the Rock of Moses.

neighbours.name: Barvan
neighbours.summary:
Gilan's chief city, known only for its bad name: no good houses, no good markets, and no great congregational mosque, only a few small ones. Its Divine aura is unusually low, 1.

Story seeds:
To Build a Mosque: Barvan wants a great mosque, its pleasure-loving governor would rather not pay, and the townsfolk cannot agree which mosque to enlarge; the characters are asked to mediate.

neighbours.name: Tiflis
neighbours.summary: The capital of Georgia since Dawid II took it in 1121.

neighbours.name: The Sabians of Harran
neighbours.summary: A cult of monotheist star-magicians centred on Harran, whom the Muslims first met in the ninth century. They are said to have died out, but some may live on, passing for Muslims to avoid trouble. The book gives no tradition record for them.

neighbours.name: The Ashipu
neighbours.summary: Priest-magicians, exorcists, among those who still worship the old gods, as at Harran or Mardin. Most of their craft is knowing demons' weaknesses (Infernal Lore) and making amulets against them; some have more active powers against demons and may belong to the Order of Suleiman. The book gives no tradition record for them.

neighbours.name: The Brass-Smiths' Guild of Arzanjan
neighbours.summary:
The guild of Arzanjan's brass-smiths, whose members can shape brass by hand: a Minor Supernatural Virtue, Lesser Power, gained by the guild's Initiation, whose script always brings the Minor Flaw Vow (guild loyalty). Organization Lore: Arzanjani Brass-Smiths' Guild serves as its Mystery's Lore. A character may start with it, with the Vow and a score of 1 in that Lore.

The power, Crafter of Brass: 1 Fatigue level, Init Quickness - 6, Terram; R: Touch, D: Conc, T: Ind. Brass the smith touches turns supple and can be reshaped, though not joined, so the pieces must still be cut out with care; in skilled hands it gives work of great intricacy and beauty. ReTe 15 (base 4, +1 Touch, +1 Conc, +1 intricacy), a Lesser Power of 15 levels, -2 Might cost.

Story seeds:
To Learn the Craft: a Verditius magus wants the brass-smiths' secret and urges a character to be initiated into the guild, which means convincing its elders their Mystery will not be spread abroad.

details.rules: Loyalty to the guild, and its secret kept.

neighbours.name: Persia
neighbours.summary:
The lands from the Tigris east to the Oxus: a high plateau some four or five thousand feet up, ringed by the Alborz in the north and the Zagros in the south and west, seven parts in ten of it desert or waste. Only the Gulf coast below the Zagros and the Caspian shore, a little under sea level, lie low. The plateau's rivers find no sea and die in sand or marsh, so the farmers, most of them tenants sharing their harvest with landlords who live in the towns, depend on qanats, underground channels that want constant, skilled upkeep. The Lurs of the Zagros and the Ghuzz of Khurasan are its chief nomads.

Its people speak Parsi, a tongue unlike the region's other languages; Arabic keeps its place in religion, but most secular books are now written in Persian, and Turkish dialects have spread among the Ghuzz and the Lurs since the Seljuks. The provinces are held by atabegs, once the tutors of Seljuk princes and now princes in their own right, or by mamluks, slave soldiers set over a land as the sultan's direct servants; nearly all have sworn to the Khwarazm-shah.

The Seljuks held Persia for almost two hundred years, an empire of two halves with a sultan of Khurasan in the east. That sultanate ended in 1149, when the Shansabani broke Seljuk rule there with Infernal help; the Ghuzz, settled in Persia as soldiers, rose in Khurasan in 1151 and held Sultan Ahmed Sanjar prisoner for more than three years. Tekish of Khwarazm rose on the empire's decline and beat Togril III in 1194; his son is the shah of 1220.

Besides the Order of Suleiman, whose sahirs are in every city, five supernatural powers matter here: the yatus, the mobeds, the Nizari Isma'ilis, the Ghuzz and the Shansabani, with the peris and pairikas all over the land. The Shahnameh, Ferdowsi's tenth-century Epic of Kings, is its people's own story, from the making of the world and the first crafts through the heroes Saum, Zal and Rostam to Alexander, the Sasanids and the Arab conquest. A fine illuminated copy, in Parsi and often seven volumes long, is a summa of Persian Lore at level 4, Quality 12, and can be read as four tractatus, on Magic, Faerie, Divine and Infernal Lore, of Quality 10 each.

Zahhak, the demon king of the heroic age who sawed Jamshid in two and ruled a thousand years from Ctesiphon until the hero Feridun ended his reign, is not one man but whoever the demon Azi Dahak possesses: a black snake grows from each of the host's shoulders, regrows when cut, and hungers for human brains. The demon first drives his host to evil and then corrupts him with promises until he learns the Goetic Arts; no host has yet resisted. Persian sahirs have fought several Zahhaks since; the last was the Shansabani sultan Mohammed al-Ghuri, beaten fourteen years ago, and some sahirs fear Genghis Khan is, or is counselled by, another.

The disease rishtah, which the Latins call dracunculus, is common in Khurasan under Mars: worms in a limb whose hot poison swells and paralyses it, most often a leg (Lame until cured), sometimes an arm or an eye. It is a Serious Choleric disease of Severity 12, Stable 4, Recovery 18, with an interval of a month. The Ghuzz cure it by burying the limb in hot sand from dawn to dusk, and the worm that creeps out sometimes lives on to become an olghoi khorkhoi.

links.note: the corpse-flies of the nasu spirit

neighbours.name: Fars
neighbours.summary:
The cradle of the Achaemenid and Sasanid dynasties, which gave its old name, Parsa, Hellenised as Persis, to the whole land. It is an atabegate of the Salghurids, who rule from Shiraz. Its climate splits it in two: the Garmsir, the hot lowlands by the Gulf, and the Sardsir, the cold uplands to the north; the desert of Mandistan lies in its south-west. Its five great cities are Arranjan, Shiraz, Darabgerd, Istakhr and Shapur. The Nizaris keep hidden communities in the southern Zagros here, among them the fortress of Shardiz.

Story seeds:
The Well of Hindijan: treasure-hunters have spent many fruitless nights at Hindijan seeking a hoard rumoured there; a certain well draws them, but its fumes kill birds that fly over it, and no one has yet gone down.

neighbours.name: Jibal
neighbours.summary:
The Arabs' 'mountains', ruled by the Zagros, which cross its southern quarter from north-west to south-east. Its four great cities, Hamadan, Qazvin, Kirmanshah and Isfahan, have each housed a dynasty or a conqueror in their turn, and Isfahan, the largest, has always done well. South of Hamadan the Lurs, half nomads, herd goats in the emirate of Luristan. The Khurasan Road runs through it from Baghdad by Kirmanshah, Hamadan and Rayy and on through the Caspian Gates into Qumis.

It is one of Persia's most crowded provinces and has sahirs to match: one is often seen borne through the air on a whirlwind of a jinni's making, or on one of Isfahan's flying carpets. The Vulture Hills and the Black Hills west of Isfahan, Kargas Kuh and Siyah Kuh, are the plain's highest and grimmest peaks and a robbers' haunt; between them the caravanserai of Dayr al-Jiss keeps four great tanks filled, by the sultan's order, for those crossing the Dasht-i Kavir.

neighbours.name: Khuzistan
neighbours.summary: Persia's oldest settled land, the Elam of Babylon's day, lying in the basin of the Karun, which comes down from the Zagros. Its well-watered plains grow sugar cane, and its rivers, all of them navigable, have been cut into canals for fields and towns. Lurs roam its north. A Ghuzz atabeg of the Hazarasp family, sworn to the Khwarazm-shah, rules it from Ahwaz.

neighbours.name: Kirman
neighbours.summary: Part of Persia on paper, nearly independent in fact. The Ghuzz crossed the desert and took it some fifty years ago, but their rule fell apart, since no Ghuzz will be ruled, and they have joined the Khwarazm-shah's army, which now occupies the province. It is mostly steppe and half desert, known for oranges, dates and pistachios, and shelters several Mazdean communities who keep their heads down after past persecution. The Jabal Kufs, south of the Dasht-i Lut, take up a quarter of it and are the Balu's country. Bardasir and Sirjan are its trading towns.

neighbours.name: Daylam
neighbours.summary: Highlands lying across Gilan and Mazandaran, a country of their own in all but name. In the tenth century Daylam held Gilan, Tabaristan, Gurgan and Qumis; now those are ruled apart and Daylam is a people more than a place. The Alborz cut it off from the plateau, and its fiercely independent folk held out against Sasanids and Arabs and were among the last Persians to take Islam. Zoroastrianism is still fairly strong here, living uneasily beside the Isma'ilis, whose fifty castles in Daylam are led by Alamut; Maimun-Diz is the strongest and Lamasar the most remote.

neighbours.name: Qumis
neighbours.summary: A province in the eastern Alborz, south of Tabaristan. Damghan, its chief town, is about the only place in it the Isma'ilis do not hold, and its emir lives besieged in his own land, treading softly with subjects any of whom may be a Nizari. The sect runs Qumis from the mountain fortress of Girdkuh. The road from Rayy to Nishapur crosses it through the Caspian Gates.

neighbours.name: The Great Desert
neighbours.summary: Al-Mafazah, the Wilderness: Persia's dry heart, which is in truth two deserts, the Dasht-i Kavir in the north and the Dasht-i Lut in the south. No province owns it. Outlaws shelter there, and apart from its three oases (Garmah, Naband and Sanij) nobody lives in it for good. The roads across it have domed water tanks every three or four leagues, which merchants do well to keep filled, and both deserts are full of jinn.

links.note: the death worm under the sand

neighbours.name: Makran
neighbours.summary: The coast towards Al-Sind, named for its fish-eaters (mahi khoran) and thinly peopled in fishing villages. Its capital Fannazbur is poor beside the cities of the other provinces, and the port of Tiz is a halt between Al-Sind and Fars. The caliphs and the kings of Al-Sind once fought over it, and the war elephants taken from Al-Sind went into the Persian army. Bands of Ghuzz left from the invasion of Kirman still roam it.

neighbours.name: Khurasan
neighbours.summary: The greatest province of Persia, the land where the sun (khor) rises. Long a sultanate of its own, it is now firmly part of the Khwarazm-shah's empire; Seistan, Quhistan and Ghur are its districts, not provinces. Merv, Nishapur, Herat and Mashhad are its great cities. The Karakum, the black sand or Desert of the Ghuzz, lies between the Caspian and the Aral Sea, bounded on the north-east by the Oxus.

neighbours.name: Seistan
neighbours.summary:
Low country round and east of Lake Zarah, into which several great rivers drain. The Shahnameh calls it Zabulistan, home of Zal and of his son Rostam, a giant of a hero. Many Ghuzz live here. Its capital is Zaranj; Dartal in the Zamin-Dawar guards the passes into Ghur.

Rostam was so huge that the Simurgh had to teach his father to cut him from his mother; his stallion Rakhsh could carry him, kill a lion and outrun any horse. In Rostam's Seven Quests he rescues his king from the demons of Mazandaran and ends by fighting the White Demon, the Div-e Sepid; in Rostam and Sohrab he kills his own son unknowing; and he died by the treachery of the king he served. Any Persian knows the tale; its details want an Area Lore. Rostam's descendants carry Mythic Blood (the catalog's general Virtue): a short-lived +3 to one athletic, riding or swimming action of their choosing, a Minor Focus in harming supernatural creatures, the Reckless Flaw, and often Large or Giant Blood.

neighbours.name: Quhistan
neighbours.summary: The 'land of the mountains' east of the Great Desert, between Khurasan and Seistan: a cool highland unlike the lands about it. It is a dependency of Khurasan on paper and part of the hidden Isma'ili state in fact; the Nizaris hold its mountain castles: Tabas, Qa'in, Birjand, Turshiz, Muminabad, Nih and Dara.

neighbours.name: Ghur
neighbours.summary:
Mountains whose people are kin to the Baluchi and to the folk of Bactria and Badakhshan more than to the Persians. When the Khwarazm-shah drove the Shansabani out, their familiar demons and evil spirits stayed: malicious jinn haunt its roads, demons walk its towns in human shape, and the Ghurs watch even their own kin for any strange behaviour. In some towns the demons rule openly and the people cannot stop them. No new ruler has replaced the vanished Shansabani; Bamiyan, Firuzkuh and Ghazni were their three capitals.

Rostam's tiger skin, which he wore over his armour and slept in, is held by the emir of Ghur. It adds +5 to Soak on top of any armour, with a Load of 1, and lets its owner recover long-term Fatigue from any night's sleep, however hard or cold the ground; but he sleeps so deeply that waking him takes a Stamina roll of 9, and he is at -1 to all he does until sunrise, unless he spends a Confidence point. Joined with his mace (in Samarkand's Shahr-i-Zindah) and his bones (in the tower at Zaranj), it is said to rouse the hero for a while to defend Persia; a quest in Rostam's tale in Elysium may point the way to both.

neighbours.name: The Khwarazm-shah
neighbours.summary:
Ala al-Din Muhammad, Sultan Mohammed II, son of Tekish, the mamluk ruler of Khwarazm who brought the Seljuks down in 1194. He went on with his father's conquest of the Seljuk lands and named himself their shah in 1205, a title the caliph has never granted; he broke the Shansabani in Khurasan in 1206, added Transoxiana in 1212, and beat the faerie Qara Khitai in 1218. His empire now runs from the Jaxartes to the Gulf, with twin capitals at Samarkand and Gurganj, and most of Persia's atabegs and mamluks have sworn to him. Kirman is under his army's occupation; the House of Healing at Gundeshapur keeps his favour.

In 1218 his cousin Inalchuq, governor of Otrar, put to death a whole Mongol trade caravan with its envoy; when Genghis Khan's ambassadors met the shah at Samarkand, he had them killed or shaved, a mortal insult, and sent back. As 1220 begins the Khan's horde is before Bukhara.

If history holds: Bukhara, Otrar, Samarkand and Gurganj fall in 1220, and the shah, hunted across Khurasan, dies on the Caspian shore at the year's end. In 1221 the Mongols sack Balkh, Merv, Nishapur and Herat, and his son Jalal al-Din is driven over the Indus; the Mongols take eastern Persia by 1227 and western Persia between 1230 and 1240.

neighbours.name: Salghurid Atabeg of Fars
neighbours.summary: The Salghurid dynasty, Turkish atabegs who hold Fars from Shiraz. The book names none of them. Like most of Persia's provincial lords they owe the Khwarazm-shah their oath, and Shiraz is their capital.

neighbours.name: Ghuzz Atabeg of Khuzistan
neighbours.summary: An atabeg of the Ghuzz family of Hazarasp, ruling Khuzistan from Ahwaz under an oath of loyalty to the Khwarazm-shah. The book gives no name.

neighbours.name: Arranjan
neighbours.summary: The westernmost of Fars's five great cities, on the south bank of the Tab, which divides Fars from Khuzistan; date palms and olive groves ring it, and it is known for soap and bitumen. Isma'ili strongholds have long crowned the hills about it, and the Isma'ilis have lately taken the city itself. Hindijan, on the lower Tab, is its port.

neighbours.name: The Well of Hindijan
neighbours.summary: A well at Hindijan, Arranjan's port, where treasure hunters have wasted many nights looking for a hoard said to be hidden in the town. Its poisonous fumes kill any bird that flies over it, so it drops in, and for the same reason nobody has yet gone down it.

neighbours.name: Darabgerd
neighbours.summary:
A round city founded by a family from Daylam, quietly Isma'ili in sympathy though it has never said so. Near it is the Kubbat al-Mumiya, the Bitumen Dome, shut by an iron door; each year the sultan's officer comes, unlocks it and boxes up the bitumen gathered since, for the court.

Story seeds:
Summoner's Salts: a sahir given a princely store of the salt of seven colours suddenly calls far greater jinn, but the salt is tainted to addict them, his jinni wants ever more, and his benefactor's favours grow larger; he needs a way out, and to expose the giver.

neighbours.name: The Hill of the Seven-Coloured Salt
neighbours.summary:
A hill near Darabgerd where rock salt of seven colours is now and then dug out.

Vis: the salt is Dedicated Vis (Realms of Power: Magic) for summoning jinn, who love it: each pawn counts as two when summoning a jinni, though not other spirits. The book gives no yearly amount. Princes keep the salt workings in their own hands and use the salt to woo or reward sahirs.

neighbours.name: Kajaran
neighbours.summary:
A small, well-off town near the Gulf, home of the Kajarani worms, an odd Beast of Virtue that can be Enriched while alive. Kept alone in a dark box for a season and fed twelve mulberry leaves a day, each folded into a pellet, a worm gives Luck to whoever fed it (it dies if two people feed it). Enriched again each year it grows, to a mouse's size and Puissant (an Ability), then a cat's and Venus' Blessing, then a dog's and Wealthy, the Virtues adding up and all lost if it dies; but in its third year its keeper cannot refuse its comforts (Compulsion) and in its fourth it begins to repel him (Fear). A worm eats any other worm it meets, and nobody in Kajaran lets one see a fifth year.

They remember Haftvad, a peasant who let his worm grow seven years into a gleaming black dragon patterned in saffron, and rode his luck to rule from Basra to Kirman, beating the first Sasanid, Ardeshir, until Ardeshir killed the elephant-sized beast with boiling lead. Haftvad's fortress still stands, hidden high in the mountains.

neighbours.name: Istakhr
neighbours.summary:
The seat of Fars's northern district, the Persepolis of the Greeks, and once Takht-e Jamshed, the capital of Jamshid, the Shahnameh's fourth king of the world: a great sorcerer who ruled every jinni and gave men armour, weaving and dyeing, masonry, wine and ships, until pride drove off the royal farr, Ahura Mazda's shining blessing, and Zahhak murdered him. Buildings of Jamshid's and Solomon's day stand in and around the city. Rice and pomegranate villages crowd the shore of Lake Bakhtigan near by; on the hills to the north-west the Sih Gundaban, three great fortresses, guard a dam in a deep gorge that holds a year's water for a thousand besieged men, and a drill ground on a flat hilltop.

The Jaam-e Jam, the Cup of Jamshid, of silver with seven bands of gold and jewels, lay hidden in Istakhr from the Arab conquest until a sahir found it a few years ago. Filled with an elixir of long life (al-Iksir, say, or a longevity potion) brewed new for its user, it works for one season and spends the elixir: its holder names any place in the world and sees it in the cup, as Summoning the Distant Image does but with no Arcane Connection, and its views of the heavens double his Artes Liberales for astrology and his Solomonic Astrology for magic.

Story seeds:
The Spying Sahir: the sahir who has the Cup of Jamshid uses it to spy on his neighbours, the characters perhaps among them, and sees a respected citizen doing something monstrous; unable to say how he knows, he steers the characters by what he knows of them.
neighbours.secrets: The sahir who found the cup uses it to pry on neighbours and rivals (the troupe perhaps among them); the book does not name him.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Kamfiruz
neighbours.summary: An oak wood amid pastures between Shiraz and Istakhr, by the town of Bayda, whose fierce lions are the terror of the herds grazing round it. The local emir has begun to hunt them down.

neighbours.name: Kish
neighbours.summary:
The island that is the Gulf's chief port, about twelve miles out, under a great walled city. It is famous for its pearls and crowded with the trade of Arabia, Africa and Al-Sind, which goes over to Huzu on the mainland and north to Shiraz. It has risen over the last century since Siraf, the old port further west, was ruined by an earthquake that went on for seven days.

Pirates from Abarkavan, the Long Island, prey on its traders and on the divers of its pearl banks, to its emir's fury; one of them is an elementalist (Hedge Magic) who plays with wind and wave.

neighbours.name: Shiraz
neighbours.summary:
The capital of Fars and of the Salghurids, made the empire's capital by the Buyids (945 to 1055), who filled it with palaces, mosques and a great wall. It is now the Dar al-Elm, the House of Knowledge, for its academies and its schools of famous poets; sitting at the middle of Fars, it takes most of the province's trade through narrow, packed markets, and it has three great mosques.

Story seeds:
The Imamzadihs of Shiraz: two rival shrines, one healing limbs and one feet, compete for an emir with an abscessed foot; witnesses to their cures are caught in riots, and the emir may ask the characters which shrine will heal him.

neighbours.name: The Imamzadihs of Shiraz
neighbours.summary:
Shiraz's many shrines to the imamzadihs, kin and descendants of the twelve Shi'i imams. Each grants its own miracle, most often the cure of a given complaint, a husband or wife, or an easy birth, and they compete for pilgrims. The shrine of the fourth imam's brother, on the Street of Butchers, has baraka for hurt limbs; the shrine of the sixth imam's daughter, beside the main square, for every trouble of the feet; and the two are bitter rivals.

The book gives no aura; the shrines take the city's 4.

neighbours.name: Shapur
neighbours.summary: The City of Flowers, which sends out irises, violets, jasmine and narcissus and above all its red rose. It makes ten scented oils from them; its attar of roses is dear enough to reach the courts of England and France.

neighbours.name: The Black Man
neighbours.summary: A forty-foot statue of a man in black stone in a cave near Shapur, three carved leaves at its feet; behind it a waterfall, and a wind that never stops blowing out of the cave. Some say it is King Shapur, others a real man God turned to stone. The old kings anointed it with oil; nobody has honoured it for centuries.
neighbours.secrets: The statue is a great div, one of the forty-five named demons (which one is unknown), bound in it long ago by a mobed. Knowing his binding would not last forever, he made the leaves green, to fade as it wore off; each anointing came with a mobed's blessing that renewed it. Under Muslim rule the rite was banned as idolatry, and only a tenth of one leaf is still green: the demon is nearly free.

neighbours.name: Yazd
neighbours.summary: The stronghold of the Mazdean faith since Islam came, and one of the few places it is still openly kept. The city is well walled, with two iron gates on the Istakhr road, and the streams from the near mountains make it so fertile, this close to the Great Desert, that it seems a paradise; the mobeds get the credit. The six pirs, mountain shrines of the Zoroastrian villages, are near by.

neighbours.name: Isfahan
neighbours.summary: Jibal's largest city, on the north bank of the Zayandah, which rises in the Zagros, sinks into the Gav-Khanah swamp on the edge of the Dasht-i Kavir, and comes up again ninety leagues off in Kirman. It is two towns: Jay to the east, inside a wall of a hundred towers, and Al-Yahudiyah to the west, where Jews have lived since Nebuchadnezzar. Ibn Sina, the Latins' Avicenna, lived and taught here. It sells silk, cotton, saffron and every fruit, but its carpets are what it is famous for: an Isfahan rug has an ivory field with one central medallion among leaves and vines, in blues, rose and indigo dyed by methods its weavers keep secret.

neighbours.name: Kirmanshah
neighbours.summary: The seat of Kurdistan, a half-independent province Sultan Sanjar made for his nephew about 1150, with a great mosque and a splendid palace. A day's march east the rock of Bustam bears carvings of Darius taking his vassal kings' tribute and, far later, of Khusraw Parviz and Queen Shirin, whose sculptor Farhad killed himself for love of her. On the road east lies Kanguvar, which the Arabs call the Robbers' Castle for good reason.

neighbours.name: Qum
neighbours.summary: After Mashhad perhaps Persia's holiest place for Muslims: the tomb of Fatima, Imam Reza's sister, with the ninth imam's three daughters beside her. Reza promised Paradise to whoever made the pilgrimage to her. The mosque of Jam Karan lies a few miles east.

neighbours.name: The Mosque of Jam Karan
neighbours.summary: A mosque a few miles east of Qum, on holy ground. In 986 the hidden Imam and al-Khidr appeared to Hassan ibn Muthih and bade him build here, and the mosque he raised has hardly an equal in Persia for its building and adornment. Its Divine aura is 7.

neighbours.name: Rayy
neighbours.summary: A strong city whose five gates open on five roads, to Qum, Hamadan, Qazvin, Mazandaran and Khurasan. The inner city, with the mosque and the officials' houses, is ditched round; the outer city rings and overlooks it, with a busy fruit market of melons, peaches and apricots. It sells blue-dyed cotton, striped cloth above all, and hardwood from the Mazandaran forests.

neighbours.name: The Shrine of Shahr Banu
neighbours.summary:
A shrine on a mountain near Rayy to Shahr Banu, a Sasanid princess and the fourth Shi'i imam's mother, whom the mountain swallowed, they say, sooner than let her enemies kill her. For centuries before, the place was a shrine of Anahita, the Mazdean yazata of water and fertility. The book gives it no aura.

Vis: Aquam, in the water of the shrine's spring, when it is drawn while Venus is in the sky; the book gives no amount.

neighbours.name: Savah
neighbours.summary: A town of camel-drivers and herdsmen whose great mosque holds the finest magical library in Persia. A hospital and a tall domed tower adjoin the mosque: the tower has the library below and the observatory at the top, and Savah's house of wisdom, every member of it of the Followers of the Star, keeps both.

neighbours.name: Ahwaz
neighbours.summary: Khuzistan's capital, beset by jinn: they make its days unbearably hot and fill its nights with biting flies, the water jinn crashing over its weir keep newcomers awake, and snakes and scorpions swarm in the fields about it. An alchemist here claims he can make gold of base metal, if only he had a few magical ingredients, above all the wood the Zagros griffins gather for their nests.

neighbours.name: Gundeshapur
neighbours.summary: The town of the House of Healing, the great medical school and hospital founded by the sahir Bakhtyshu, a Nestorian of Harun's council, and still run by his descendants; the Seljuk sultans paid for it and the Khwarazm-shah holds it in honour. It is also the town's largest house of wisdom.

neighbours.name: Ramhurmuz
neighbours.summary:
A rich town living on silk and perfume, with a modest library. Its sahirs once took in one of the famous sorcerers of Soqotra, who studied with them for some years and, too trusting, gave away much of his island's lore, among it many perfume recipes, which the sahirs turned into a thriving trade. Seeing he had been cheated, he left, and cursed the district: every year gnats and biting midges swarm over it.

South-east of the town, near Fars, is the district of the Zutt.

neighbours.name: Bardasir
neighbours.summary: A trading city between western Persia and Khurasan. The governor's palace sits in green gardens on a very tall hill outside it, a second fortress guards the gate and a third looks down on the houses from the middle of the town; for all that the Ghuzz sacked it, and Sirjan has since outgrown it.

neighbours.name: Jiruft
neighbours.summary:
A city on the Div Rud, the Demon River, which runs so hard that waterwheels all over the town drive the working of indigo, cotton and grain. Lions from the forests about it hold the city under siege; anyone coming must pass through the dark woods, and its trade has dwindled to a trickle these last years.

Story seeds:
The Lion-Shah: the jinni who rules Jiruft's lions asks the characters to protect the lions of Kamfiruz from the emir hunting them and bring them to Jiruft, offering his thanks and the lions' in return.

neighbours.name: The Forest of Jiruft
neighbours.summary: The woods round Jiruft, whose lions a jinni, the lion-shah, took for his own about ten years ago. His glamour, spread over the forest, has given it a Faerie aura, and the lions have been a little Warped by it. The book gives no strength; 3 is assumed.

neighbours.name: Mazandaran
neighbours.summary:
The lands between the Caspian and the Alborz: Gilan, with Daylam to its south, Tabaristan (its chief city Amul) and Gurgan, whose capital shares its name. The Arabs never took it, kept out by the mountains and by its old Mazdean nobility; the Bavand family held it for two hundred years, until the Nizari Isma'ilis brought them down in 1125, and the Nizaris rule its politics now. It is the ancient Hyrcania, the land of the tigers: hot, wet and very fertile, blessed by Ahura Mazda in the Zoroastrians' eyes, with houses built of wood rather than brick and a famous hardwood, khalanj. Its old demons are those Rostam fought, the White Demon among them.

Three groups of magicians fight over it: the mobeds of Daylam, one of Zoroastrianism's last strongholds; the Nizaris in their Alborz castles, whose faith seeks to win every man and be rid of those who refuse; and the yatus of Mount Damavand. None will ever agree with the others: yatus and Nizaris fight over vis, mobeds and Nizaris over the local rulers, and the mobeds loathe the yatus as pagans and, they suppose, devil-worshippers.

Hyrcanian vis. Vis is plentiful here: the yatus say Damavand is the source of all vis in the world, the mobeds that it is Ahura Mazda's gift. It gathers in whatever is odd or single: the one white egg among a hen's brown ones, the ear of wheat with thirteen grains, the driftwood furthest along the shore. A character may hunt for it, chasing rumours and dead ends through a land the size of a small county for a season: Perception + Area Lore: Mazandaran + a die against 9 finds a pawn, and each point over either adds a pawn or halves the time (both may be had; beating it by 8 might give five pawns in eleven days). To the roll add one of the magnitude of a vis-finding spell's Target or Magic Sensitivity; a Realm Lore, no higher than the Mazandaran Lore (with any Lore but Magic Lore, half the vis found, rounded up, is tainted by that realm); and the aura, if the whole search lies in a Magic aura. Ground searched in the last season costs -15, in the last six months -9, in the last year -3, whoever searched it; the storyguide may raise the Ease Factor where magicians or magical beings are thick. Elsewhere the same roll may be used with that land's Lore against 12 in wilds, 15 in settled country and 18 in a city, for less. It finds no renewable sources, which come from stories; most sahirs of the region, yatu or Nizari, find or are given a Personal Vis Source early on.

Suggested vis sources (not in the book), for the storyguide to use, change or ignore, each found by a story and not by the roll: the thirteenth hen's egg laid each spring in a Daylami village where hens lay twelve (Animal, 2 pawns); the single white flower that opens on a khalanj tree in a Tabaristan valley each midsummer (Herbam, 3 pawns); and the piece of driftwood that comes ashore furthest up the beach after the first autumn storm (Aquam, 2 pawns).

links.note: the earth jinni of a quarried cave
the swift tigers that hunt its gazelles

neighbours.name: Gurgan
neighbours.summary: The capital of Gurgan, the westernmost province of Mazandaran, near the Caspian end of the great wall that bears its name.

neighbours.name: Mount Damavand
neighbours.summary: The mountain that towers over all Tabaristan, its snowy peak seen for hundreds of miles across Persia's plains. The Simurgh nests here, and the tyrant Zahhak is thought to lie imprisoned beneath it. On its lower slopes are seven settlements, each with its own house of wisdom of sahirs mostly of yatu descent: closed houses, which take no other sahirs, kept by the pagan yatus apart from the Order's other families. The yatus guard an Initiation Script for a Major Focus against the enemies of Persia; the rite works only within the Wall of Gurgan's aligned aura.

links.note: the great bird of the mountain

neighbours.secrets: The first Zahhak was not killed by Feridun: with an angel's help he was chained and buried under the mountain. The demon has long since left him, but he lives on there, kept from death by the holy bonds, an ancient survivor of the heroic age who might teach something to those facing a new Zahhak.

neighbours.name: Baghl's Cave
neighbours.summary:
A dark cave in the Elburz, once quarried until its jinni, Baghl, drove the miners away. He asks chiefly to be left with his lovely rock formations, though he will sometimes talk with scholars of theology. As a spirit of the place, the cave is an Arcane Connection to him (+1 to the Penetration multiplier). The book gives it no aura; 3 is assumed.

Vis: 1 pawn of Terram a year, as a quartz-crusted stalactite at the back of the cave.

neighbours.name: The Great Wall of Gurgan
neighbours.summary:
A vast rampart from the Caspian's east shore east and north to the Pishkamar Mountains, more than 120 miles long, with 35 forts about every 30 miles: red brick, 25 feet thick and some 20 high, strengthened with steel and adamantine (an unbreakable metal some magicians make from diamond), with a canal down its middle the whole way. A Magic aura of 5 runs all along it. Alexander built it, the story goes (so it is also the Sadd-i-Iksandar), to keep the children of Gog and Magog out of Persia; yet the Ghuzz came in a century ago, and were asked to stay.

Perhaps that is because of the breach at the fort nearest the Gates of Alexander, the wall's western end by the Caspian. Since it was found, the local sahirs have noticed that the wall's aura alignment (Realms of Power: Magic), which gave spells aimed at giants twice the usual aura bonus, is gone. Anyone who looks can see the gap was made on purpose and held open by magic that is not Solomonic. Mazandaran's sahirs care little: the Ghuzz do not threaten them.

Story seeds:
Sealing the Breach: to meet a danger to Persia, the Mongols, a Zahhak or something unseen, the characters seek the yatus of Damavand's initiation into a Focus against Persia's enemies, which works only in the Wall of Gurgan's aura; first they must mend the deliberate breach in the wall and face whatever made it.

neighbours.name: Alamut
neighbours.summary:
The Nizaris' chief castle and the seat of their grand master, in Rudbar, the valley of the Shahrud. A king of Daylam, out hunting, saw his eagle settle on the rock and built a castle there named aluh-amut, the eagle's lesson; it has grown into a fortified village. The rock rises sheer on every side to a flat top crowded with buildings, with storerooms cut into the bedrock and a spring of its own. Amid the dust and stone lies a lavish garden, which gives the fortress its Magic aura of 3 and holds a way into the Magic Realm, where the Nizaris' initiates are taken to a paradise insula.

The sect's other named castles: in Daylam, among fifty, Maimun-Diz (the strongest) and Lamasar (the most remote); in Quhistan, Turshiz, Qa'in, Birjand, Muminabad, Dara, Tabas and Nih; in Qumis, Girdkuh; in the Zagros of Fars, Shardiz. Arranjan and the hills round it are theirs too.

Hasan-i Sabbah, a sahir of Nishapur, fled here after he murdered his boyhood friend Nizam al-Mulk, the Seljuk vizier and grand vizier of the Order of Suleiman, and it was here that Nizar's followers took refuge after the Isma'ili schism.

neighbours.name: Maimun-Diz
neighbours.summary: The strongest of the fifty Nizari castles of Daylam.

neighbours.name: Girdkuh
neighbours.summary: The great Nizari mountain stronghold from which the sect runs Qumis. It takes a toll from everyone who passes, for it sits on the only road from western Persia to Khurasan that does not cross the Great Desert.

neighbours.name: Damghan
neighbours.summary: The chief town of Qumis and nearly the only one there the Isma'ilis do not hold. Its emir rules a province that besieges him, never sure which of his subjects is a Nizari.

neighbours.name: The Caspian Gates
neighbours.summary: Sirdara to the Persians: the endless narrow gorge through which the road from Rayy to Nishapur crosses the mountains of Qumis. Carts go in single file between sheer cliffs, slowed further by water streaming down the rock and by the swarms of snakes that infest it; merchants still prefer it to the Great Desert.

neighbours.name: The Dasht-i Kavir
neighbours.summary:
The salt desert of the north, about 500 miles from west to east and 200 from north to south. Its middle is almost rainless, but it has marshes, wadis and stretches like steppe, and a great salt lake in the west, and many birds, sand grouse and great bustards, besides the Persian gazelle and the Hyrcanian tigers that hunt it.

Its oases: Garmah, halfway between Isfahan and Tabas, three hamlets round a small fort, with palms and pasture, whose emir must keep the desert roads open; and Naband, between Kirman and Quhistan, whose guard house does not stop desert raiders hiding in its domed water tanks.

neighbours.name: The Rig-i Jinn
neighbours.summary: Dunes in the middle of the Dasht-i Kavir where a tribe of jinn lives, mischievous more than malicious; the caravans go round. Its Faerie aura of 3 is the tribe's own glamour and moves with them. Travellers who meet them see a green oasis where none should be, and are fed or wounded as the jinn please; either way the oasis moves while they are in it, and when the jinn draw off the travellers may be tens of leagues from where they began.

neighbours.name: The Dasht-i Lut
neighbours.summary: The 'emptiness desert' of the south, some 300 miles along its north-west to south-east line and 200 across: salt flats on a low plateau in the east, mostly sand in the south-east, and far less life than the Kavir. Its oasis Sanij, in a valley joining Kirman to Seistan, is home to many people, whom the Balu raiders who know it well never leave in peace.

neighbours.name: The Gandom Beriyan
neighbours.summary:
The 'toasted wheat': the middle of the Dasht-i Lut, a volcanic waste of black lava cut by ravines and sinkholes and scoured by a fierce wind, the hottest place in Persia and empty of any plant or beast. The cruellest of the jinn tribes live here, in an Infernal aura of 4 tainted with a Debauched aura of exhaustion, so no one may spend Confidence while in it.

Few come willingly: it is a place of Infernal pilgrimage, where a villain may be chased before he gives himself further to Hell; those fleeing the Balu may blunder in, and be saved by their pursuers, who would not feed the land more victims than they must; and as the hottest spot on earth it may serve a Mystery's initiation, or the forging or unmaking of a thing of power.

Story seeds:
Why Go to Hell?: few go willingly to Gandom Beriyan: to catch a villain before he gives himself fully to Hell, by blundering in while fleeing the Balu (who may then rescue them), or to forge or unmake an item of power, or for a mystery's initiation, in the hottest place on earth.

levels.name: The burning heart
levels.notes: A Tartaran regio at the waste's centre, where the air burns and the rock runs molten; one of the mightiest corrupt jinn of Persia lurks in it.

neighbours.name: The Gedrosian Desert
neighbours.summary: The arid coast of Makran, the ancients' Gedrosia, famous for being all but impassable; it beat the armies of Cyrus, of Queen Semiramis and at last of Alexander's unbeaten veterans, and only scattered fisherfolk live on it. It is full of pagan ghosts, soldiers of every army that has died trying to cross it since antiquity. As restless dead they answer necromancers and other summoners readily, but most are so lost in despair and the memory of want that they can say little of use about their past.

neighbours.name: Zaranj
neighbours.summary:
Seistan's capital, on a branch of the Helmund, so near Lake Zarah in flood time that the swelling lake almost reaches it. A walled inner town is ringed by outer suburbs; above-ground channels bring water to every house, and nearly every house has a cellar where its people live through the stifling summer. Salt marshes, drowned each year when the lake rises, lie round it, and sand beyond them. From early summer into autumn the baad sad va bist rooz, the wind of 120 days, blows from north to south, wrapping the land in dust; some think jinn live in it.

Story seeds:
Rostam Roused: Rostam's tiger skin is the emir of Ghur's, his mace lies forgotten in a tomb of Samarkand's Shahr-i-Zindah, and bringing both to his body may wake the hero for a time to defend Persia; with the Mongols coming, Persian sahirs may try, and a tale of Rostam in Elysium may give clues.
neighbours.secrets: The 120-day wind is a host of air elementals (Realms of Power: Magic) on their yearly migration, playing as they pass.

neighbours.name: Rostam's Tower
neighbours.summary: A fluted tower in Zaranj with no door, stair or any way up. The bones of Rostam and his horse Rakhsh are thought to lie on its top: their bodies were laid out to sun and vultures in the Zoroastrian way, the bones never gathered, and the tower sealed as their monument. Brought together with his tiger skin and his mace, the bones are said to wake the hero from his death-like sleep for a time, to stride out once more in Persia's defence.

neighbours.name: Dartal
neighbours.summary: The city of the Zamin-Dawar, the Land of Gates, named for the passes into Ghur; it keeps a strong garrison of horse guards against the warlike Ghurs beyond the mountains. The flocks of the Zamin-Dawar give Persia much of its wool. The Zur Mountain, near by, once had a shrine to a solid gold idol with ruby eyes, carried off as booty at the Muslim conquest.

neighbours.name: Herat
neighbours.summary:
The Pearl of Khurasan, under the ruins of a citadel of Alexander's. It has changed hands many times in the last hundred years but has built a name for brasswork, still its chief export. The fire temple of Sirishk is two leagues north, with a Nestorian church between it and the city, and south of Herat lies a land as lush as a garden, watered by many canals.

Story seeds:
The Riddles: a ghoul controls the emir of Herat, who has demanded a visitor neither clothed nor bare, neither walking nor riding, to speak to him neither in nor out of doors, or the city falls; whoever solves it must then answer the ghoul's three riddles, and only a killer meeting a string of impossible conditions can slay it.

neighbours.name: Merv
neighbours.summary:
A great oasis city of the Silk Road, 'the meeting place of great and small', whose vast market is said to sell everything. Once it called itself the largest city in the world; but the Ghuzz plundered it in 1153, it has since passed among Khwarazmians, Ghuzz and Ghurids, and Nishapur has taken its place in Khurasan. Sultan Sanjar, the last of the great Seljuks, lies here under a dome of blue tiles so tall it shows a day's march off.

Its libraries are famous. The Great Mosque has two, the 'Aziziyah of over 12,000 books and the Kamaliyah with somewhat fewer; the libraries of the colleges of the Samanidiyah, the 'Umaydiyah and the Khatuniya are kept here too; and the small Dumayriyah's 200 books are priceless, many of them unique. What matters most to the sahirs is Nizam al-Mulk's library, the grand vizier's, now held among Merv's collections, and the town's house of wisdom keeps its books of magic.
neighbours.secrets: Faeries keep stalls in the market beside the townsfolk and help earn Merv its name. They draw their life from trading with mortals but supply nothing themselves: each deal they make is with another mortal who has the thing, so getting anything rare means a chain of favours, each faerie asking for something else, from a pebble with a white spot to the Sasanid king's crown. The trick is to know when to stop.

neighbours.name: Mashhad
neighbours.summary: Mashhad ar-Rizawi, the place of Reza's martyrdom: the city grew round the tomb of the eighth Shi'i imam. The Sunni caliph Mamun surprised everyone by naming Reza his heir, and when Sunnis rose in violence at the news, Reza died suddenly before he could take it up; the Shi'a say Mamun repented and settled the matter by murder. A pilgrimage here is held worth 70,000 to Mecca, and people come from all over Persia.

neighbours.name: The Shrine of Imam Reza
neighbours.summary: The rich shrine over the eighth imam's tomb at Mashhad, the holiest place in Persia for its Muslims. Its Divine aura is 6.

neighbours.name: Nishapur
neighbours.summary: Named for the first Sasanid king, Shapur I, who briefly made it his capital, it commands the way east. Like most Khurasan cities it is ruled by its market, whose streets are lined with merchants' hostels and where almost every trade is found; nearly all the turquoise and malachite that reaches the Middle East and Europe comes from mines near by. Its house of wisdom trained Nizam al-Mulk, Hasan-i Sabbah and 'Umar Khayyam, three friends who swore to share any greatness one of them won: Nizam al-Mulk became vizier of the Seljuks and grand vizier of the Suhhar, 'Umar asked only the means to study, and Hasan, secretly an Isma'ili, took a post to come near his friend and murdered him.
