The Order held its hand at its dying grand vizier's wish. 'Umar Khayyam, astronomer, poet and sahir, later led the house, and died in 1123.

neighbours.name: The Footsteps of Imam Reza
neighbours.summary: Prints in the rocky road all the way from Nishapur to Mashhad, held locally to be the imam's footsteps on his last journey. Whoever walks the whole road setting his own feet in each print is said to be blessed in his next venture; but wear and malicious jinn, who lay false trails, make some prints hard to find. Finishing it should be a short story testing the walker's faith, rewarded with the Intuition Virtue for the length of his next venture.

neighbours.name: Bamiyan
neighbours.summary: A rich city without walls in the east of Ghur, till lately one of the Shansabani's three capitals, from which a branch of the family ruled Bactria and Badakhshan. Its people are unbelievers who honour two great idols on the mountainside.

neighbours.name: The Idols of Bamiyan
neighbours.summary: Two statues cut from the living rock in a pillared chamber high on the mountain above Bamiyan, its walls carved with birds covered in beaten gold. The townsfolk call them Surkh and Khing, Red and Grey, twin faces of one god in their tangled faith. Now and then the idols walk out of their niche, bringing a Faerie aura with them: when Khing walks the people feast it and hang it with flowers, but when Surkh is abroad they hide indoors and shake. The book gives the aura no strength; 3 is assumed.

neighbours.name: Firuzkuh
neighbours.summary: The Ghurids' summer capital, the 'turquoise mountain', for the turquoise (and silver) in its hills. The Shansabani used it as a retreat to hide their wickedness: enemies brought there in secret were drowned in the Hari, and some say it was the heart of their devil-worship. The palace stands empty, haunted by the ghosts of their victims.

neighbours.name: The Minaret of Firuzkuh
neighbours.summary: A minaret of baked brick more than 200 feet high on a bend of the Hari, covered in glazed tiles in alternating bands of Qur'anic verse (from the sura of Maryam, on the mother of Jesus), geometric patterns and calligraphy in several scripts. The jinn of the Hari attack it, and a flash flood has lately swept away the mosque it belonged to, but it stands, warded powerfully against supernatural beings. Sahirs have studied it for years; all they have learnt is that the wards are Divine. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Ghazni
neighbours.summary: Once the capital of the mamluk of Ghur, from which a Shansabani branch ruled Khurasan, and now forsaken by them. Its Bahramshah mosque has star-shaped minarets covered in geometric patterns, and the city is famously rich: even its meanest buildings are decorated, the poorest peasant wears a gold necklace or bracelet, and the great drip with jewels.
neighbours.secrets: Its wealth is a False God's gift, through that demon's Wealth of Nations power (Realms of Power: The Infernal) that the Ghaznians worship in secret.

neighbours.name: Kabul
neighbours.summary: A city much visited by merchants, who climb its one fortified road to trade with the strange merchants of Mythic Hind. The Persians want its indigo, which fetches a high price in the west, and also myrobalan, a greasy, speckled powder spicy like pepper or cardamom that physicians prize for its cures; taken with wine it brings pleasant visions and with water horrible ones, and either way it is ruinously addictive, so the markets are full of its slaves, vacant-eyed and dark of tooth. A demon known only as the Shadowed One rules the city, bound up somehow with the myrobalan trade; no one has seen him, and four lieutenants with demon-given powers govern for him.

neighbours.name: The Yatus
neighbours.summary:
Persia's old sorcerers, wholly secular where the mobeds served the faith, and loathed by the Mazdean priests. Ancient kings kept cadres of them with their armies, and the Greeks' unreadiness for their magic helps explain the early victories of Darius and Xerxes. Most were faerie wizards, said to have invented the Ars Fabulosa (Realms of Power: Faerie), Faerie Summoning and the arts round it, which oral lore traces to Canaanite necromancy, the root of all summoning. Darker, Goetic yatus brought down the mobeds' persecutions that ended Persia's magical warfare.

When the Suhhar was founded, Persia gave it several yatu lineages that had outlived the Mazdean purges and the Arab conquest, and with them came True Names and the Virtue Invocation of Names of Power. Yatus live today in western Persia, Iraq and the north-west provinces; most are sahirs who join Faerie Summoning to the Solomonic arts, Storytelling chief among them, and the rest faerie wizards of the Ars Fabulosa. Faerie blood is common among them, and being often pagan they quarrel with many sahirs and keep to closed houses of their own, such as the seven on Damavand. They fight the Nizaris over vis in Mazandaran, and the mobeds detest them.

neighbours.name: The Ghuzz
neighbours.summary:
Magic-blooded tribesmen from the steppes north of Persia and east of the Caspian, said to descend from Gog and Magog; their giant blood is plain to see. Big, warlike and famously ungovernable, they would be far more dangerous if they could hold together or stay loyal long enough to make an army. They live in many southern provinces, Kirman, Makran and Seistan above all, and breed huge horses; their magic kin ride mounts the size of elephants and sometimes keep eagles as big as a man. Invited in as soldiers, they rebelled in 1151, plundered Merv in 1153 and ruled Kirman for a time; now they serve in the shah's army, and one of their families rules Khuzistan.

Every Ghuzz has the Large Virtue, save those in whom Gog and Magog's blood runs strong, usually their leaders: these are magic kin with Giant Blood and a Greater Immunity to having their minds swayed, by Leadership, Charm, Folk Ken, Inspirational or even Command the Masses, a Greater Power Virtue (Major, Supernatural) common among their chiefs, which makes a group of men strongly inclined to obey one order and lets him lead in battle without spending his turn on it (ReMe 30). Many Ghuzz, kin or not, have the Rebellious Flaw.

neighbours.name: The Shansabani
neighbours.summary:
Ghur's ruling family, who count Zahhak their first forefather. Sultan Ala'uddin Hussain, the World Burner (Jahansoz), took Ghur from the Ghaznavids with his demon patrons' help, and he and his kin held Ghur and then Khurasan in an iron grip, in which troublemakers simply vanished. Their wars looked east to Hind, not west or south, to Persia's luck. Three branches ruled: Bactria and Badakhshan from Bamiyan, Khurasan from Ghazni, and Ghur itself from Firuzkuh.

The last sultan, Mohammed al-Ghuri, was Zahhak's host; a Nizari killed him on the bank of the Indus in 1206 and the Khwarazm-shah forced the family out of Khurasan. They never gave Ghur up, nobody has been named in their place, and they have all disappeared: gone to Mythic Hind, some say, or into hiding. Their demons stayed behind.
neighbours.secrets: One rumour that will not die puts the Shansabani heir at Genghis Khan's court.

neighbours.name: The Zutt
neighbours.summary:
A half-nomad tribe from south-east of Ramhurmuz near the edge of Fars, who say they came from beyond Al-Sind. They travel in brightly painted wagons and dress in vivid silks and deep-dyed linen; they are thought thieves, and the Khuzistanis greet them coldly when they come to trade. Their women are strong folk witches (Hedge Magic). They have been met as far off as Egypt and Samarkand, and some of the Atsingani covenfolk of Provence look much like them. A Zutt family now owns the golden idol of Zur, which has begun walking home to its mountain.

Story seeds:
The Idol of Zur: the golden ruby-eyed idol taken from Mount Zur at the conquest, now owned by a Zutt family, has for years been walking slowly home; the characters meet the family following it, and no one knows what its return will bring.

neighbours.name: The Balu
neighbours.summary: The tribesmen of the Jabal Kufs, much feared by Persians: travellers say they stone their victims so as not to dull their swords, need neither food nor drink, and are as tireless as their war camels. They hate the Ghuzz but count them foes worth their blades, and they raid the oasis of Sanij. They carry strong Jinni Blood and often a Greater Immunity to thirst, ride to raid with their jinn kin beside them, and have wise men versed in Faerie Summoning and Bonding (Realms of Power: Faerie); some war leaders are bonded to a desert or mountain jinni and use its powers.

neighbours.name: The Peris and Pairikas
neighbours.summary:
The peris are Persia's courtly faeries, nearly all female and so lovely that a pretty girl is called peri-faced. They have a lesser nymph's statistics and part (Realms of Power: Faerie), the lover who ensnares, though they seldom rule plants; small male attendants, sprites with brightly coloured birds' wings, sometimes wait on their every whim.

The pairikas are another matter: the Persian name for the Aerial Powers (Realms of Power: The Infernal), demons that sahirs treat as corrupt jinn. They are met all over Persia, mostly as the crushing heat of the desert or the terror of an earthquake.

neighbours.name: The Carpet-Weavers of Isfahan
neighbours.summary:
Isfahan's makers of magical carpets, most of them Touched by Magic (City & Guild): a weaver adds an effect's magnitude and its uses a day to a base Craft Total of 12, can put only effects of two Hermetic Forms into his work, and a carpet works only for the one it was made for.

Dadvand's family has woven flying carpets since the Sasanids and has patrons among the Suhhar; they cost a fortune for the skill they need. His Steed of the Air rises twice a day and carries its owner and all he holds through the air as fast as a running horse (ReAn 15, Ease Factor 16 to make). He weaves other rugs too, such as one whose air of health speeds healing.

Yarankush weaves carpets that guard their owners. His Murderers' Chagrin, woken twice a day, makes a noise of its own for a round whenever anyone but its owner touches it while he lies or sits on it (CrIm 3, Ease Factor 14): a boon to any great man in these days of hidden murder. Since saying you own one defeats its purpose, nobody talks of them.
neighbours.secrets: Yarankush is a Nizari, and weaves into each carpet's design a hidden sign that tells the sect's killers not to step on it.

neighbours.name: The Silk Road
neighbours.summary:
The way to Serica, the land of silk, which is taking shape once more as the century opens: by putting down the endless banditry of the east, the Mongols' invasion, strangely, makes the road safer for merchants and missionaries. It has existed since antiquity, open or shut by turns, and is not one road but a web of caravan stages joined by caravanserais, branching and meeting again through desert, steppe and mountain as the caravans go north-east from Baghdad, through Khurasan and on into Transoxiana, Badakhshan and the Wakhan, past the edge of the Mythic Middle East and into the supernatural realms beyond.

Local rulers keep caravanserais, stone stations with water and a small garrison, a day's journey apart (ten to fifteen miles). Asses, camels, horses or mules carry the goods as the ground allows; great caravans come down from the Volga Bulghars and the northern forests through Merv, Baghdad, Samarkand or Khojend, and go on west by Venetian hands or east by Sogdian ones. Some are towns on the move: Ibn Fadlan saw one of up to 3,000 beasts and 5,000 men. Such a caravan could hide a wandering covenant, or carry a troupe of the region's own.

The Asian elephant is still kept in small numbers in the east, by nobles as a curiosity and by the Khwarazmian army as shock troops; elephants fear nothing that crawls but flee a pig's squeal. Ghosts of ancient war elephants can be called up from their bones on old battlefields across Arabia, Persia and Transoxiana, and the bones of the faerie war elephants of Hind that Alexander's armies met lie in the far eastern mountains and the southern deserts of Persia.

links.note: the two-humped camels of the caravans

neighbours.name: Transoxiana
neighbours.summary:
Mawara'n-nahr, the Lands Beyond the River, Turan to the Persians: the borderland past the Oxus, always at the edge of civilisation. The Khwarazm-shah rules it in name. It takes in the old oases of Farghana, Sogdia and Bactria, the river-mouth province of Khwarazm and the jinn-ridden Kyzylkum, with the endless steppe to the north-east and the Pamir and the Paromisidae walling it to the east.

Qutayba's Arabs swept over it in the seventh century, and Islam's tide broke there on the edge of the steppe. Islam changed as it went: strict Sunni ways took little root, but ecstatic Sufism, with its likeness to the nomads' shamans and its charismatic holy men, did better, and many who profess Islam still keep pagan beliefs and folk customs tied to the local Faerie and Magic spirits. Nomad overlords have come and gone and the river oases have had dynasties of their own; no one power has held both herdsman and townsman since the old Turk Empire, until now.

Two great rivers bound and shape it, a border of trade and changing cultures between the wild steppe beyond the Jaxartes and the towns south of the Oxus. A third, the lesser Zeravshan, 'the golden', runs past Samarkand and Bukhara and dies in the desert before it reaches a sea. To the north-west lies the Bahr Khazar, the Caspian, beyond which the Khazars once ruled, nomads who took up Judaism and held Islam back in the ninth century before fading into the steppe; the tales they left have bred Faerie jinn that ape their kingdom. Travellers past the Caucasus to the sea's far shore may find the Amazons' secret isle (Rival Magic), and beyond it the outer reaches of Jinnistan.

Story seeds:
The Accursed Turanians: the Turanians, a once-holy tribe led astray by Hell, made war on the Iranians, and the soldier who killed Zoroaster raised the fortress Arvandasp by sorcery; their Infernal relics, the prophet's death-blade among them, may still lie north of the Oxus.
Caravans: a great caravan, a moving town of thousands of beasts and men stopping at caravanserais a day apart, makes a cover for wandering magi or a shield for native travellers, and a source of tales of trade and discovery.

the shamans who ride with the Mongols

neighbours.name: Khwarazm
neighbours.summary: Transoxiana's farming heart, a province of canals and gardens at the Oxus mouth, and home of the warlike Khwarazm-shah, Sultan Mohammed II Iskander, whose deeds have brought the Mongols down on it. It grows great crops of cotton and keeps big flocks of sheep and herds of cattle in the marshes among its canals; it trades chiefly, in costly furs from the Bulghar lands among much else, and above all in Turkish slaves: young nomads bought or stolen from the steppe, schooled in Islam and sent to every corner of the Islamic world.

links.note: the elephants of the eastern armies

neighbours.name: Sogdiana
neighbours.summary: Since antiquity a land of merchants and go-betweens, still a place of crossroads and caravans: the main roads from Baghdad run through it by Samarkand to the Turkish lands beyond. Once the heartland of the Manichean heresy, it holds a passing mix of trading faiths, Sunni Muslims, Nestorian Christians and Jews.

neighbours.name: Farghana
neighbours.summary: The broad open valley north-east of Sogdiana, the furthest east that Islam's first wave reached. It is famous for horses, metalwork and above all weapons, and has good oil and bitumen; Arab armies fill clay pipes with its oil as fire bombs in sieges, a trick the Mongols will learn. The Heavenly Horses of its valley head, said to be sired by river dragons or divine steeds on the wild herds, are sought by magi and Gifted sahirs alike, for the Gift does not trouble them, and envoys from Serica are said to come great distances for a single one.

links.note: the blood-sweating horses of the valley

neighbours.name: Bactria
neighbours.summary: Bactriana, lately called Tokharistan: the lands between the Oxus and the Caucasus Indicus, long a melting pot and a breeding ground of revolt. Cyrus made it a satrapy; it fought off Alexander, then became the heart of the Seleucid empire and of an independent Greek kingdom. Sakas, Kushans, Sasanids, Hephthalites and Arabs conquered it in turn, but its back country keeps many classical monuments and ties to the Faerie powers of Greek myth: outside the Theban Tribunal no part of the Mythic Middle East has more Greek buildings.

neighbours.name: Badakhshan
neighbours.summary: Mountains famed for rubies, sapphires and other jewels, rising into the Caucasus Indicus south of a great northward bend of the Oxus and cut by its chief tributary, the Nahr Dirgham (the Badakhshan or Kokcha river). The ancients called it Balascia and set it on the north face of the south-eastern slopes of Mount Imeon. Rid now of the Shansabani of Bamiyan, whose demons ruled it from the south, it is a borderland of the old world, known to the traders who cross it from north-west to south-east.

links.note: the giant eagles of the high valleys

neighbours.name: The Wakhan
neighbours.summary:
The narrow land along the Oxus from lower Badakhshan up to its fabled source, home of the Vakhi, shy herdsmen whose Parsi is so odd that speakers of it are at -3. A trade route has climbed the valley to Serica since antiquity, though no merchant yet says he has made the whole journey and come back; now and then strange travellers and pilgrims arrive in the west claiming to have come the other way, with tales of the mountains and of the cities of their homes in the Taklimakan beyond.

Story seeds:
The Faerie Road to Serica: the upper Oxus valley is one long narrow Faerie aura, 2 near Ai Khanoum and 6 in the Wakhan, with regiones off the path that lead to dead ends, lost kingdoms or the realms of Faerie, Arcadia most often.

neighbours.name: The Oxus
neighbours.summary:
The Jahyun of the Arabs, the Turks' Amu Darya, wrongly taken for Gihon, a river of Eden, and always a frontier of the classical world. The people of Qarabolaq in the high Pamir say it is born of the eerie Lake Zorkul near by; the old geographers, that it melts out of an ice cave under a glacier high in the Wakhan. In winter the lower Oxus and the Jaxartes freeze, so caravans, and now nomad armies, cross with ease.

Its delta's spirit was once one great Magic spirit; the clash of peoples on its lower banks has split it into a throng of lesser ones as the river splits into channels and canals towards the Aral Sea. Just short of the sea the great dykes of Gurganj, magically strengthened with jinn enslaved by the sahirs of before Islam, turn the river from its natural course into the canals that water the province. Faerie, Infernal and Magic river spirits, and perhaps Divine ones, are bound along that broken lower course, each with its own name and loyalty, gathering at times into shifting alliances and courts. One, the captive Magic spirit Ahurani or Anahit, the remnant of a fertility yazata older than Zoroaster that the Sogdians adopted, is yoked to the shah's harvests; the faerie lords called Old Jahyun and the Son of the Oxus are the most fickle and the strongest, and a clever magus or sahir might strike a bargain with one against the other.

Story seeds:
A River Runs Through It: the Oxus and Jaxartes freeze each winter because Faerie jinn win their yearly struggle with the Magic spirits of the banks, letting nomads and their stories across; in summer the old spirits rule again and the water flows to the fields.
Spirits of the Oxus Delta: the Oxus's great spirit has split into many lesser ones along the canals, held by Gurganj's dykes, which pre-Islamic sahirs strengthened with enslaved jinn; Ahurani the old fertility spirit is yoked to the shah's harvests, and Old Jahyun and the Son of the Oxus may each be bargained with against the other.
neighbours.secrets: The winter freeze is the outcome of a running struggle between the Faerie and Magic jinn who claim the lands on either bank. In winter the faeries rule and the rivers ice over, letting nomads, and their stories, cross between steppe and town, feeding the faeries on the strife; in summer the old Magic spirits take back the rivers and let them run to water the towns downstream.

neighbours.name: The Old Bed of the Oxus
neighbours.summary:
The river's first course, which runs six days' march west across the desert to the Caspian near the fishing town of Khalkhal. Its spirits have all been bound into the works and canals round Gurganj, and nothing magical lives in it now, but a failing Magic aura of 2 lies along its dry length.

Vis: Aquam, as small clear pools that form along the dry bed on cool nights while Aquarius is rising; the book gives no amount.

neighbours.name: The Jaxartes
neighbours.summary:
The Sayhun, or river of Shash, gathered from many mountain streams in Farghana and running through it past the desert homelands of the Ghuzz Turks into the north-east of the Aral Sea by many channels. More than the Oxus it is the true line between Iran and Turan, Persian and Turk, farmer and nomad. Unlike the Oxus, one Faerie being rules it, and meddles in every tale of nomads breaking in.

Near the old town of Talas lie the ruins of a nomad fort, and just outside them ends a road from Arcadia to a faerie image of the steppe.
neighbours.secrets: The old river spirit feeds on the townsmen's dread of the steppe's barbarians: every few centuries it calls a faerie host under a new name down the Arcadian road by Talas, one more wave in an endless cycle of ruin, each slightly different, each breaking on civilisation's shore. The Mongols may be only its latest telling.

neighbours.name: The Aral Sea
neighbours.summary: The Lake of Khwarazm: shallow and reedy, with fine fishing in its south, though no one counts it navigable.

neighbours.name: Jabal Jaghrahaz
neighbours.summary: A small island with a single low hill in the south-east of the Aral Sea, in a Magic aura of 4. The water round it never thaws. The local people are sure a mighty water jinni, the marid Jaghrahaz, lives there, but nobody dares cross the ice to look.

neighbours.name: The Kyzylkum
neighbours.summary: The red sands between the two rivers, on the south-east edge of Khwarazm and the north-west of Sogdiana, haunted by jinn. For all its crescent dunes, its gentler eastern edge is full of game: gazelle, golden eagles, deer and koulan, the wild ass. Its north belongs to the waral, giant lizards of real wit, whose leaders walk upright and speak the local tongue, though their magic seems slight.

neighbours.name: Gurganj
neighbours.summary:
Al-Jurjaniyah, a leading town of the trade roads and one of the shah's two capitals, which has moved up and down the Oxus's west bank over the years to dodge its floods and the anger of the native river spirits.

If history holds, the Mongols besiege it in 1220 and after five months break the great dyke in frustration: the Oxus floods the town once more and runs again to the Caspian, and the river spirits, set free, turn on the Khwarazmians who held them. When the Mongols leave, only bodies and the outline of broken walls remain.

neighbours.name: The Gutluk-Temir Minaret
neighbours.summary: The tallest brick minaret of the Mythic Middle East, over 180 feet, looking out over the watered province. For all its holy form a Magic aura of 7 surrounds it, and it is the hub of the web of fetters and wards that holds the Oxus spirits to the dykes. The local community of sahirs keeps those wards up, meets in the tower, and sees that the canals go on feeding the province's famous fields. It stands right in the Mongols' way; its few survivors may be among the first sahirs to carry the news west.

neighbours.name: Kath
neighbours.summary: Once the capital of Khwarazm and seat of its native shahs, a fine city on the Oxus's east bank, until flood after flood washed it down to second rank. The mausoleum of Il-Arslan looks out over a great necropolis to its north.

neighbours.name: Otrar
neighbours.summary:
A town on the east bank of the Jaxartes. In 1218 a rich Mongol caravan came here with a message for the shah; the governor Inalchuq, the shah's cousin, jailed and killed all 450 men of it with their envoy, as spies, or for their goods, and the second embassy was shamed. On that insult from a petty officer the horde has come down on the land.

If history holds, Otrar holds out five months in the first half of 1220 before it falls. Inalchuq is taken alive and killed with molten silver poured into his eyes and ears, and the town is levelled, its people killed or enslaved.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Otrar
neighbours.summary:
What the Mongols leave of Otrar, in a Perfidious Infernal aura of 6 tainted with the sin of Deceit (the aura comes with the town's fall, if history holds, in 1220). Lies told among the ruins ring truer: the Ease Factor to see through one rises by the aura.

Uqana haunts them, the Muslim merchant the Khan sent as his first envoy with a personal message of friendship, killed by a fellow Muslim: an apparition (Realms of Power: Magic) who cannot rest because his message was never given, though the Khan has avenged him, and whom the Mongols' trail of ruin makes hard to talk into going on. Forced by magic, he might tell much of the Mongol leaders' plans; but forcing or deceiving him in this aura may cost dear.

neighbours.name: Samarkand
neighbours.summary:
Marakanda to the Greeks, Sogdia's old capital on the upper Zeravshan, taken by one conqueror after another and still among the most crowded and cosmopolitan cities of the region; Alexander said it was finer than he had heard. It is the eastern capital of the shah's empire, and the first paper mill of Islam was built here after Talas.

If history holds, Genghis Khan's armies besiege it in the spring of 1220, and for all its new walls it falls in five days; its surrendered garrison is put to death in batches, and its people are marched out for the sack and shared out as Bukhara's were.

neighbours.name: The Shahr-i-Zindah
neighbours.summary:
The 'tomb of the living king', a street of tombs east of old Marakanda, named for its central shrine, the grave of Qusam ibn-Abbas. The other tombs are doors into a city of dark Faerie jinn and ghul, which gives the street a malevolent Faerie aura of 5 by day and an Infernal aura of the same strength by night. The shrine keeps a small Divine aura of 2, a lonely refuge in the dark.

Rostam's mace lies forgotten in one of its tombs, carried to Turan by his enemies after his death: a superb two-handed mace (as a warhammer) giving +3 to Attack and Defence and the Inspirational Virtue to whoever holds it.

neighbours.name: Bukhara
neighbours.summary:
An old trading town on the Zeravshan below Samarkand, in the middle of the Kyzylkum. In the ninth and tenth centuries it was the Samanids' capital and the heart of Islam's learning, home country of the poets Firdausi and Rudaki; Ibn Sina read in its famous library, and al-Biruni thought its book bazaars unequalled. It has a large Jewish community, one of the biggest of the Diaspora not to speak Hebrew. A sahir of its house of wisdom tends Job's Spring.

As 1220 opens Genghis Khan and much of his horde are camped before it. If history holds, it falls within a fortnight: every defender left is killed, the townsfolk are driven out (craftsmen sent as slaves to Mongolia, young men forced into the army, the women worse used), and a fire burns the mostly wooden town, so that by winter's end it is smoking ruin. The whole place then lies under a Malevolent Infernal aura of 3 (Realms of Power: The Infernal), save round the Kalyan minaret, and the unburied dead wander it, open to any necromancer's call. Its book collections are lost, and poets will mourn them as a second Alexandria.

Story seeds:
The Lost Books of Bukhara: after the Mongols burn Bukhara, poets and Merinita storytellers mourn its libraries until the grief may give a faerie library life; its books turn up on odd stalls and in forgotten stacks, and a reader who wishes for it is drawn into Arcadia, to visit once and leave with only a token.
The Wishing Tree: in the village of Kasri Orifon, barren women crawl under the arch of a dead mulberry, home to a faerie jinni of fertility; passing beneath it leads into a tiny Faerie regio.

neighbours.name: The Kalyan Minaret
neighbours.summary:
Bukhara's great minaret, in a Divine aura of 7, one of the few things left standing when the Mongols are done, spared by Genghis Khan himself: a gust took his hat as he looked up at it, and stooping for it he said it was the first thing he had ever bowed to. He spared the tower, but not the sheikhs: he killed two hundred holy men and had their heads thrown down the well near by before climbing the pulpit to make his famous speech. From its rotunda of sixteen arches the muezzin called the faithful and watchmen kept lookout; a frieze of diagonal brickwork lettered in Arabic rings its base.

It belonged to the Po-i-Kalyan mosque, whose ruins about it keep a Divine aura of 5, an island in the Infernal aura that will lie over most of the ruined city. The mosque's well lies under an octagonal platform near by, and the grave of an imam whom the tower's builder, Arslan Khan, slew in a rite lies under the minaret's foot.

Story seeds:
The Sheikhs Beneath the Well: under an octagonal platform by the Po-i-Kalyan mosque a dry well leads down to a heap of skulls in a small Magic aura, each an Arcane Connection to summon its restless sheikh; an imam the minaret's builder slew lies beneath the tower.

levels.name: The round chamber above the rotunda
levels.enter: A devout Muslim who climbs the spiral stair just before dawn.
levels.notes: A small terrestrial Divine regio, a round room that appears above the minaret's top.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Isma'il Samanid
neighbours.summary: The half-buried tomb of Isma'il Samanid (r. 893 to 907), the Samanid dynasty's founder, just outside Bukhara, long forgotten by its dissolute townsfolk; if history holds, the dust of neglect hides it from the horde and it comes through untouched. Over its main door is carved a circle inside nested squares, a Zoroastrian sign. Because mobeds once used it, it has a Magic aura of 3 by night and a Divine aura of the same strength by day.

neighbours.name: Job's Spring
neighbours.summary:
The Chashma-Ayyub, a small mausoleum at the edge of Bukhara's farmers' market, newly built over a little spring in a Faerie aura of 3; unlike other tombs it holds no one. Folk say Job struck the ground with his staff here and water came, though the tale may cover an older pagan one. A sahir of the town's house of wisdom, which paid for the building, comes once a year.

Vis: faerie-tainted Terram and Aquam, which the faerie jinni of the spring gives in a bargain for acting out the old story within its walls; the book gives no amount.

neighbours.name: The Wishing Tree of Kasri Orifon
neighbours.summary: In the main square of Kasri Orifon, a village just east of Bukhara, the dead trunk of an old mulberry twists into an arch. Childless women crawl under it hoping to conceive.

levels.name: Beneath the arch
levels.enter: Crawling under the arch of the trunk.
levels.notes: A small Faerie regio, just big enough for a grown person, the home of a faerie jinni with power over fertility.

neighbours.name: Balkh
neighbours.summary:
A great old city, for long the home of Zoroastrianism, since Zoroaster was born and is buried inside its walls; it sheltered the emperor Yezdgird from the Arabs, but has since taken wholly to Islam. Its Greek name, Bactra, gave Bactria its own. The fire temple of Naw Bahar is in one of its suburbs.

If history holds, the Mongols sack it in 1221.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Ai Khanoum
neighbours.summary:
Ruins where the Jahyun meets the Nahr Dirgham, once a centre of Hellenism: Alexander founded the place as Alexandria on the Oxus, and the Seleucids made it the city of Eucratidia. What is left of a gymnasium, a theatre nearly as big as Epidauros's and several temples of the Greek gods, Zeus and Dionysus above all, gives it a Magic aura of 4.

An altar of Alexander lies hidden in one of the temples on the city's edge. The altars (Ancient Magic) are linked to one another and to over seventy sites: a magus casting at Arcane Connection range with his hand on one may reach any shrine, city or temple tied to it as though through an Arcane Connection worth a +4 Penetration multiplier. It could bring Seekers into the region, or be a lifeline home for Hermetic settlers far into strange lands.

Story seeds:
The Altars of Alexander: the altar hidden in a temple at Ai Khanoum links to some seventy sites; a spell cast at Arcane Connection range while touching it reaches them all at a +4 Penetration multiplier, a way into the east for Seekers or a lifeline home for colonists.

neighbours.name: The Gymnasium of Ai Khanoum
neighbours.summary: The best kept of Ai Khanoum's buildings, in a Magic aura of 7 centred on a pillar inscribed to Hermes and Hercules together.

neighbours.name: Sogdian Rock
neighbours.summary:
The site of Alexander's battle with the rebel satrap of Sogdia, Oxyartes of Balkh, father of the fabled beauty Roxane. Only little-known mountain paths reach it, and only a handful of local tribesmen know just where it is. The ghosts of the thirty men who fell in the climb still haunt it and have no love for the heirs of their Persian foes.

A candidate covenant site: a superb natural fortress, full of caves and cut cisterns that could store food and water for a siege, in a Magic aura of 3, perhaps higher deep in the caves. Remote as it is, it could be a base for Hermetic magi exploring the Mythic Middle East.

Story seeds:
A Covenant on the Rock?: the Rock is a natural fortress of caves and cisterns in a Magic aura of 3, stronger perhaps in its depths, reached only by paths a few tribesmen know and haunted by the thirty who fell climbing it for Alexander: a base for magi exploring the east.

neighbours.name: Khojend
neighbours.summary: A small trading town at the mouth of the Farghana valley, built by the ruins of Alexandria Eschate, the furthest town Alexander founded. If history holds, the Mongols lay waste the Jaxartes towns as far as Khojend in 1220.
neighbours.secrets: Another altar of Alexander is hidden under the town or in the ruins beside it.

neighbours.name: Osh
neighbours.summary: The easternmost town of Farghana, just below the Jaxartes's source in the Pamir, and the northernmost of the caliphate: where certainty ends and stories of what lies past the map begin. It is the last caravan halt on the Great Khurasan Road from Baghdad; beyond it merchants follow legends, not tracks, up into the mountains towards the faerie city of Khashgar and the dreaded desert road to Serica.

neighbours.name: The Mines of Lahzvard
neighbours.summary:
Limestone beds along the Badakhshan river at Lahzvard, the only source of lapis lazuli Mythic Europe knows (its name comes from the town's). The greedy jinn of Zubaydah, a fort named after Harun al-Rashid's favourite wife, oversee the chief workings, and heavily guarded loads go west to Europe's painters and magi, or east to Hind, Serica and perhaps the mountain lands of Faerie beside them.

Lapis is often taken for sapphire. Its pure pigment, ultramarine, is prized for illuminating Hermetic texts as a strongly resonant material, though kuanos (azurite) often stands in for it. Its bonuses: +3 as an aphrodisiac, ground; +5 to keep limbs healthy; +5 to cure boils and ulcers; +6 against a demon's Obsession. Carved as an eye, set in gold and laid on an altar of Ra on a month's last day, it is Enriched to give Lesser Immunity to demons' Obsession; melted with lead to strip its gold flecks and ground onto the eyelids, it works as Venus' Blessing.

Vis: a Lapis Lazuli of Virtue holds 2 pawns of Corpus.

Story seeds:
Untouched Stone: an old magus needs a man-sized block of fresh lapis untouched by hands or magic for his longevity potion, and it must come from Lahzvard by mundane roads through the Mongol chaos, a fortune too big to hide from bandits.

neighbours.name: The Faerie Road to Serica
neighbours.summary: Past the Badakhshan river's mouth, the whole upper valley of the Oxus lies under one very long, narrow Faerie aura, fenced by the ridges north and south. It is only 2 on the edge of Ai Khanoum and grows as one climbs east, reaching 6 in the Wakhan proper, where its Warping helps make the nomads so silent (the Reclusive Flaw). Many Faerie regiones open off the path, according to the traveller's mood, aims and Faerie Sympathies: some lead only to dead-end canyons and death, some hold lost kingdoms and cities on the shore of a creeping desert, and the most sought lead into the worlds of Faerie, Arcadia most often, though one who goes alone is likelier drawn into Eudokia to settle the crisis that drove him past the Order's knowledge.

neighbours.name: The Roof of the World
neighbours.summary:
The Bam-i-Dunya: the high plateaus of the Pamir knot, the north-west of the Caucasus Indicus and the ranges running south and east out of the House of Islam. The peoples of its valleys have always stood between Rome and Persia in the west and Serica in the east. Islamic legend makes the chain part of the Mountains of Qaf, a homeland of the jinn; the classical writers, the lower flanks of Mount Imeon, the mountain at the centre of the world, where some Criamon magi think the Axis Magica stood before Criamon passed into Twilight.

An unspoilt Magic aura of 4 at least covers it all, broken by higher auras and by regiones of other realms among the ice. Its valleys, strewn with diamonds the size of a fist, are the roosts of the great ruq, eagles that can lift a man in one claw like a mouse.

Story seeds:
Janaindar, the City Above the Clouds: nomads speak of a city at the Magic Realm's edge on a peak above the clouds, reached only by magic or a ruq, whose people claim an ancient magical race as ancestors: Nephilim, Hyperborea, or a hidden covenant of old magi?

neighbours.name: Janaindar, the City Above the Clouds
neighbours.summary: In the nomads' legends, a lost city on the edge of the Magic Realm, seen above the clouds on a great peak on a clear day and all but impossible to reach save by magic or in a ruq's claws. Its strange folk look human but say they come of an ancient magical race that once ruled the earth.
neighbours.secrets: The book leaves its truth open, offering a lost Nephilim settlement, the real Hyperborea in Turkistan, an old and secluded covenant of elder magi, the heirs of a rival tradition founded by Viea, Trianoma's sister, a final hiding place of the Zoroastrian mobeds, a high covenant site, or the Diedne's last sanctum.

neighbours.name: Turris Lapidae, the Stone Tower
neighbours.summary:
In Ptolemy's Geography, the halt in the little mountain kingdom of Sarikol where caravans for Sera Metropolis, the Seres' capital, stopped. Some say the fort above it marks the halfway point between Europe and the east; others that the town stands half in the world and half in Faerie, a gate to Arcadia. The tales come from the merchant Maes Titanos, whom Ptolemy's own source, the pre-Hermetic wizard Marinus of Tyre, thought an invention, a faerie or an infernalist.

In the Mythic world it is a sizeable town at the end of classical travel eastward, and one of the bounds of the Order's knowledge. No Redcap or Mercere magus claims to have been there or inside the tower, and some Merinita think it can only be reached along the Arcadian paths their House knows.

neighbours.name: Khashgar
neighbours.summary:
The best known of the legendary cities of the road east in this century: an oasis where the routes from north and south meet before splitting round the Taklimakan towards the Land of Silk. Scholars argue over its origin and where exactly it is, but all agree that men, jinn and other Eastern faeries jostle in its streets with angels, demons and sorcerers of every tradition but the Hermetic. Nominally Muslim since the late ninth century, it suffered persecution under the faerie Qara Khitai and has lately fallen to the Mongols without a fight, which its people, mortal and magical, seem hardly to mind.

Its Yekshenbar, the Sunday market, sells anything: desert robbers rub shoulders with weary merchants, and fine silks, knives and jewels lie beside magical wares, with slaves, mundane and magical, for a price. Some Merinita say they have reached its market through Arcadia, and suspect that the city exists in more than one version at a time, or that the whole town lies in a regio reached from many places in Mythic Europe.

neighbours.name: Yenghissar
neighbours.summary: A small village on the road to Khashgar, which a wild desert storm spirit, a buran, laid waste every seven years, ruining its crops and herds, until a sahir bound it.
neighbours.secrets: The sahir who bound the buran is Infernally aligned and used the Goetic Art of Binding (Realms of Power: The Infernal); the spirit rages in his ancestral sword, ever trying to wreak elemental havoc round its careless captor.

neighbours.name: The Taklimakan
neighbours.summary:
A desert of death beyond the mountains, whose name means that those who go in never come out: oasis towns and the ruins of lost peoples, searing heat, cruel winds and malicious demons, all luring travellers from their caravans to die slowly of hunger and thirst. Two auras of a steady 7, one Magic and one Infernal, wander across the sands, winding about each other like opposing storms, and as they spiral they swallow and uncover ancient Faerie regiones, deserted ruined cities or living oases peopled by jinn from before Islam. The record keeps the Magic aura; the Infernal one is as strong.

The dunes off the main track are dreaded as the home of the qara buran, the black hurricanes, bloodthirsty wind spirits that fall on caravans as sandstorms and part travellers from camels and friends. They are much like elemental jinn, though some seem closer to the Infernal Aerial Powers; they split their loyalty between the Gok Buran, a fearsome Daimon in a still stronger Magic regio deep in the sands, and its rival, a Duke of Hell called Great Lop.

Story seeds:
The Black and the Blue: the black hurricanes, wind spirits that tear caravans apart as sandstorms, split their loyalty between the Gök Buran, a great daimon in a stronger Magic regio at the desert's heart, and its rival Great Lop, a Duke of Hell.

links.note: the storm demon bound in the Yenghissar sword

neighbours.name: The Great Steppe
neighbours.summary:
The sea of grass across the breadth of Asia, from the Sea of Azov and the plain of Hungary in the west as far as the Ordos and the endless eastern horizon, which even the Roman empire at its height only touched. Herodotus called its shore Scythia; no other land Hermetic magi know is on its scale, and out of it pour the Mongols.

Its nomads share a belief in Khan Tengri, the Great Sky, common forefather and overlord: a vast spirit drawing on the Magic realm, an Elder Daimon in Hermetic terms, a Kosmokrator of the steppe and sky, as the spirit of the Hercynian Forest is in the west. Unlike that spirit, no Mercurian rite has weakened it and no town or Dominion has touched it save at its fringes: a reservoir of power for a magus who would finish the last work of Hercynius, folding Merinita's nature magic into Hermetic theory.

Where towns press on the steppe's edges, Tengri has given up some of its power to lesser spirits, genii loci of grasslands from a valley to a kingdom in size (Magic Might 30 to 45). Such a spirit may hold its own, keeping a magical steppe (the plains by the Sea of Azov, the Dzungarian basin, eastern Mongolia); may waste away and leave a mundane one (Pannonia, and the Hungarian plain, now a promontory of Divine pasture); or may be replaced, most often by a faerie fed on the nomads' descendants' tales: the towns along the Jaxartes border such a Faerie steppe.

A few of the Mongol army are shamans of Great Tengri, who summon spirits to scout, spy and fight for them, bargain with them or bind them into weapons, using any spirit that serves, demons included; each has a familiar spirit of his homeland, like a qareen.

neighbours.name: Tashkent
neighbours.summary: The Turks' City of Stone, once the greatest Arab town past the Jaxartes: a city of canals famous for its vines, and the market between the Sogdians' heirs and their Turkish neighbours. The shah sacked much of it in 1214 and the Mongols laid it waste in 1219; under Mongol rule it is already being settled again and taking back its trade, and marks the line between civilisation and the wild.

neighbours.name: Talas
neighbours.summary:
Where in July 751 Ziya ben Salih's Muslim army met a strange force from beyond the eastern steppe, the Arabs' furthest reach east; craftsmen taken there brought papermaking into Islam. Nearly five centuries on, here the shah beat the faerie Qara Khitai in 1218 to make Transoxiana his. The Mongols razed the town to the ground in 1219 on their way to Otrar.

Story seeds:
The Endless Nomad Cycle: near Talas a road from Arcadia ends by an old nomad fort, and down it the Jaxartes spirit sends a faerie horde under a new name every few centuries; the Mongols may be only the latest telling.

neighbours.name: Great Khan of the Mongols
neighbours.summary:
Temujin, Genghis Khan, Great Khan since 1206, master of the nomad empire coming down out of the east. Khashgar has fallen to him, and Tashkent and Talas were razed in 1219; as 1220 opens he is camped before Bukhara, come to punish the Khwarazm-shah for the caravan killed at Otrar and the envoys killed and shamed. He calls himself God's punishment on a sinful people.

His generals are mostly gifted soldiers rather than his kin, masters of strategy whose great strength is knowing the ground and the enemy; their best trick is a feigned retreat that draws a foe into a long, wearing chase before turning on him. His troopers are fierce horse archers in fur-lined leather; shamans of Great Tengri ride with them. By the simplest reading he is a brilliant mundane general and history runs its course.

If history holds: by the end of 1220 he has taken Bukhara, Otrar, Samarkand and Gurganj and harried the shah to his death; in 1221 his armies sack Balkh, Merv, Nishapur and Herat and drive Jalal al-Din over the Indus, while Jebe and Subadei begin their great raid into Russia. He dies in 1227, holding the east as far as eastern Persia; his heirs take western Persia, Georgia, Armenia and northern Iraq in the 1230s, the Seljuks of Asia Minor in 1243, and Baghdad in 1258, where they roll the caliph in a carpet and trample him, and are checked only by Egypt's Mamluks in Syria in 1260.
neighbours.secrets: What the Khan truly is the book leaves to each troupe, offering, with none chosen: an Infernal horde, its leaders Angels of Punishment, demons of the Avengers of Evil posing as God's vengeance, or the Khan a new Zahhak possessed by Azi Dahak; the Spawn of Gog and Magog, a horde ridden out of Arcadia in the endless nomad cycle, the Khan a dark faerie monarch and his officers court faeries; the legions of Prester John, faeries playing a pious part, born of garbled tales of the Qara Khitai's defeat of Sultan Sanjar; the Vengeance of God, a true Divine host of punishment; Blood of Heroes, the Khan and his generals scions of Ares or of Attila; or a Spirit Votary of Great Tengri, who made his bargain on the holy mountain of Burkhan Khaldun and wields elemental powers great enough to force the Order of Hermes to unite against him. Some Persian sahirs already fear the Zahhak.

neighbours.name: The Qara Khitai
neighbours.summary: The Kara-Khitai, a mysterious nomad dynasty from the far east whom the book casts as Eastern faeries. Their confederation, which counted Nestorian Christians among its tribes, beat Sultan Sanjar on the Qatwan steppe near Samarkand in 1141, and garbled tales of that battle may lie behind the legend of Prester John. They lorded it over Khashgar, oppressing its Muslims, until the Khwarazm-shah Muhammad II broke their faerie host in 1218 and took Transoxiana; Khashgar has since gone to the Mongols.

neighbours.name: Amerabad, the City of Amber
neighbours.summary: One of the whole cities the jinn keep inside the shifting borders of Jinnistan, and the one the tales name first. The book gives it only that line: its streets, rulers and ways in are the storyguide's to make.

neighbours.name: Golden Baghdad
neighbours.summary:
The faerie reflection of Baghdad as it was under Harun al-Rashid, its greatest caliph: roofs of gold, streets of marble, and the tales of the Thousand and One Nights played out again and again, whether or not a visitor joins in. A traveller may overhear Sinbad the Sailor telling his voyages to Sinbad the Porter, go fishing with Judar, ride out beyond the walls in search of Solomon's ring with Bulukiyya, or help Hasan the goldsmith of Basra win a jinn bride; he may even find himself living one of those parts. Its bazaars sell the hidden folk's kohl, seldom for coin. The poet Abu Nuwas, once of Harun's court, lives on here as a creature of the tales.

Its ways in are scattered all over mundane Baghdad. One may be an ordinary doorway that happens to open onto it, another a gate only Second Sight, Faerie Sight or a like power can see, and where the Guardian is part of the Threshold a visitor can cross into Faerie without noticing. So many Baghdadis stray across by accident that it counts in the city as a fair excuse for being missed, and most of them have been there at least once. The Order of Suleiman has tried to chart the entrances, but they open, close and move as they please and differ for each traveller, so only a few steady ones are known for sure. Sahirs still argue whether the strange beings met in the mundane city belong there or have wandered out of the golden one.

neighbours.name: Khashgar of the Jinn
neighbours.summary:
The legendary oasis city where the roads from north and south meet before they part around the Taklimakan for the Land of Silk, and the best known of all the cities of the eastern journey. Scholars quarrel over where and what it is, but agree that men, jinn and other eastern faeries crowd its streets beside angels, demons and sorcerers of every tradition but the Hermetic. Its Sunday market, the Yekshenbar bazaar, sells anything at all: brigands and tired merchants trade silks, knives and jewels beside magical wares, and slaves, ordinary and otherwise, are to be had for a price.

Muslim in name since the late ninth century, it suffered under the faerie Qara Khitai and has lately passed to the Mongols without a fight; neither its human nor its magical people seem to mind the change of masters. Merinita who say they reached its market through Arcadia think several Khashgars may stand at once, or that the whole town lies in a regio with doors at many places in the mundane world. Its traders pay the scholars no heed.

neighbours.name: Al-Khadar, the Green Ocean
neighbours.summary:
The great ocean beyond the ring of the known world, past the pale blue seas off Persia and past the merchants' Erythraean Sea: a wall of magic and of metaphor that only jinn, heroes, sorcerers and Muslim saints have crossed. Few claim to have reached its far shores, or its drifting islands with their trees bearing human heads and their thinking apes, and those who say they came back tell of it in parables and lies, as Sinbad the Sailor did.

Islamic cosmology puts whole worlds out beyond it, peopled by terrible angels, strange men, outlandish jinn and stranger things still. Hermetic scholars of the Keepers of Tales place those lands in Eudokia, in the Faerie realm, while Criamon magi read the tale of Buluqya as a road into the Magic Realm that leads out of the Circle of Time.

neighbours.name: The Court of Golden Baghdad
neighbours.summary:
The faerie caliph of Golden Baghdad and his two companions: a Harun al-Rashid, with Ja'far the Barmakid, his vizier, and Masrur the eunuch, his executioner, who go about the city at night in disguise to see how its people behave, rewarding the good and punishing the wicked, and who may call on a guest after dark.

Sahirs have told of meeting him since a few years after the real caliph died in 809. It begins harmlessly, with a talk with three strangers, and usually turns into a wild adventure across the Threshold. Many sahirs take him for the faerie ruler of the golden city, who invites only those he judges able to do something for its good.

Story seeds:
The Wandering Caliph: for four centuries sahirs have told of meeting Harun al-Rashid with his vizier and executioner, a chance talk with three strangers that ends in Golden Baghdad; they think him the faerie city's ruler, choosing guests for what they can add to it.

details.wants: Visitors who can add something to the glory of his city.
details.offers: Reward for the good, punishment for the wicked, and a place in the tales.

neighbours.name: Adur Farnbag
neighbours.summary:
The first of the three Royal Fires of the Mazdeans, on Mount Kavarvand in Fars, called the shining mountain for the holy fire that spills from its slopes. The Royal Fires are held to have been lit before the world was made and carried out on the back of the ox Srishok to spread the faith and guard mankind. Adur Farnbag, the fire of the priests, is counted the holiest of the three, the earthly image of the yazata Atar who burns before Ohrmazd. It first burned in Khwarazm and was later brought here. Mazdeans still come to the mountain as pilgrims.

Its temple stands in a regio of Divine 8; the book gives the mountain itself no aura.

levels.name: The temple of the Royal Fire
levels.see: Holy flame streams out of the mountainside where the way stands open.
levels.enter: The way opens on the mountain's west face at dawn and on its east face at dusk.
levels.notes: A terrestrial Divine regio holding the fire temple of Adur Farnbag. An ervad or any higher initiate adds his Theology: Zoroastrian (the book's Theology: Mazdean) to every Ability and magic roll he makes inside it. A temple fire kindled from this flame gains a further +1 to its Divine aura.

neighbours.secrets: The mobeds who brought the fire from Khwarazm still live on Kavarvand, kept alive across the centuries by the Gifts of Gayomart.

neighbours.name: Adur Gushnasp
neighbours.summary:
The second Royal Fire, the fire of warriors and nobles, at Takht-i-Suleiman, the Throne of Solomon, in a half-moon valley in the mountains of Jibal. A small, deep lake fed by a spring from below fills the top of a low flat hill, and on its shore stands a fire temple in remarkably good repair, whose walls are also the edges of a Divine regio of 8 where the fire rests.

The book gives the hill no aura of its own.

levels.name: The temple of the Royal Fire
levels.enter: The temple's own walls are the regio's bounds.
levels.notes: A weapon forged at a fire lit from Adur Gushnasp and quenched in the lake gives +4 to calls on God's aid in battle (RoP:D) whenever the warrior it was made for fights with it, for as many years as his Theology: Zoroastrian. In anyone else's hand it loses the gift for good.

neighbours.name: Adur Burzen-Mihr
neighbours.summary:
The third Royal Fire, the fire of farmers and craftsmen, in Mihr, a plain village on the road to Nishapur. The ruins of an old fire temple hide the way into a Divine regio of 8, where the temple still stands and the fire burns.

The book gives the village no aura of its own.

levels.name: The temple of the Royal Fire
levels.enter: Through the ruins of the fire temple.
levels.notes: Here the temple is whole and the holy flame burns. A tool left in the regio for a year is purified and gives +4 to its owner's Craft or Profession rolls made with it, for as many years as his Theology: Zoroastrian; if anyone else so much as touches it, it loses its purity for ever.

neighbours.name: Naw Bahar
neighbours.summary:
A fire temple in a suburb of Balkh, the city where Zoroaster was born and lies buried, built under the Sasanids to rival the Ka'ba at Mecca. Precious stones stud its walls, brocade curtains hang everywhere, and centuries of anointing have left the walls and floors smelling sweetly of perfume. A cupola 375 feet high crowns the main hall, and 360 chambers for its mobeds ring it.

It is no longer a working temple, yet it keeps a Divine aura of 5, and neither time nor treasure-hunters have touched it; its floors stay clean of dirt and vermin. The few who dare to go in say a fire burns at its centre, though no one is ever seen there.

Story seeds:
Naw Bahar: a fire still burns at the heart of the empty temple outside Balkh, tended by no one anyone sees, and its Divine regio hides a small Zoroastrian community; few dare go in.

levels.name: The temple within
levels.see: A fire burning at the temple's heart, with no one tending it.
levels.enter: By going into the temple and on towards its fire.
levels.notes: The first level of a terrestrial Divine regio reached through the temple; the book numbers none of its levels.

levels.name: The hidden community
levels.notes:
The higher levels of the regio.

Secrets
A small community of Mazdeans lives here, out of the world's reach.

neighbours.name: Lake Zarah and Mount Khajeh
neighbours.summary:
The lake of Seistan, near Zaranj, whose waters carry a Divine aura of 2. The Nestorians say the three magi set out for Bethlehem from its shores; the Mazdeans that it keeps the seed of Zoroaster, and that when the world's renewal draws near three virgins will go into it and bear the saviours of mankind.

Out of the water rises Mount Khajeh, a flat-topped black hill with an ancient fire temple and two deserted forts, together called Qal'a-e Sam after Saum, Rostam's grandfather.

neighbours.name: The Cypresses of Kishmar
neighbours.summary:
At Kishmar near Turshiz Zoroaster planted a cypress grown from a branch he had carried from Paradise, to mark King Goshtasp's conversion; it outgrew every cypress there had ever been. In 861 the caliph al-Mutawakkil had it pulled up and hauled across Persia for beams in his new palace, and was killed the very day it arrived.

Several cypresses in Quhistan are said to have grown from its seed, and some truly have. Each has a Divine aura of 1 out to five paces, tempered with Calm (RoP:D). Fallen branches fed to a Mazdean temple's sacred fire raise that temple's aura by 1 for as long as they burn; wood cut from the trees does not.

neighbours.name: The Pirs of Yazd
neighbours.summary:
Six holy shrines in the mountains around Yazd, the heart of the faith since Persia became Muslim and one of the few lands where Mazdeans still worship openly. Each year the Zoroastrian villages go to them on pilgrimage together, an occasion as much for feasting and dancing as for prayer.

The book names none of the six and gives them no aura; they take the Divine 3 this pack gives a holy place left unnumbered.

neighbours.name: Sirishk
neighbours.summary:
A Zoroastrian fire temple on a hilltop two leagues north of Herat. Unusually, a mobed still lives and serves in it, and the faithful come up from the hills around to worship. Shamiran castle, just behind the temple, may be part of why it has lasted. A Nestorian church stands between it and the city.

The book gives it no aura; it takes the Divine 3 this pack gives a holy place left unnumbered.

neighbours.name: The Mazdeans
neighbours.summary:
The followers of Zoroaster, who worship Ohrmazd, the Wise Lord, and hold to good thoughts, good words and good deeds. Their priests, the mobeds, gave their Greek name of magoi to magic itself: once they commanded angels and spirits, read the heavens and turned one substance into another, and at their height may have nearly matched Hermetic magic. Little is left. Zoroaster, born more than six centuries before Christ, converted the emperor Vishtaspa and was murdered by Turanian warriors at prayer in a fire temple at Balkh; his disciple Osthanes spread the faith through Persia. Alexander burned its temples and books, the Sasanids raised it again and, under the high priests Tansar and Kartir, gave it a Church with a hierarchy, which put down rival faiths; the Arab conquest broke that Church for good, though the priesthood survived. Muslims count the Mazdeans people of the book and dhimmis, and Zoroaster a prophet, yet call them gabars and fire-worshippers and press them to convert. Most who held out have gone to the poor, remote south-centre of Persia, and more drift east every year.

Where they are. Yazd, where the faith is still openly kept, its six mountain pirs drawing yearly pilgrimages and its mobeds credited with the fertile land round the city; secretive villages in Kirman, which keep their heads down after hard persecution; Daylam, a stronghold of the faith where its mobeds, the Nizaris and the yatus of Damavand fight over vis, rulers and souls, and which holds Hyrcania's plenty to be Ohrmazd's gift; scattered believers in Azarbayjan; the one living mobed of Sirishk near Herat; and a hidden community in the regio of Naw Bahar at Balkh. With the Order of Suleiman relations have always been strained: a few Persian priests became sahirs, and the mobeds' purges of the Goetic yatus long ago ended the old Persian art of magical war.

The priesthood. It passes from father to son, its priests marry, and it has no single head, so it settles doctrine as a college. An ervad performs the ordinary services; the martab ceremony makes him a mobed, who may perform them all; a dastur leads the priests of a district or a great temple (the Senior Clergy Virtue). The higher ranks are lost. Few mobeds have The Gift, many have True Faith, and only full mobeds wield holy power; a mobed who has the Ameratat gift can live about two hundred years, as the high priests Vishtana, Tansar and Kartir and Osthanes, the first Prince of Magi, did. Their holy magic, Mysteries and initiations are the Mobeds tradition's chapter; RoP:D's Zoroastrian holy magi, and the small Hermetic mystery cult of Zoroastrian magi, are kin to them.

Fire and the Dominion. Fire is the sign of Ohrmazd's presence and of truth, kept burning always on clean dry wood in an iron urn on a stone dais in a square, vented temple, fed and prayed over five times a day. A household lamp or hearth (atesh dadgah) raises the Divine aura by 1, to at most 3; the atesh adaran, joined from four fires, by 3, to at most 5; the atesh Behram, joined from sixteen, by 6, to at most 10. The aura is strongest at the flame and fades to the temple's walls and the community's fields, and where Mazdeans live among Muslims or Christians it is likely to be in Schism. The daily Yasna lifts the aura round the fire by 3 for an hour, to at most 8.

The rites. The Bareshnum, ten days of washing with sand, water and consecrated bull's urine before two priests and a dog, which everyone undergoes once and which gives one Faith Point the first time; the daily Padyab ablution; the Nahn bath and the Riman for those who have handled the dead; every purification but the Padyab drives out a possessing spirit and ends any temporary non-Divine effect. The Videvdat service from midnight to dawn; birth lamps that raise a room's aura by 1, to at most 3; the Navjote, which gives a child of twelve to fifteen the sacred cord and shirt and a Faith Point, and puts his name beyond use as a True Name; marriage, which gives both a Faith Point; and the dakhma, the Tower of Silence, after which no magic can touch the soul. Haoma, the sacred plant, helps potions of health, fertility, spirit-sight and long life.

The calendar. Twelve months of thirty days, each day and month sacred to a divine being, five extra days, and no week. With no leap year the dates have slipped, so communities keep either the Shenshai (Imperial) or the Fasli (Ancient) reckoning. Seven festivals of five days honour the Ameshaspand, the greatest No Roz, the New Day, which in 1220 falls on 27 January (Shenshai) or 26 February (Fasli). While a festival lasts, a temple's aura bars any Infernal being whose Might is under ten times the aura, and wounds one that gets in each hour by the aura's score, unsoakable on the last day. Their astrologers count a World Year of twelve thousand years, with a second saviour due about 1350.

Holy and unholy beings. Ohrmazd is the one God of every faith of Abraham. Under him are the seven Ameshaspand, archangels of his aspects: Vohu Manah (Bahman), Asha (Asavahisht), Khshathra Vairya (Shahrevar), Spenta Armaiti (Spendarmad), Haurvatat (Hordad), Ameretat (Amurdad) and Spenta Mainyu; then forty named yazdan, among them Mithras, Haoma, Atar and Vayu, who may be invoked like saints by one made pure by the Nahn; and the frohar, the guardian spirits of all good things, who lead the dead to the Chinvat Bridge. Against them stands Ahriman, the Devil himself, with the daevas Aka Manah, Indra, Saura, Naonghaithya, Taurvi and Zairich and forty-five lesser named demons. The faith keeps no relics in the Christian way, but many holy objects carry Faith scores; the greatest is the Staff of Yoisht Frayana, who answered all ninety-nine riddles of the sorcerer Akhtya and sent him to Hell: Faith 5, with the powers Grant Serenity, Expel Demons, Celestial Immunity and Acknowledgement of Evil (RoP:D). The book names no one who holds it.

Heresies. The Zurvanites, who gave Ohrmazd a father, Zurvan or Time, and called free will an illusion; the Mazdakites, ascetics vowed to poverty; and the cult of Mithras, strong in the empire's western provinces after Alexander. None survives in 1220, but their relics and monuments may.

Scriptures. The priests carry the Avesta in memory; temples hold parts of it, in Avestan and Gathic (Dead Language: Avestan reads both). The Yasna, the chief liturgy: Summa on Theology: Zoroastrian, Level 9, Quality 4. The Visparad: Summa on Dominion Lore, Level 4, Quality 3. The Videvdat, the law against demons: Summa on Theology: Zoroastrian, Level 6, Quality 6. The Khordeh Avesta and the Yasht: each a Tractatus on Theology: Zoroastrian, Quality 6. Also named: the Dadistan i Menok i Khrat, which says astrology came from the Spirit of Wisdom to Zoroaster, and the Arda Viraz Namag. Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, the Persian epic, in Parsi and seven volumes: a fine copy serves as a Persian Lore Summa of Level 4 and Quality 12, and a Tractatus, Quality 10, on each of Magic, Faerie, Divine and Infernal Lore. The book's Theology: Mazdean is the catalog's Theology: Zoroastrian, and its Mobed Lore is Organization Lore: Mobeds.

Story seeds:
The Demon-Blooded Paladins of Manochir: Alexander broke up the paladins of Manochir, tried to end the line of a white-haired, demon-blooded son of their greatest knight, and buried their arms in the desert, a mace said to fell an elephant at one blow and a belt that kept its wearer from harm; a cache of them would be a prize, if untainted.
A Heretical Revival: a Hermetic follower of the Cult of Mithras finds scrolls in a European Mithraeum tying his cult to the Mazdeans and hinting where in Persia Mithras was born; how will he take a living faith that counts Mithras a divine spirit?

details.rules: A hereditary priesthood of men; constant ritual purity; a sacred fire must never go out or be fouled.
details.wants: To keep their fires alight and their faith alive at the edge of the Muslim world.
details.offers: Purification, the lore of the old magi, and True Names.
